News.title: Barcelona fire LIVE: 'Explosion' heard as blaze burns 25 hectares and residents told 'stay indoors'
News.content:
A huge fire has broken out in Barcelona, with smoke visible from a Ryanair flight amid unconfirmed reports of an explosion

A large fire is burning in Barcelona, with around 35 hectares of land affected and residents in two neighbourhoods told to stay indoors.

Mobile phone alerts have been sent to people in Torre Baró and Ciutat Meridiana, warning them to close their doors and windows and not go outside due to the vegetation fire.

People posting on X have reported hearing an explosion, while a high-voltage tower in the area is believed to have been damaged. The explosion report has not yet been confirmed by authorities.

Spain’s 112 emergency service has received 1,074 calls about the blaze, while firefighters continue to tackle the flames.

The emergency warning tells residents: “Close doors and windows and do not go out on the street. In case of emergency, call 112.”

News.title: Angela Rayner urged to U-turn on rent controls decision after study shows benefits
News.content:
Angela Rayner urged to U-turn on rent controls decision after study shows benefits

EXCLUSIVE: Dozens of MPs have written to Angela Rayner warning the Government that it has an 'opportunity to fix the foundations of our housing system for the long term'

View 2 Images Housing Secretary Angela Rayner last month said the Government was not planning to bring in controls despite previous speculation (Image: Toby Shepheard/PA Wire)

Dozens of MPs have written to Angela Rayner urging her to U-turn on her decision not to bring in rent controls in England.

‌



The Housing Secretary last month said the Government was not planning to bring in controls despite previous speculation.

‌



But new research showing tenants could save up to £1,418 a year if rent controls are introduced has reignited calls.

‌



The study, commissioned by the Joseph Rowntree Foundation (JRF) and carried out by the Autonomy Institute, tests three rent-control pathways introduced from 2027/28: a cap linked to inflation (CPI), a nominal freeze and a moderate approach that limits in-tenancy rises to inflation (CPI) and between-tenancy rises to inflation (CPI) plus 2%.

By 2031, per tenancy, tenants would be annually saving £1,418 if rents were frozen, £701 if moderate rent controls were brought in or £130 if CPI inflation-tracked rent controls were introduced, researchers said. The rent-control pathways are modelled alongside two other reforms: restoring full mortgage-interest deductions for landlords and applying National Insurance to landlord property income.

View 2 Images By 2031, per tenancy, tenants would be annually saving £1,418 if rents were frozen, the study shows (Image: Getty Images)

‌



The letter to Ms Rayner, organised by Labour MP Chris Hinchliff and signed by 26 MPs so far, backs the study and warns the Government it has an "opportunity to fix the foundations of our housing system for the long term".

It says: "On average rent now takes 36% of a renter’s salary, rising to almost half of their pay in some areas just to keep a roof over their heads. With so much of people’s income going on housing, it is little wonder that a third of renters are living in poverty.

"The impacts don’t stop at the front door either, when rent take up such a large chunk of a pay packet you aren’t able to spend in local cafés, restaurants or shops.

‌



"These extortionate rents are the elephant in the room when we talk about the cost of living. The Prime Minister is right to support a mass council housebuilding programme to lay the long-term foundations of a housing system based on meeting need. However, renters are feeling the pain of high rent today and rent controls are essential to easing that pressure."

It is signed by mostly Labour MPs plus a few Green MPs, as well as Your Party MP Jeremy Corbyn.

In 2023, Mr Burnham - who was then the Greater Manchester mayor - called for freezes to private sector rents during the cost of living crisis.

‌



But Ms Rayner told the BBC last month: "I don't think that rent freezes, rent controls, is a way forward at the moment. Three years ago, Andy called for that because there was a significant crisis in the rental market. We implemented between then the Renters' Rights Act which is giving renters more power and control."

She added that controls had not "necessarily brought rents down" where they had been imposed in other places in the UK, such as Scotland. Other critics warn rent controls could increase the housing crisis by putting off people from renting out their house.

Nearly a fifth of UK households now rent privately, and high rents have strained living standards for two decades.

‌



The new report, Rebalancing the market: Designing feasible rent controls, models the private rental sector from 2027 to 2031 using data from the 2024 English Private Landlord Survey and the latest Office for Budget Responsibility forecasts.

Dr Will Stronge, chief executive at the Autonomy Institute said: "Rent controls have often been dismissed as unworkable, but our modelling shows that a modern, well-calibrated cap paired with fair treatment of landlord costs can improve affordability for tenants without triggering the kind of landlord exodus that would leave renters worse off.

"Desperately-needed regulation of rents doesn’t pose a risk to the sector if it comes along with tax reform for landlords”

Article continues below

An MHCLG spokesman said: “We have no plans to introduce rent controls. International examples show they don’t necessarily bring rents down and our landmark Renters’ Rights Act already protects tenants from excessive rent increases. The Act limits rent rises to once a year, gives tenants strong powers to challenge above-market increases and bans rental bidding wars - giving renters the security they deserve.”

News.title: Former nurse extradited to UK denies having sex with mental health patient at London hospital
News.content:
Former nurse extradited to UK denies having sex with mental health patient at London hospital

Former nurse Jason Forde appeared at Wood Green Crown Court after being extradited from Barbados over allegations involving a mental health patient at Homerton Hospital in Hackney.

View 2 Images The allegations relate to a woman who was being treated at a mental health unit on the site of Homerton Hospital in Hackney. (Image: Humphrey Nemar)

A former nurse extradited to the UK has denied having unlawful sexual activity with a woman who was receiving treatment for a mental disorder at a London hospital.

‌



Jason Forde, 56, pleaded not guilty to eight counts at Wood Green Crown Court on Tuesday afternoon over alleged offences dating back to the 2000s.

‌



The allegations relate to a woman who was being treated at a mental health unit on the site of Homerton Hospital in Hackney, east London.

‌



Appearing in court via video link, Forde denied having sexual intercourse with the woman at the unit, which was part of the East London and City Mental Health Trust - and now operates under the East London NHS Foundation Trust.

View 2 Images Forde pleaded not guilty to the charges at Wood Green Crown Court (Image: MyLondon)

‌



He also denied charges alleging that he engaged the woman in other sexual activity while she was in his care in the east London borough.

Prosecutor Paul Fairley told the court it had taken "many, many years to achieve" Forde's extradition from Barbados, with the 56-year-old landing at Heathrow Airport earlier this summer.

Forde denied one count of "having sexual intercourse with a woman who was a mental defective" contrary to section 7(1) of the Sexual Offences Act 1956, and one count of "having unlawful sexual intercourse with a patient," contrary to section 128(1) of the Mental Health Act 1959.

Article continues below

He also denied three counts of "sexual activity with a person with a mental disorder impeding choice" contrary to section 30(1) of the Sexual Offences Act 2003 and three counts of being a care worker engaged in "sexual activity with a person with a mental disorder" contrary to section 38(1) of the Sexual Offences Act 2003.

Forde was remanded into custody.

News.title: Man in his 40s dies swimming in sea off Devon
News.content:
Man in his 40s dies swimming in sea off Devon

The unnamed man from Sussex, aged in his 40s, died despite the best efforts of paramedics after he was pulled from the waters off a Devon beach earlier this week

View 4 Images The man died after getting into difficulty off the coast of Devon (Image: Getty Images)

A man has died after getting into difficulty in the sea off the Devon coast in another summer drowning incident.

‌



Devon and Cornwall Police confirmed they were called by HM Coastguard at 3.30pm on Monday over concerns for the welfare in the coastal village of Strete. The service said the unnamed man, who in his 40s and from Surrey, was pulled from the water after members of the coastguard, police and paramedics rushed to the scene.

‌



A spokesperson said the man was sadly pronounced dead at the scene, and added that the death was not being treated as suspicious.

Heartbreak at death of youngster days after parents and sister drowned in Shoreham READ MORE :

View 4 Images Paramedics were sadly unable to save the man, who died at the scene (Image: Getty Images)

Confirming the man's death, a spokesperson for Devon and Cornwall Police said: "Police were called by HM Coastguard at 3.30pm on Monday, August 24 following concerns for the welfare of a man at Blackpool Sands, Strete. The man had got into difficulty while swimming in the sea and was recovered from the water by HM Coastguard.

‌



"He was treated at the scene by paramedics. Sadly, the man, who was in his 40s from Surrey, was pronounced deceased at the scene. His death is not being treated as suspicious and a file will be prepared for the coroner."

The man is the 52nd person to die after getting into the water this summer, which has proven particularly deadly for people venturing into the water to cool off during severe hot weather. Three heatwaves have scorched the country since May, leading thousands of people to flock to the coast, rivers and other water sources in a desperate bid to escape sky-high temperatures nearing 40C.

View 4 Images Sara El-Khawas, 14, died with her parents

‌



The man's death follows the devastating Shoreham drownings, during which four members of the same family died after getting into difficulty in waters off the coast of the West Sussex port town at around 2pm on August 18.

Palestinians Saja El-Khawas, six, her sister Sara El-Khawas, 14, and her parents Hassan El-Khawas, 55, and Zeina Alayn, 37, died last week after entering the water at Kingston Beach, which is near Shoreham Port. Despite the best efforts of paramedics, who were called to the scene at around 2.40pm.

Sara, Hassan and Zeina sadly died on the scene, while Saja died three days later after she was rushed to hospital. A spokesperson for Sussex Police said the deaths were being treated as a "tragic incident" without third-party involvement.

‌



View 4 Images The deaths of Hossam El-Khawwas and his family were ruled a tragic accident

Sussex Ch Supt James Collis said: "This heartbreaking update is one we all feared in the aftermath of Tuesday's tragic events. The impact of this tragedy has been felt across the country, and I know the Shoreham community, emergency responders and all involved will continue to be affected for a long time to come.

"I would like to thank all of the public who have shared their sympathies and kind words." The Mirror has launched the Save Lives For Sam water safety campaign to tackle the UK's growing drowning crisis.

Article continues below

Backed by MPs, Olympic champions, national water safety organisations and bereaved families, the campaign is calling for urgent action to make our waters safer. That includes compulsory water safety lessons in schools, a nationwide public awareness campaign, better lifesaving equipment at high-risk waterways, the introduction of Sam's Law , and a dedicated Minister for Water Safety.

Find out more about the campaign and how you can support it here.

News.title: Should Brits get their licences taken away for dangerous driving videos? Take our poll and have your say
News.content:
Should Brits get their licences taken away for dangerous driving videos? Take our poll and have your say

As a ghoulish social media trend sees young motorists risk everything on the road for likes, but should those who upload dangerous driving videos face serious penalties?

View 2 Images Liberty Mitchell, 21, filmed herself speeding and swerving in a Mini Cooper for Snapcha (Image: Gloucestershire Police / SWNS)

Campaigners are calling for those who upload dangerous driving videos to be stripped of their licences, to prevent further bloodshed.

‌



While those who are found guilty of a drink-driving offence automatically lose their licence, no such legislation is in place to tackle an alarming online trend. As seen by the Mirror, young people are turning to social media platforms such as TikTok to share content of themselves, risking their lives on the road in the name of likes.

‌



Some of these clips show youngsters going 'ghost mode', speeding along narrow, winding country lanes with their lights off. Others partake in wrong way motorway driving stunts. This is a deadly trend that cannot be normalised and, as seen in recent weeks, the effects of reckless driving, whether filmed or not, can be catastrophic.

‌



In the early hours of Saturday, August 22, two police officers, PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, died following a nightmare collision near Middlesbrough, Teesside.

A Volkswagen Passat travelling the wrong way on the A66 dual carriageway collided head-on with the police vehicle that had been assisting in a search for the car. All five occupants of the Passat - Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Theo Rae, 17, Cole Robert Worthy, 17, Jakub Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18 - died instantly.

‌



It quickly emerged that a TikTok profile believed to belong to Saddington frequently featured footage which glorified dangerous driving. One video, deleted shortly after the crash along with the account, appeared to show Saddington in a high-speed police chase alongside four other youngsters.

View 2 Images PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, were both killed in the horror wrong-way smash (Image: Getty Images)

This tragedy came mere days after another wrong-way motorway crash in County Kildare, Ireland. Five teenagers - Jeremy O'Brien, 18, Alex McCarthy, 17, Joey Carthy, 15, Jack Kennedy, 17, and Kamil Pustkowski, 17 - died when their BMW, travelling the wrong way down the M9 motorway at more than 74mph, crashed head-on into a Hyundai.

‌



The Hyundai had been carrying three sisters, Ella, Niamh, and Alma Kinsella, in their 20s and 30s, and a seven-year-old boy, all of whom were driving to Dublin Airport for a family wedding. The five teenagers were killed at the scene, while the three sisters sustained severe injuries. The young boy suffered a broken leg.

It's an issue that has sparked concern for some time. In December 2022, newly qualified driver Liberty Mitchell recorded Snapchat videos of herself speeding at almost 100mph in a 60mph zone.

Overtaking three vehicles on the wrong side of the road near Aldsworth, Gloucestershire, the then-18-year-old lost control of her Mini Cooper and caused a multi-car pile-up, killing taxi driver Octavian Codreanu and his passenger, teacher Moyra Whelan.

Article continues below

This week, the Government has demanded that social media companies remove any content which shows people driving dangerously. Speaking with reporters during a visit to Kyiv on Monday (August 24), Prime Minister Andy Burnham stated: “Anybody who glorifies dangerous driving is doing something that’s truly reprehensible.”

News.title: Gordon Ramsay's daughter Megan engaged 8 months after Holly's wedding to Adam Peaty
News.content:
Gordon Ramsay's daughter Megan engaged 8 months after Holly's wedding to Adam Peaty

Gordon Ramsay has revealed that his rarely-seen daughter Megan is engaged, eight months after her sister Holly married Olympian Adam Ramsay-Peaty, which sparked a family war

Megan Ramsay features alongside her dad on Hell's Kitchen

Gordon Ramsay has revealed his daughter is engaged, months after Holly's wedding. Holly, 26, tied the knot with Team GB Olympian, Adam Ramsay-Peaty, 31, in December last year, at Bath Abbey.

‌



But while Adam and Holly's wedding was shrouded by controversy following his dramatic fall-out with his family, this is far from the case for Gordon's daughter, Megan.

‌



Chef Gordon confirmed the exciting news of Megan's engagement during an interview on the American talk show, Live with Kelly and Mark, earlier today. Speaking on the show, the 59-year-old said of Holly's wedding: "Yeah, it was just one of those amazing moments. And the speech, it's just your little girl, right?

‌



View 2 Images Gordon Ramsay has announced his daughter, Megan, is engaged (Image: megan__ramsay/Instagram)

"I bawled my eyes out. I was a hot, freaking mess, man. I'm telling you. Honestly, it was just so emotional but the day goes so quick, right?" He went on to add: "And then last week, our other daughter announced her wedding as well. So it's rolling..." A spokesperson for Gordon, confirmed to the Mirror that Megan is engaged.

Megan, 28, maintains a low public profile and doesn't have any public social media accounts. It's also not known who her fiancé is. However, four years ago, Gordon revealed he was unhappy with her decision to reunite with an ex-boyfriend.

‌



View 2 Images Megan got engaged earlier this month (Image: Gordon Ramsay/Instagram)

Speaking on The Kelly Clarkson Show at the time, he said he had spoken to Byron during a "terrifying FaceTime call." He said at the time: "I did something really bad last week. Megan started seeing her ex-boyfriend again and his name's Byron...

"He was OK to begin with, a little bit wet. You want a man to date your daughter, and he was just a little bit pathetic. I want to kill the little f***er! I kid you not, I found out his telephone number from our youngest daughter, Tilly.

‌



"She gave me it and said, 'Dad, don't do anything', and I said, 'No, just give me it, if anything's wrong I need his number on my phone.' So I waited to find out when they were having dinner together and I FaceTimed him. He answered the phone and the thing was shaking.

"I said, "Byron, it's me! Not your future father-in-law, you little f***!' Megan leant over and pushed and cut me off, which was so rude!" But despite this, Gordon has a good relationship with his daughter Tilly's boyfriend, Henry Farrow, a sports podcast host.

He's also extremely close to Adam Ramsay-Peaty, who is preparing to welcome his first child with Holly. Speaking previously about Adam, he said: "He's a gent, he's an absolute thoroughbred. Adam is so grounded. He's not walking out as Olympic champion with his head up his a***."

‌



That close relationship was seen during the swimmer's appearance on the High Performance podcast, when host Jake Humphrey read out a text Ramsay had sent about his then-future son-in-law.

"I want you to know he's an amazing young man with such a great attitude," wrote Hell’s Kitchen star Ramsay last year. "Honestly, I could not ask for a more down-to-earth, respectable future son-in-law. What he's achieved is incredible, and he's not done yet. Looking forward to catching up soon."

After hearing what Ramsay had to say, Peaty was overwhelmed and returned the favour. "That makes me emotional. I don't want to cry on the podcast, but it makes me very emotional," Peaty said.

News.title: SUV drivers in UK city to pay new tax as council introduces England first payments
News.content:
SUV drivers in UK city to pay new tax as council introduces England first payments

Angry motorists in Bath are hitting back at the council's plans to introduce new charges based on the size of their vehicles, which come on top of existing emissions charges

View 5 Images Many motorists have been left furious by the move (Image: Getty Images)

SUV owners driving in one of the UK's most picturesque cities will soon have to fork out cash for a specialised tax introduced by a local council.

‌



In an England first, Bath has become the first city in the home nation to introduce an "SUV tax", which will charge drivers more to park bigger cars at home. The decision was taken by Bath and North East Somerset Council, which plans to introduce size-based pricing for residents' parking permits.

‌



But angry motorists have hit back at the plans, which came following a public consultation in 2025, stating the council is doing things that "don't make sense".

‌



View 5 Images Bath residents already pay emissions charges (Image: Getty Images)

The authority revealed it would be pushing ahead with the plans following its consultation last week, despite the angry backlash, ushering in a first for England. A similar policy was pursued in Wales last year, with another scheme dubbed an "SUV tax" introduced in Cardiff.

The Bath version of the scheme would see supplementary charges introduced for larger vehicles, while smaller vehicles are handed discounts.

‌



The policy was launched on August 25, and would in action see owners of smaller Smart cars get a £20 permit discount every year. Drivers who opt for much larger cars, however, including the Land Rover Discovery or Ford Galaxy, would pay up to £41 more. The highest premiums would be reserved for Ford Transit owners who sprung for the manufacturers' largest option.

View 5 Images Car owners could be asked to fork over more than £100 extra for the largest cars (Image: Getty Images)

They would have to pay a maximum of £112, a price Bath's council says will help encourage large car owners to spring for smaller, safer models.

‌



The charges for car size would be applied on top of emissions-based payments motorists are already asked to make based on how polluting their cars are. The size-based charges are planned to operate on a similar system, and, where no data is available, be based on people's self-submitted photo evidence.

The council also says it will increase the cost of a residents' parking permit by 20% generally and begin phased increases to the cost of visitor permits.

View 5 Images The council also plans to increase residents' parking permit costs by 20 percent (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Defending the decision, council cabinet member Joel Hirst said: "Research shows that larger vehicles like SUVs pose a greater risk to pedestrians and cyclists in collisions, with children particularly vulnerable.

"By introducing size-based permit charges, we are encouraging the use of smaller, safer and cleaner vehicles." Bath residents have slammed the plans as "outrageous" and claimed they will unfairly target families and people with disabilities, who need the larger vehicles for their additional needs.

Bob, 63, a retired Bath taxi driver, said he might not mind the policy if Bath's council was actively improving the city's public transport service. He said: "I was driving in this town for 20 years, and at the time, I had to pay something like £80 to £100 for residential parking."

‌



View 5 Images Some residents have said they believed the pricing plan was a 'good idea' (Image: Getty Images)

"If that weren't bad enough, they then add injury to insult by saying, 'now we're going to charge you by the size of your car as well. The things they are doing don't make sense. I wouldn't mind so much, but they're not improving the public transport system. I don't think it's going to improve the congestion in the city, because it doesn't matter how much they put the charges up - people will still pay the charges.

"People will still come into the centre of town because they have to, to function." Despite the concern, some residents were in favour of the changes, including 63-year-old Jayne Mallon, who said previously: "I think it's a good idea. Bigger vehicles should pay more - they take up more space and give out more pollution."

Article continues below

Similar charges were introduced last autumn in Cardiff, which became the first local authority in the UK to introduce a parking premium for larger vehicles. They said the plans were "to encourage drivers to switch to smaller vehicles," amid a backlash against large SUVs.

The council said it carried out initial public consultation on the proposals in Bath last year. It said feedback showed that 50 per cent of respondents supported introducing size-based charges or discounts for residents' parking permits.

News.title: Mum of teen killed in wrong-way M9 crash apologises to family left in hospital
News.content:
Mum of teen killed in wrong-way M9 crash apologises to family left in hospital

Mourners today gathered for the funeral of Jack Kennedy, 17, who died alongside four others after the car they were travelling in was driven the wrong way down the M9 motorway in Ireland

Jack Kennedy: Funeral held for teenager killed in M9 crash in Ireland

The mother of one of the five young people killed when their car went the wrong way down the M9 in Ireland, before crashing into another car, has apologised to a family left in hospital.

‌



The funeral mass for 17-year-old Jack Kennedy, who died in the crash on the M9 in Co Kildare last weekend, also heard calls to “please, please, please, stop” engaging in criminal activity.

‌



Sisters Ella Hendricken, Niamh Kinsella and Alma Kinsella, who are aged in their 20s and 30s, were rushed to hospital after their car was struck by the vehicle travelling the wrong way. They were travelling with a child, who was also hospitalised, when their Hyundai was hit by the BMW at around 3am on August 16.

‌



Garda officers were stationed in Kildare ahead of Jack's funeral today, but less than was seen at the services held last week for the other four who died in the crash.

View 4 Images Jack Kennedy

Police probe as several motorists seen driving wrong way on M6 following crash READ MORE :

Jack died alongside Jeremy O’Brien, Kamil Pustkowski, Joe Carthy and Alex McCarthy when their car collided head-on with the other vehicle.

‌



Jack’s mother Sarah spoke at the funeral at St Michael’s, Athy, Kildare, on Tuesday morning. She apologised to the family still recovering in hospital as a result of the crash.

“Five young boys made a bad choice,” she said. “Five young boys paid the ultimate price. Five families lost their babies. Five families got a life sentence. May they all rest in peace.

View 4 Images The cortege for Jack Kennedy makes its way through Athy, Co Kildare, ahead of his funeral at St. Michael's Parish Church (Image: Evan Treacy/PA Wire)

‌



“Secondly, we all want to send our deepest, heartfelt apologies to the families who were injured. You are all in our thoughts and our prayers. We pray to God that you all make a full recovery and once again, we are sorry.”

In the eulogy, Canon Frank McEvoy referred to anger that has been expressed on social media surrounding the incident. He said: “Words can hurt, and words have the power to heal. It’s also true of actions. Our actions can hurt people, and our actions can heal people.

“In all those situations, we’re responsible for the words that we use, and above all, we’re responsible for the actions that we take.”

‌



He said the feeling in the parish after the crash was “one of shock, confusion, disbelief, and above all, anger”. “Anger is a very dangerous emotion, and when it starts to curdle and get going in the community, anything can happen,” he said.

View 4 Images Ella Hendricken (L), Niamh Kinsella (C) and Alma Kinsella (R) were seriously injured in the crash

“When you watch social media and you watch the responses and you hear what people are saying, that’s the result of bad actions and very often, then, in all of that, there’s so much hurt created for the family.

‌



“Sarah put it so well, she doesn’t wish any of you to walk in her shoes, to have to bury her son. There’s no great future in all of that.

“And again, as I say, the dust has settled somewhat, and the week has passed by, there is something I want to say, and especially to Jack’s friends, and it’s this – if you’re considering continuing this criminal activity, will you please stop?

“Just one word, stop. Because this is the end of it."

‌



View 4 Images Jack was one of the five teenagers who died in a motorway crash in Co Kildare earlier this month (Image: Evan Treacy/PA Wire)

“This is a family broken, and the consequences of that will happen to you too, for you yourself, for your families, the communities in which you live in, and then you’ll have the innocent victims, like the people who are in hospital trying to recover.

“There is no need for it. So again, I say to you, please, please, please, stop.”

Article continues below

One of the items brought to the altar was a car to represent Jack’s “love for cars”.

Young, Wild & Free by Snoop Dogg and Wiz Khalifa played as the coffin was taken from the chapel for a private cremation.

News.title: Dolly Parton: The life of an iconic country singer
News.content:
Iconic country musician Dolly Parton has died at the age of 80, her family announced on her social media.

"Sadness lies with us, not with Dolly," Parton's nephew Brian Seaver said in a video announcement.

In a seven-decade career, Parton won 10 Grammy awards, sold more than 100 million records worldwide, and wrote in excess of 3,000 songs.

Parton took her writing seriously, and considered herself a songwriter over everything else. "It's my way of expressing myself," she said. "It's my therapy."

She was also a savvy businesswoman who wasn't afraid to make tough decisions. Armed with a quick wit and southern charm, she took control of her show business career that spanned more than 60 years.

Follow for live updates and read more about Dolly's life.

News.title: Father's house rammed before son died in A66 crash
News.content:
A house rammed by a car before the fatal A66 crash in Middlesbrough belonged to the father of a teenager who died in the incident.

Cole Worthy, 17, was one of five young men who died when a Volkswagen Passat travelling in the wrong direction hit a Cleveland Police armed response vehicle, also killing two police officers.

Before the crash at 03:39 BST on Saturday, police had received multiple reports of two cars driving dangerously around the town and a Volvo XC60 was seen ramming properties.

The BBC understands that, after his father's home was rammed, Worthy and the four others set out in the Passat. Police said they were linking the activities of the Volvo XC60 and the Passat.

There is no suggestion Worthy's father was involved in criminal activity.

PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died in the crash, as did Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and Worthy.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct said officers had been pursuing the Passat for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when it turned on to the dual carriageway.

Both vehicles were operating with cloned number plates but were picked up by automated number plate recognition technology.

News.title: Man dies in crash after police pursuit
News.content:
A man has died and two women have been injured in a crash after a police pursuit near Stratford-upon-Avon.

Officers tried to stop a black Audi on Birmingham Road shortly before 17:30 BST on Monday but the driver failed to pull over, Warwickshire Police said.

A pursuit began and 15 minutes later the Audi crashed into a white Ford Puma, the force added, with the Audi's 19-year-old male driver confirmed dead at the scene by paramedics.

The driver of the Ford, a woman, was seriously injured and remains in hospital in critical condition, while injuries to a second woman - her passenger - were serious but not believed to be life-threatening. An investigation by the police watchdog is under way.

Officers said after failing to stop, the Audi made off in the direction of the A46 before travelling back towards Stratford on the A439 Warwick Road where the crash occurred.

A number of other cars were damaged during the pursuit, police said.

Warwick Road was closed on Monday from the Marraway roundabout to its junction with Ingon Lane and Sand Barn Lane, with the stretch remaining shut on Tuesday morning.

It later reopened.

News.title: Trump says all mines cleared from Strait of Hormuz
News.content:
US President Donald Trump has said that the US Navy has removed or detonated all mines in the Strait of Hormuz - the vital waterway which Iran has largely closed since the beginning of the war in the Middle East.

"Iran has been notified that any ship or boat placing new mines will be immediately and systematically destroyed," Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform.

There is no comment from Iran.

Closure of the strait has caused wild fluctuations in the price of oil on world markets. Trump has often said the US has control of the area - but Iran has fired against vessels it says have sought to cross without its permission.

Some 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to transit the Strait of Hormuz before the war, which began on 28 February with US and Israeli air strikes against Iran.

In addition to closing the strait, Iran retaliated against Israel and against US bases in the region as well as US Arab allies in the Gulf.

A ceasefire aimed at facilitating talks to end the war has collapsed and there has been intermittent exchange of fire between the US and Iran.

However, this week the US announced a raft of economic sanctions against Iran.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that any nation financially partnering with Iran would be isolated.

Iran and the US signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) in June - a 14-point document which set a 60-day deadline to reach a deal on the Strait of Hormuz, before substantial negotiations on resolving the nuclear issue - allegations that Iran is building a nuclear weapon, which Tehran has consistently denied.

However, that deadline has now expired and talks have collapsed leading to the new US sanctions that Trump believes will lead to the collapse of the Iranian regime.

Iran has been under sanctions for most of the time since the founding of the Islamic Republic in 1979 and Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh said Tehran was "fully prepared" for the wider sanctions, which he added would lead to "another defeat" for the US.

Its economy, however, has suffered as a result of the war - and a blockade of Iranian ports that the US has been maintaining for weeks not to allow trade to continue.

On Tuesday, China - the biggest buyer of Iranian oil - said it was firmly opposed to what it called the US's "illegal unilateral sanctions" and would take "all necessary measures" to safeguard its rights.

The US announcement comes ahead of planned talks between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping next month.

Washington is likely to be wary of potential retaliation from Beijing, which processes the majority of the world's rare earths and other critical minerals, crucial in the manufacture of many high-tech products.

Beijing has already tightened export controls on rare earths as part of previous trade negotiations with the US.

News.title: Spanish government says sorry to people of Ceuta for migrant crisis
News.content:
The Spanish government has apologised to the people of Ceuta for the migrant crisis that has affected the city for weeks and it has unveiled plans to overhaul the country's immigration laws.

"I want to apologise to all those who may have felt, or who even still feel, abandoned or not sufficiently cared for," Defence Minister Margarita Robles told a parliamentary committee.

"I have witnessed first-hand your feelings of anxiety, of abandonment, of lack of safety."

At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta, a Spanish exclave in North Africa on 30 and 31 July.

Most of the migrants swam around the border fence and at least 100 people died during the mass crossing, according to figures from Ceuta's mayor, Juan JesÃºs Vivas.

The vast majority of the migrants returned to Morocco within hours of their arrival, but several thousand remain in Ceuta, many of them children, and most sleeping rough on beaches or streets.

The Socialist government of Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez has been under mounting pressure to resolve the situation, with many residents and the local authorities in Ceuta, which has a population of 84,000, complaining that it is unsustainable.

The SÃ¡nchez government has now declared a situation of interest for national security in the city, centralising management of the crisis. Territorial Policy Minister Ãngel VÃ­ctor Torres has been tasked with co-ordinating the response, relieving the Ceuta local government of that responsibility.

News.title: Who does Iran trade with and what could Trump's 'economic D-Day' mean?
News.content:
The US has said "the single greatest financial offensive ever" will help it and Israel end their ongoing war with Iran.

However, Iran is no stranger to these tactics.

The regime has faced near continuous US sanctions since the Islamic Revolution of 1979. In that time, it has developed deep trade ties with several countries which either have a history of ignoring US economic pressure themselves or cannot afford to stop trading with Iran.

As a result, Iran says it is "fully prepared" for the new US sanctions and many economists argue the impact of Washington's latest move will be limited.

So, who does Iran trade with? And could what the US has called an "economic D-Day" have any real impact on Iran?

News.title: Yellow weather warnings issued as thunderstorms and flooding forecast
News.content:
Yellow weather warnings have been issued by the Met Office as heavy rain and thunderstorms are forecast to break out over parts of the UK later this week.

The warnings span Wednesday and Thursday and include parts of east Wales, the Midlands, northern England, East Anglia and southern England - including London.

It is likely to be the one of the most widespread outbreaks of heavy rain across southern and central parts of the UK this summer.

While good news for regions plagued by drought, significant accumulations could lead to flash flooding where the ground is too dry and hard to absorb the downpours. Lightning, large hail and gusty winds are also possible.

News.title: Inspectors to assess police after Henry Nowak murder
News.content:
An inspection into how a police force responds to violent incidents has been launched in the wake of Henry Nowak's murder.

The 18-year-old student was stabbed in Southampton by Vickrum Digwa, who lied to police and insisted he had been the victim of a racist attack.

Hampshire Police officers initially arrested Nowak and placed him in handcuffs as he lay dying.

His Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Service (HMICFRS) will assess the force's processes, training and how officers are supported to make sound and impartial judgements.

The inspection was requested by Hampshire Police and Crime Commissioner Donna Jones, who said the public "must have confidence" in the force.

"This inspection will provide an independent assessment of the force's training, processes and culture, including the handling of allegations of racially aggravated assault," she said.

"Henry's family deserve answers, and the public deserve reassurance that their police service is equipped to recognise victims and provide the highest standard of care when it matters most."

News.title: Young care leavers dying early a 'national tragedy'
News.content:
Young adults who have left care have a death rate around four times higher than the general population, a new review, external shows.

Often left alone "with no safety net," the report says the consequences can be catastrophic.

On turning 18, people leaving care in England often lose "significant levers of support", the Government-commissioned report concluded, as it warned the so-called "care cliff" must be addressed.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4 Today, report co-author and broadcaster Ashley John-Baptiste, who grew up in care, called the deaths a national tragedy.

There were 112 deaths of care leavers aged 18 to 24 notified in 2025, which the review said equalled about 130 deaths per 100,000 care leavers.

John-Baptiste recalled his own experience of turning 18 and moving out of the last of four foster homes he'd lived in.

"I was made to live alone and work out how to be an adult," he said.

Unable to afford a bed frame, he says he slept on a mattress on the floor of his council flat and felt a deep sense of abandonment and isolation.

News.title: Boy, 3, injured in crocodile attack returns home
News.content:
A three-year-old boy who was seriously injured in a crocodile enclosure has been discharged from hospital and is settling back in at home, his family has said.

The child returned home "a few weeks ago" and is "happy to be home, playing with his toys, sleeping in his own bed and being a big brother", his parents said in an update posted online.

The boy was visiting Johnsons of Old Hurst near Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, with his family on 18 June when he was attacked by at least one of the animals.

In an update shared on a fundraising page on Monday, the boy's family said it was "nice to have us all back together in the comfort of our own home".

Cambridgeshire Police arrested and bailed a 30-year-old man from Norfolk on suspicion of attempted murder after the incident.

News.title: Legendary rugby league winger Boston dies aged 92
News.content:
Tributes have been led by prime minister Andy Burnham who said he was a "giant of a man in every way".

"Heartbroken to hear my friend Sir Billy Boston has died," he said on social media.

"Billy was one of the greatest rugby league players of all time but also one of the kindest and most down-to-earth people you could ever wish to meet.

"He always had time for people and gave so much to back to his adopted home, Wigan.

"I will miss him greatly and am thinking today of Billy's family, still grieving the recent loss of his beloved wife Joan."

Wigan owner Mike Danson said: "Billy Boston was everybody's hero, including my mum's.

"His achievements in rugby league were extraordinary, and his knighthood was a fitting recognition of a career that brought great credit to Wigan and to the game.

"But Billy's legacy was not simply what he achieved. It was the humility with which he carried it. Despite everything he accomplished, he remained a quiet, dignified and deeply respected man.

"He leaves behind an example that will endure for generations. Our thoughts are with his family and those closest to him.

"A great man, and a true Wigan legend. He will be remembered with pride and affection."

In a statement, Wales Rugby League said: "Today, rugby league has lost one of its greatest-ever players, Wales has lost one of its finest sporting sons, and our sport has lost a truly special gentleman."

The WRU also paid tribute, calling Boston "one of the best loved and most iconic figures in the history of Welsh sport".

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy added: "He was, in my view, the greatest rugby league player of all time and one of the nicest people I've ever had the privilege to know."

News.title: Former police officer charged with raping woman while on duty
News.content:
A former police officer allegedly raped and strangled a woman while on duty, according to the policing watchdog.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said ex-constable Rikki Hall had been charged with two counts of rape and one count of non-fatal strangulation.

The 33-year-old is accused of attacking the woman while on duty in Swansea city centre in February 2024.

Hall, who resigned from South Wales Police during the IOPC investigation, has also been charged with possession of a firearm and two counts of misconduct in public office.

He will appear at Bristol Magistrates' Court on Thursday.

The IOPC said its investigation began in February 2024 following a mandatory conduct referral from South Wales Police.

"A substantial file of material was submitted to the Crown Prosecution Service in February 2025 and, following further lines of enquiry being undertaken, charges were authorised by the CPS," it added.

News.title: 'We just want to get home' - dozens stranded in Tunisia after cancelled Belfast flight
News.content:
Dozens of people from Northern Ireland have been left stranded in Tunisia after their EasyJet flight home was cancelled, with the airline telling them it had no other flights available for another 10 days.

One man told BBC News NI he has spent Â£4,000 on travel home for his family-of-five, while another woman, Georgina Doherty, said she and her six children were trying to get home after the death of her mother-in-law.

Others described running out of medication for health issues, while EasyJet were also criticised over a lack of support and communication.

EasyJet has said it is operating an additional direct flight to Belfast on Tuesday night, and that it was "very sorry" for the inconvenience.

BBC News NI understands more than 100 people were booked onto the cancelled flight that was due to leave Enfidha-Hamamet Airport for Belfast International three days ago.

Stuart McCartney, from Dromore, County Down, said he had spent thousands on accommodation and flights to get his family home via a flight to Brussels.

"I'm willing to pay Â£4,000 to get us home, if needs be, and then battle for reimbursement if I have to after that," he said.

"But we shouldn't have to pay. My holiday was a fraction of what I'm paying to get home right now."

McCartney said EasyJet provided two nights of accommodation but then told the family to find alternative accommodation for the rest of the delay.

He said his mother Katherine, who accompanied his wife and children on the trip, relies on heart medication and they have had to keep a close eye on her remaining supply as the delay continued.

An EasyJet spokesperson said that the company "have been doing everything we can to support Mr McCartney, providing hotel accommodation and meals and we will be reimbursing expenses that may have been incurred".

Georgina Doherty, who is originally from Londonderry but now lives in County Donegal, told BBC News NI the last few days have been an "absolute nightmare" for her family.

Her husband returned home a day before they were due to fly back due to his mother taking ill. She has since died, with Doherty and her six children stranded in Tunisia.

News.title: More than 70,000 social and affordable homes to be built across England over 10 years
News.content:
Ministers have announced where more than 70,000 social and affordable homes will be built in England over the next 10 years as part of an initial allocation of almost Â£10bn in a bid to address the housing crisis.

Funding has been granted to Greater Manchester, the West Midlands, West Yorkshire, South Yorkshire, North East England, and Liverpool. An additional Â£6bn was previously announced for London.

It is the first part of a wider plan to build 300,000 social and affordable homes, under the government's Â£39bn social housebuilding programme.

Housing charities welcomed the news but said it was still not enough to meet demand, while the Conservatives said it was an "unfunded spending commitment".

Social housing provides affordable homes at a low cost, managed by social landlords. It includes affordable rented properties as well as low-cost home ownership, such as shared ownership, and can be provided by local authorities and housing associations.

Earlier this year, before he became prime minister, Andy Burnham had called for the entire Â£39bn affordable housing budget for England to be spent on homes for social rent - which means the cost of the unit is about half that of market rents, and there are strict criteria for who can apply for it.

"I would actually devote all of it to social housing," Burnham told The Social Housing Podcast in May.

But of the new homes announced on Monday, 60% would be for social rent.

Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook told BBC Breakfast he did not accept Burnham had failed to meet his previous commitment, saying the government had taken a "pragmatic approach" and wants to "get money out the door".

He said the next tranche of funding would be more focused on council houses - which are usually also classed as homes for social rent.

It is understood ministers decided against giving councils more of the funding announced in the first tranche because they did not believe councils would be in a position to build the required number of social homes.

News.title: Andrew Tate exaggerates and did not own supercars in photos, his lawyers say
News.content:
Controversial influencer Andrew Tate portrays himself as "uberwealthy" but did not own cars and a yacht featured on his social media and exaggerated his lifestyle for online attention, his legal representatives have said.

Tate and his brother Tristan are currently being held in a Florida jail but are seeking release on bail while they await the outcome of extradition proceedings.

They were arrested last month after British prosecutors unveiled new charges including alleged sexual offences against them, which both men deny.

Prosecutors have argued the Tates are a "flight risk", citing the brothers' past statements about their wealth and influence and having multiple identities to evade the law.

In a legal submission to the court, the brothers' legal representatives said the Tates' business model "depends on online attention".

"The outrageousness of the posts by them and about them is the point. The more hyperbolic and outlandish the post, the more likely it will generate views and likes, which in turn generates income. In short, they are playing a role," it says.

At times Andrew Tate has also exaggerated and used hyperbole for "comedic effect" with no intention to be taken seriously, the submission argues.

"The government alleges that the Tates are a risk of flight based on their social media claims that they are 'self-proclaimed billionaires' who own 'high-end vehicles, private jets, and a custom $50-million-dollar superyacht and have unrestricted access to traditional funds, cryptocurrency, and bitcoin,'" it says.

"But the government has not established these grandiose claims are true," it adds.

News.title: Man jailed for killing student over fake Rolex row
News.content:
At about 17:00 GMT on the night he died, Oladipo left his girlfriend's flat carrying a plastic bag of leftover snacks and was on the phone to her while he walked back to his accommodation nearby to watch football.

But outside the De Montfort University's Innovation Centre, he was met by Dennis who was captured on CCTV walking up and down in the "busy" area.

"It took less than 30 seconds for the two men to come together, to struggle and for the defendant to leave," Osborne told the court.

The court was told Oladipo's girlfriend heard him say "why did you come up and stab me?" over the phone before asking for her to call the ambulance.

A post-mortem examination showed he had suffered six wounds, five to the chest including one which penetrated his heart, and one to his thumb.

Despite being taken to the Leicester Royal Infirmary, he was pronounced dead just over an hour after the stabbing, which took place near the DMU campus.

Giving evidence in his defence on Wednesday, Dennis said he was "fearful" for his life when Oladipo approached him with a knife, adding he was "wrestling" to prevent the 20-year-old from stabbing him.

In cross-examination, prosecutor Jane Osborne KC asked if Dennis knew he had stabbed Oladipo, to which he replied: "I didn't know and I didn't know he was hurt, and I didn't intend to cause any serious harm."

Jurors were shown CCTV footage of Oladipo and Dennis walking towards each other, with Osborne suggesting Dennis used his hands to open a folding knife.

Dennis denied the suggestion he had a knife in his possession, and said he did not leave his accommodation with one.

Addressing Dennis, the prosecutor said there was "bad feeling" between Dennis and Oladipo - and suggested Dennis left his accommodation with a knife "to settle it".

Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins has refused to say which countries the Trump administration is relying on for its plan to temporarily surge beef imports into the U.S. to ease consumer prices.

“I am not privy to talk about that,” Rollins told reporters on Tuesday. “I think the conversations are still going on,” she added, saying that President Trump and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer were involved.

In a Truth Social post on Friday, President Trump claimed he had reached a deal to allow up to 300,000 metric tons of meat destined to become ground beef into the U.S. to be sold at reduced prices for the next 90 days without tariffs or quotas. The plan, Trump said, would “substantially lower the price of ground beef for working American families.”

A White House official told The Independent last week that Trump would “formally sign an executive order” to execute the agreement “within the next two weeks.”

Since Trump returned to office last year, the price of ground beef has risen from $5.45 per pound to $6.85 per pound, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

open image in gallery Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins on Tuesday did not name the countries the U.S. is importing beef from as part of its plan to lower consumer prices ( Reuters )

On Monday, an Arizona border crossing reopened to Mexican cattle, as fears have eased over the spread of the New World screwworm through Mexican cattle imports. The U.S. plans to open more border crossings as part of the beef plan.

The Trump administration’s beef deal has met with stiff resistance from ranchers and Republicans, who argue that allowing more imports will do little to change the underlying conditions that have sent beef prices spiking, such as low herd sizes because of drought.

"Despite high beef prices in grocery stores, prices paid to farmers and ranchers for their cattle have fallen sharply over the past two months, and beef packing plants are shutting down across the U.S.,” American Farm Bureau Federation President Zippy Duvall said in a statement after the plan was announced.

"Further undercutting a fragile recovery by swamping markets with foreign products and attempting to manipulate prices threatens to wipe out any progress that has been made,” he added.

“I’ve advised President Trump against this course of action for a year because American ranchers have been struggling against the packer monopoly for decades, and this will further harm them — most of whom are MAGA Republicans,” Senator Tim Sheehy of Montana, a Trump ally, said after the president's announcement.

The Trump administration argues the temporary surge in imports won’t impact farmers over the long term and merely represents a fraction of the beef imports that normally would’ve been coming into the U.S. anyway, but for the screwworm.

open image in gallery Ranchers have argued against intervening in the market, while the administration argues the plan is a short-term measure to relieve American shoppers from high prices ( AFP/Getty )

Agribusiness experts, meanwhile, have doubts over whether the plan will lower prices.

"The administration obviously has a lot of incentive to try to be able to say that they’re doing something about high beef prices in particular," Derrell Peel, an agribusiness professor at Oklahoma State University, recently told the Associated Press. "Beef has been singled out because it is an expensive product and because it’s just high profile."

"I don’t expect to see any measurable impact on cattle prices or beef prices soon," he added.

The White House previously negotiated for thousands of tons of beef imports from Argentina to lower prices, and the president has accused major meat packers of conspiring to keep prices high.

The questions surrounding the beef program come as the Trump administration has reignited its trade war with Canada and continues to strain global fuel prices through the Iran war.

The high-profile mixed doubles event at the US Open begins on Tuesday with several star pairings set to take to the courts at Flushing Meadows.

It was confirmed on Saturday that Serena Williams, who returned to tennis in June, will team up with defending men’s singles champion Carlos Alcaraz in New York.

World No 1 women’s player Aryna Sabalenka and 24-time Grand Slam champion Novak Djokovic are the top seeds, with the all-American pairing of Jessica Pegula and Taylor Fritz the second seeds.

There will also be a qualifying event, made up predominantly of specialist doubles players, before the main draw starts on Tuesday. The defending champions are the Italian doubles pairing of Sara Errani and Andrea Vavassori.

Here’s everything you need to know for the US Open mixed doubles event.

When is it?

The main draw starts on Tuesday 25 August with the first round and quarter-finals. Play starts at 4pm BST (11am local) on Arthur Ashe Stadium and 3pm BST (10am local) on Louis Armstrong Stadium.

The semi-finals and final will headline a special night session on Arthur Ashe Stadium on Wednesday 26 August, starting at midnight BST (7pm local).

What is the draw?

First round

Katerina Siniakova/Henry Patten bt. Aryna Sabalenka/Novak Djokovic [1] 1-4, 4-2, 2-10

Elina Svitolina/Gael Monfils bt. Alexandra Eala/Felix Auger-Aliassime 4-1, 4-1

Belinda Bencic/Flavio Cobolli [4] bt. Taylor Townsend/Alexander Zverev 4-2, 4-2

Serena Williams/Carlos Alcaraz vs Erin Routliffe/Lloyd Glasspool

Karolina Muchova/Jakub Mensik bt. Kristina Mladenovic/Marcelo Arevalo 4-1, 2-4, 10-7

Emma Navarro/Tommy Paul bt. Amanda Anisimova/Learner Tien [3] 5-3, 4-2

Mirra Andreeva/Andrey Rublev bt. Sara Errani/Andrea Vavassori 1-4, 4-1, 11-9

Diana Shnaider/Casper Ruud vs Jessica Pegula/Taylor Fritz [2]

Quarter-finals

Svitolina/Monfils bt Siniakova/Patten 5-4, 4-5, 10-8

Bencic/Cobolli [4] vs TBC

Muchova/Mensik bt. Navarro/Paul 4-1, 5-3

Andreeva/Rublev vs TBC

Semi-finals

Svitolina/Monfils vs TBC

Muchova/Mensik vs TBC

What is the format?

For every match up to the final, matches will be best-of-3 sets, with sets to four games and a 10-point tie-break instead of a third set.

For the final, it will be a traditional set to six games and a 10-point tie-break instead of a third set.

All matches will have sudden death deuce.

Sara Errani and Andrea Vavassori won last year’s new-look mixed doubles event ( Getty )

Prize money

Round 1 (qualifying) - $10,000

Round 2 (qualifying) - $20,000

Round 1 (main draw) - $40,000

Quarter-finals - $120,000

Semi-finals - $250,000

Finalist - £500,000

Winner - $1,000,000

Where can I watch it?

Matches in the United Kingdom will be broadcast on Sky Sports Tennis.

In the United States, ESPN2 will present live coverage, with the final on ESPN and ESPN+.

National Park Service emergency responders have been recruited to work on President Donald Trump’s beautification projects in Washington, D.C., including fountain renovations and repairs to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, according to a new report.

Nearly 300 employees from the Park Service’s “incident management team” — which responds to wildfires and other emergencies — have been deployed to the capital, CNN reported, citing internal documents and agency workers.

“It just shows how much DC operations are getting priority above all other park units and staff,” an unnamed Park Service employee told the outlet.

The employees reassigned to Washington, D.C., previously worked at parks across the country, including in Alaska and California. Their duties have since included cleaning up the East Potomac golf course, according to CNN.

The Trump administration pushed back on the CNN report with an Interior Department spokesperson telling The Independent that "NPS sets up incident management teams for all sorts of things, from major events to major projects" and that "people were not pulled from the front lines of wildfires."

open image in gallery Nearly 300 employees from the Park Service’s “incident management team” have been deployed to the capital ( AFP/Getty )

“President Donald J. Trump has done more to make our nation's capital a shining beacon than any other president in the history of this country,” a spokesperson told The Independent. “The Department of the Interior, the National Park Service and our U.S. Park Police had the honor of being part of this effort to Make D.C. Safe and Beautiful.”

Since returning to office, Trump has devoted significant resources to revitalizing Washington’s public spaces, including reviving defunct fountains, gilding statues and repairing the Reflecting Pool — a multimillion-dollar effort that has produced mixed results.

The administration has also pursued grand projects like a massive ballroom at the White House, which the president says is critical for national security, and plans for a 250-foot victory arch along the Potomac River.

open image in gallery Since returning to office, Trump and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum (pictured left) have devoted significant time and resources to revitalizing Washington’s public spaces ( Getty Images )

Incident management employees work across the country’s 63 national parks, responding to planned events such as Fourth of July fireworks displays as well as “unplanned emergencies,” including wildfires, floods, hurricanes and search-and-rescue operations, according to the Park Service. The team includes firefighters, radio operators and liaison officers.

“The immediate NPS response for parks significantly impacted by severe weather and other natural disasters is often coordinated by an NPS incident management team,” the agency’s website states.

One Park Service employee described the deployment of nearly 300 team members to Washington for Trump’s “safe and beautiful” initiative — a federal effort to clean up and improve public spaces — as “crazy abnormal.” The staffer noted that only about 60 personnel were brought in for D.C.’s National Cherry Blossom Festival.

Incident management team members have also been tasked with preparing “highly detailed status reports” for Interior Secretary Doug Burgum’s office, CNN reported. One employee said these “operational details” are typically overseen by less senior officials.

“It’s highly unusual,” the staffer said. “Political folks have wanted to know even the tiniest details, and it’s always about schedule. Will it be on time?”

open image in gallery Incident management employees also assist with other unplanned events, such as floods and search-and-rescue operations ( National Park Service )

The employee said the Parks Service is also operating with reduced resources because of staffing cuts spearheaded by former special government employee Elon Musk’s DOGE initiative, as well as a hiring freeze.

The Park Service workforce has been cut by nearly 25 per cent since 2025 through terminations, early retirements and federal buyouts. Trump’s proposed 2027 budget would eliminate an additional 3,967 full-time positions, reducing staffing by 31 percent from 2025 levels.

The Interior Department’s reliance on the incident management team in Washington appears likely to continue. According to internal documents, the department is requesting “continued support through September ” in order to “sustain the great work underway” by relocated staff.

open image in gallery Incident management employees respond to both ‘planned events’ and ‘unplanned emergencies,’ such as wildfires ( Getty Images )

Exactly what work the employees might be assigned in D.C. remains unclear. Trump, fresh off hosting his Freedom 250 IndyCar race this past weekend, has expressed interest in refurbishing a golf course in the capital.

“The wholistic approach which is common practice across the entire Parks system, from team members across the district and country, to celebrate our nation's 250 demonstrates what makes this country great,” the Interior Department spokesperson also told The Independent. “Across D.C., residents and visitors are excited to see the streets are safe and the city revitalized to the grand destination it was meant to be.”

The Associated Press reported earlier this week that the Park Service received a federal directive earlier this year to deprioritize maintenance projects nationwide in favor of other priorities, including work on the Reflecting Pool and initiatives connected to America’s 250th anniversary.

The Atlantic also reported that Trump recently used nearly $700,000 in taxpayer funds allocated to the Park Service to replace a White House walkway, despite claiming that he had paid for the project himself.

Pennsylvania has reported the first measles deaths in the United States this year, and the first in the state in 35 years.

Both deceased individuals - who are not being identified by the state - were unvaccinated residents of Lancaster County, according to health officials.

There has been a historic resurgence of measles in the U.S. this year, which can lead to fever, brain swelling, pneumonia, and death.

“And all of this suffering and hospitalization and death is entirely preventable. Why is it that the most vulnerable among us, our children, are forced to suffer our ignorance,” Dr. Paul Offit, an infectious disease expert at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, told The Independent in an email.

Two doses of the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine can prevent measles. The majority of infections are in people who are unvaccinated.

open image in gallery There has been a historic resurgence of measles in the U.S. this year, which can lead to fever, brain swelling, pneumonia, and death ( CDC )

Pennsylvania has had 393 confirmed measles cases this year and 86 reported infections in the past week.

“Because measles was largely eliminated in the Commonwealth for more than three decades, people are not familiar with this disease and don’t fully understand the potential severity of the illness,” Secretary of Health Dr. Debra Bogen said.

The U.S. has confirmed 2,777 measles cases in 47 states and D.C. in 2026, the majority in children and teenagers, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

There have been 36 new outbreaks of the highly-contagious illness across the country, accounting for the majority of cases.

Maryland, which borders Pennsylvania, declared measles outbreaks in three counties Monday, following an investigation of 14 new cases in unvaccinated residents. Maryland has 31 cases, including 27 reported since July 15, state health leaders said.

“No public exposures have been identified in these cases. There is currently no evidence of widespread community transmission, as most cases occurred among household contacts,” the Maryland health department said.

Health officials say that the risk for measles infection remains low if people have been fully vaccinated. Two doses of the shot provides 97 percent lifetime protection against infection, the CDC says.

Without it, there is a 90 percent chance someone will become infected after breathing in infected particles or touching contaminated surfaces. Infections can spread for up to two hours after a person who is infected leaves the area.

Pennsylvania's MMR vaccine rate was at 92.7 percent in kindergarteners over the last school year, below the 95 percent rate needed for community immunity that limits the spread of the disease.

open image in gallery Measles cases in the U.S. this year. The darkest blue shows the states with the highest number of cases and the lightest blue shows states with 1-5 cases. Grey states have no cases ( CDC )

Just under 86 percent of kindergarten-age students in Lancaster County had gotten the vaccine, data shared by LancasterOnline showed.

Experts say that vaccine hesitancy in the U.S. is largely to blame for rising measles rates, which have worsened since the pandemic.

A new Trump administration plan to split up the shot could further worsen hesitancy, too.

The Trump administration's public health strategy, spearheaded by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., has also seen vaccine skeptics added to advisory panels and misinformation about vaccines spoken about inside the federal government, including regarding how many vaccines children are given.

"They give — I mean, for a little baby to be injected with that much fluid?" President Donald Trump told reporters in September. "Even beyond the actual ingredients, they have sometimes 80 different vaccines … It’s like you’re shooting up a horse."

The number of vaccinations before the age of 18 is typically between 30 to 50, doctors say.

The Big Ten became the first conference Tuesday to adopt a rule prohibiting football players who have signed professional contracts from returning to play at its schools as college sports finds itself mired in lawsuits and disputes over eligibility.

The matter came to a head Monday when the agent for former Mississippi tight end Dae’Quan Wright said Wright could be heading to LSU thanks to a state-level court order allowing him and others an unexpected fifth year of eligibility despite a NCAA rule change in June impacting players who graduated from high school in 2022. There are a number of lawsuits in dispute around the country.

The Big Ten said that administrators unanimously approved the rule to prohibit football players who have signed a professional contract, were on a professional roster at any point or declared for the NFL draft as an underclassman without withdrawing, from maintaining eligibility for athletic competition at a conference institution. It did not rule out restrictions in other sports like basketball.

Wake Forest athletic director John Currie, chairman of the Atlantic Coast Conference ADs group for the upcoming season, said his colleagues plan to discuss the issue in Wednesday’s regularly scheduled call.

“I don’t think anybody in our league likes the idea of taking away opportunities from existing college students and graduating high school players, which is exactly what is happening when a school signs a player out of an NFL camp to their team,” Currie wrote in a text message to The Associated Press.

Duke coach Manny Diaz said the Power Four conferences need to present a unified front. The Big 12 and Southeastern Conference have not announced steps they could take or returned messages seeking comment, though the SEC ripped the potential for pros back in college in a statement late Monday.

“I think you’ll see more leagues start to govern themselves since we’re having such a hard time finding it at a national level,” Diaz said. “I think everyone understands it’s absolutely absurd. We can enjoy the fact that the players can benefit financially from playing in college now. At the same time, recognize the ultimate truth that we’re not a professional sports franchise. We are a collegiate, scholastic school activity, and we’ve got to rein that in.”

Agent Drew Rosenhaus told the AP on Monday that Wright had been waived by the Cleveland Browns and, if he clears waivers, will join Lane Kiffin’s roster at No. 11 LSU. Wright played two seasons for Kiffin at Ole Miss.

Wright was among a group of players who sued in a Louisiana court, saying the new NCAA rule granting five years of eligibility to most athletes should apply to him and others who were not “grandfathered” into the rule, which did not include the high school Class of 2022.

Los Angeles Rams coach Sean McVay said reversing the college football-to-NFL pipeline was mind-boggling.

“I don’t know enough about it, other than the fact guys that can be in NFL camps, if it doesn’t go down for them, they can go back to college,” McVay said. “I mean, I feel like I took a freaking gummy. I don’t even understand it. It’s true. I mean, looking at this stuff, I’m like, surely that’s not real. But I just try to stay in my lane. But I would say it’s very unique and it’s very different.”

TCU coach Sonny Dykes, whose team plays North Carolina on Saturday in Ireland, said eligibility issues are out of control.

“”It’s a rudderless ship right now,” he said. “My question is, OK, you go and you take 10 guys off of an NFL roster and play them, who’s going to tell you that you can’t? Who’s in charge? What are they going to do? Your guess is as good as mine. I mean, I don’t know who’s in charge of football anymore. I applaud the Big Ten for doing that. I think that showed some leadership.”

Diaz said players returning from the NFL would be taking roster spots belonging to players who have gone through summer conditioning and preseason camp.

“I think there’s morale issues, there’s real-life consequences,” he said. “This is not pro sports where we just have the waiver wire and we just cut a dude and bring a dude in.”

In its statement, the SEC said it opposes professional athletes returning to play college sports.

“College athletes, not professional athletes, have been at the heart of the Southeastern Conference,” the SEC said. “Individuals who choose to leave college athletics, sign professional playing contracts, and compete professionally should not then be permitted to return to college competition. Allowing that to occur will blur the line between college and professional sports, create significant competitive equity concerns and reduce opportunities for high school and current college athletes.”

The SEC concluded its statement by calling on Congress to pass a bill regulating college sports.

Earlier this summer, a Texas judge cleared the way for quarterback Brendan Sorsby to play at Texas Tech despite admitting to gambling in what usually leads to an NCAA ban. Texas Tech supported the move, saying it was important to Sorsby's mental health, but other members of the Big 12 Conference and the Big 12 itself indicated strong opposition and Sorsby eventually decided against trying to play again in college.

Diaz said an overriding problem is that college sports are being legislated by individual judges whose rulings tend to benefit the interests of local universities. The NCAA is fighting all the cases, and recently won a procedural step in a federal case in Denver.

“So it’s bad policy,” Diaz said. “You wouldn’t run any other type of corporation, organization, anything else the way we’re being run right now. And so I hope the leagues do step up because somebody has to right now, because when there’s a vacuum, this is what you see.”

___

AP Sports Writers Aaron Beard and Stephen Hawkins and AP freelance writer Dan Greenspan contributed to this report.

News.title: Palmer and Rogers show promise of star double act for Chelsea
News.content:
“I am very happy for Cole,” Alonso said. “I have really enjoyed seeing him play with the dynamism and the freedom and the responsibility... when Cole feels this way we have a better team and a better Cole.”

Palmer makes it look very easy in this form, capable of switching the direction of play a beat before anyone else spots the opportunity. He and his old Manchester City academy friend Rogers came off before the end, Palmer having demonstrated some discomfort chasing a ball. Asked afterwards how ready he felt, Palmer responded in kind. “Did you not watch the game? I’m only joking, I’m ready... it was a difficult season with injuries and whatnot, but through the summer and since I’ve been back I’ve worked extra hard.”

If there was an attacker to compare with him on the other side it was King, who looks even better. The 19-year-old was way ahead of Arbeloa’s two young Real Madrid imports. García toiled away and took his chance, but César Palacios struggled for any impact in a position tucked in on the left. Oscar Bobb and King gave Fulham some edge but the concern, as ever, will be where Fulham get their goals.

Arbeloa pushed his full-backs high and encouraged Sander Berge to drop deep to get on the ball in the first passing phase. The Norwegian delayed too long in challenging João Pedro for Chelsea’s third – backing off and allowing Palmer to overlap to receive the pass.

Sánchez had not been the only concern for Chelsea. Back in the team, Levi Colwill misjudged a challenge on King in the first half and was relieved that the card was only yellow. Roméo Lavia took a wild swing at Calvin Bassey and was also booked. Moisés Caicedo was not fit to play. Enzo Fernández was on the bench and would come on in the second half to the kind of reception from opposition fans to which he will quickly become familiar.

There was a grin from the Argentine at those who berated him from the home stands when he returned at half-time. Fernández worked hard to transmit a general sense that the abuse did not land, although he will be relieved that the Chelsea fans were supportive. His future still feels very much in play.

It was Palmer’s subtle ball through that gave João Pedro the chance with 32 seconds of the game played. The ball came forward immediately from Lacroix’s firm header from defence. The Frenchman delivered a very accomplished assist for Rogers’s first-half goal. Before that King had equalised. There was an exchange with Timothy Castagne, and King looked up just inside the box and decided to have a swing at it. Sánchez was close enough to grasp the ball and somehow failed to do so.

Sánchez would later push a Castagne shot in the direction of García, who stooped and nodded the ball over the goalkeeper after Palmer had scored Chelsea’s third. This second error was unfortunate, but it is the kind of thing that happens to a goalkeeper as erratic as the one for whom Chelsea’s hierarchy seem to have such patience.

At Telegraph Recommended, we test hundreds of products each year, and we rely on our community members to help verify our experts’ findings.
