World.title: The 2026 NFL season hasn't even started yet and the Jacksonville Jaguars are already taking a massive L
World.content:
I tend to talk a lot about college football uniforms more than NFL uniforms, but that all changed Tuesday morning.

The NFL rolled out their "Rivalry" series of uniforms for all eight teams from the NFC North and AFC South, and by and large, they did a pretty nice job.

The league partnered with Nike to deliver some uniforms that feature a good bit of franchise history and community pride stitched into each team's garments, and I have to say I'm a fan of the overall concept.

CINCINNATI REDS DEBUT CITY CONNECT UNIFORMS AND THEY ARE AN ABOMINATION

I've always been a bigger fan of college uniforms and felt the NFL threads were a bit too "corporate" and "samey" for my liking, but almost all of these are sweet looking alternate kits.

All of them except for one team, that is.

JACKSONVILLE JAGUARS SET AT 8.5 WIN TOTAL AFTER SURPRISING 13-4 SEASON AND WILD CARD LOSS TO BUFFALO

The Jacksonville Jaguars, being an AFC South team, were included in the "Rivalry" uniform rollout, and if I'm being blunt, they massively swung and missed their intended target with these monstrosities.

Okay, let's start with the positives. At least they aren't the "Color Rush Thursday" mustard uniforms the Jags wore back in the late 2010s.

Well, that's about the only positive I can find, so let's dive in, shall we?

This is way too busy for my liking. The helmet, jersey and socks, and pants all being different colors is murder on my eyes. It looks like a 13-year-old kid customized Jacksonville's uniforms in Madden and picked the most garish combinations possible.

Why didn't they go with a black helmet like the good old days?

Or, if they wanted to do the teal lids, at least get a matching jersey and make the pants white.

And, oh Lord, the pants!

You might not be able to tell, but if you look closely enough on the graphic, those are indeed, spotted pants.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

You know, like a jaguar?

People like to rag on another team from the Sunshine State, the Florida Gators, for their "Gator Skin" jerseys, and rightly so. But these pants are just as egregious and deserve just as much flak.

And believe me, they are catching some heat from fans on social media.

The season hasn't even started yet, and the Jags are already taking L's all over the place.

On the bright side, if Trevor Lawrence throws for 400 yards and three touchdowns while wearing these and Jacksonville wins their division this year, everyone will look back fondly on these uniforms a few decades from now.

Time heals all wounds. Hell, just look at how popular the "Creamsicle" jerseys are in Tampa.

World.title: Trump administration says it might demolish the Kennedy Center if court blocks renovations
World.content:
The Trump administration is, for the first time, threatening the demolition of the Kennedy Center if the arts institution isn’t allowed to follow its plans for the site, including adding President Donald Trump’s name to the front of the building.

“Without those efforts, the Center will deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down, with a determination to follow on what to build on the site, such as a large outdoor amphitheater overlooking the Potomac River that has been proposed, by some, for many years,” Justice Department attorney Brantley T. Mayers wrote in a court filing on Monday.

The filing notes that any potential outdoor amphitheater would “fail to adequately honor” President John F. Kennedy, “but would be simpler and more economical to build, operate, and maintain.”

The DOJ attorneys called the Kennedy Center “structurally unsound, fundamentally unsafe, and embarrassing to the Nation’s Capital.”

They say the center’s board, which was handpicked by self-appointed chairman Trump, “recognizes that President Trump’s efforts and prestige provide the sole hope for the Center’s financial survival, and structural renewal.”

“The Board also underscores, and the undisputed evidence demonstrates, that without the prominent recognition of The Trump Administration, and President Trump’s efforts, the donors will not contribute, and the Center will continue to be in a financial and structural death spiral. The Trump Administration, and President Donald J. Trump, should, therefore, be given the respect and dignity of acknowledgement,” the filing says.

It notes that Trump “obtained $258 million in funding from Congress for capital restoration, and has marshalled a new donor base to finance an endowment for the Center,” but does not say what has happened to that money.

The filing makes a dramatic twist in the monthslong saga to renovate the historic arts institution, which has faced multiple legal challenges and criticism from Democrats, musicians and members of the Kennedy family.

This language is a shift from what Kennedy Center Executive Director Matt Floca has used in recent months to describe what the board has said are necessary renovations. Floca has said the renovations would include a “total replacement of stage lifts and rigging systems” and wide-ranging electrical work and leak prevention that could be completed within two years if the facility was shut down during the renovations.

He said in a court filing earlier this year that the “exterior of the Center’s main building will not be materially affected” and “the planned construction, renovation, and renewal efforts will not tear down the Center to its structural steel.”

Mayers’ filing Monday suggested only Trump and his people could save the arts institution.

The administration has “committed an enormous amount of time and energy in planning for the forthcoming renovation and restoration of this building, a task which President Trump, given his unrivaled expertise and experience in real estate and construction, and prominence as President, is uniquely qualified to accomplish,” Mayers wrote Monday in opposition to a motion from Rep. Joyce Beatty, D-Ohio, to block the administration from closing the center completely.

“Even Beatty should prefer a healthy, restored Center to a decaying hulk that is doomed to inevitable destruction or collapse. The Court should allow the Board and President Trump to bring the Center back to a level of greatness far higher than it has ever had before. This would be the fitting tribute that President Kennedy so well deserves.”

Beatty has claimed the closure decision was rushed and that board members weren’t presented with enough information about various scenarios before having to vote on it.

The congresswoman did not immediately respond to a request for comment about DOJ filing.

She is challenging the Trump-appointed board’s renewed bid to add Trump’s name to the front of the building. A judge found the board’s earlier bid to do so was unlawful and compelled it to remove the president’s name from the building, which is supposed to be a “living memorial” to the slain president.

Trump is appealing and the board voted this month to add his name back to the building in a slightly different way- going from the since-stricken “The Donald J. Trump and John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts” to “The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump.”

There is a hearing scheduled on the planned name change and closure in D.C. on Thursday afternoon. The judge said in his earlier decision that only Congress has the power to rename the site.

The immigrant father of a sailor who is on board the beleaguered USS Abraham Lincoln is back with his family on Tuesday after being detained by immigration authorities over the weekend.

The family confirmed the release of Luis Manuel Aviles in a statement posted on social media by his son Joshua Aviles, a Navy handling airman. Joshua Aviles has been deployed on the aircraft carrier for nine months, which is considered a U.S. military record for uninterrupted time at sea.

“Luis has been released back to our family. We are grateful for all of the support for both Luis and Josh throughout this situation. At this moment, our family is taking time to be together. While we await the return of our proud Navy sailor, we kindly ask for your understanding and respect,” the statement reads.

The Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement did not respond to multiple requests for comment about the release of Luis Manuel Aviles.

DHS confirmed over the weekend that Border Patrol arrested Luis Manuel Aviles on Saturday during a traffic stop in Key West, Florida, where the family lives. The agency said he entered the U.S. illegally at an unknown date and location and was being held in ICE custody.

Originally from Nicaragua, Luis Manuel Aviles, 47, has been living in the U.S. for 20 years. He’s mostly worked as a handyman for hotels in Key West, according to his youngest son, Luis Aviles, and stepdaughter, Katty Delgado.

In an interview with Noticias Telemundo on Sunday, Luis Aviles said his father “never hid, he always did things the right way,” adding that he was working toward getting legal status and had complied with his paperwork and visits to ICE’s offices.

Delgado told NBC News on Saturday that her stepfather had a work permit, a Social Security card, a driver’s license and an active asylum case. Joshua Aviles, along with another family member, had filed immigration petitions requesting he remain in the country legally, according to the family.

Asked to confirm whether Luis Manuel Aviles had a Social Security number, a work permit or pending immigration cases, as his family indicated, DHS said in an email on Sunday, “Having a family member in the military is not a free pass to violate our nation’s laws.”

“Military service by an immediate relative does not automatically grant parole, lawful status, or immunity from immigration enforcement,” the email reads.

The immigration detention of Luis Manuel Aviles gained national attention after his son, Joshua Aviles, posted about it on Facebook on Saturday while on board the USS Abraham Lincoln.

“I just got a call that my dad was taken by ICE. If you know my dad, you know he is a hardworking, humble man who is always willing to help anyone if he can,” the post reads. “We have done everything through immigration to get his green card approved, and we are just waiting.”

The post continues: “This is heartbreaking for me. I don’t know how I can mentally continue working 12+ hour days knowing that my dad is somewhere, possibly being treated like a criminal. My dad’s only ‘crime’ was coming to this country to give my siblings and me a better life.”

The Navy said Saturday that the Lincoln had officially left the Middle East en route to the West Coast, a journey that could take a month or more.

World.title: CIA director flies unannounced to Moscow to hold talks, source says
World.content:
WASHINGTON — Central Intelligence Agency Director John Ratcliffe flew to Russia to hold unspecified talks in Moscow, according to a person with knowledge of the matter.

The person declined to say whom was Ratcliffe meeting with or what was the focus of the talks. The CIA declined to comment.

It’s Ratcliffe’s first known trip to Moscow as CIA director. He made headlines with a visit to Venezuela in January to meet with interim President Delcy Rodríguez about two weeks after the U.S. military seized President Nicolas Maduro in a raid in Caracas.

He also traveled to Cuba in May to meet with government leaders. He was the highest-ranking Trump administration official to visit the island, which is under severe economic pressure after the U.S. tightened sanctions.

News of Ratcliffe’s travel came as mystery swirled around a U.S. military transport aircraft that landed in Moscow, according to tracking data.

It was not known who was on board the plane and why it was in Moscow. When asked, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he did not have information about the aircraft.

Neither U.S. military officials, the White House, the U.S. Embassy in Moscow nor the Russian Embassy in Washington immediately respond to questions about the flight’s mission.

Two planes, a C-130 cargo plane and a C-40, landed in Riga, the capital of Latvia, as part of the same mission, according to a U.S. official. The C-130 then went on to Russia, the official said.

Data from FlightRadar24 tracking site showed a plane approached Vnukovo International Airport in Moscow just after 10 a.m. local time (3 a.m. ET) after taking off from Riga two hours earlier.

It had departed from the U.S. Air Force’s Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on Sunday just before 5 p.m. ET, the data showed. That plane had apparently left Moscow on Tuesday afternoon, according to flight radar data.

CBS News and Axios first reported on the CIA chief’s unannounced visit.

CIA directors sometimes act as envoys for presidents in high-stakes talks with adversaries. Former President Joe Biden turned to then-CIA Director William Burns to relay stern warnings to Russia before and after President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

World.title: Dolly Parton, country music icon, dies at 80
World.content:
Dolly Parton, who rose from a loving if impoverished upbringing in the mountains of East Tennessee to become the “Queen of Country” music, a Hollywood star and a beloved American icon, has died, her family announced Tuesday.

She was 80.

Parton’s nephew, Brian Seaver, announced the news in a video posted on her Instagram. He did not provide details about her death.

“My name is Brian Seaver, son of Cassie Parton, and I’m representing the Parton and Owens family today announcing the passing of my aunt, Dolly Rebecca Parton Dean, Sister, Sis and Granny to one generation and Gigi to the next,” Seaver said in a video.

Dolly Parton in 1970. Michael Ochs Archives / Getty Images file

“This video announcement is something Dolly asked of me years ago, before I fully absorbed it as a future reality. As her head of security for more than two decades, a role my father Larry held before me, I have imagined the heaviness of this moment but haven’t truly felt it til now,” he added.

Seaver added that Parton “lived in the light and is in the arms of Jesus, surely met by (her late husband) Carl, her parents, and countless others.”

“Rest in peace, Aunt Dolly — Aunt, Granny, Gigi. May God bless Dolly Parton, and may God bless you all. She will always love you,” Seaver said at the end of the video statement.

Her death comes after Parton announced in May that she was canceling a Las Vegas show and had been undergoing treatment for kidney stones for several years.

"Lord, they dig more stones out of me a year than the rock quarry in Rockwood, Tennessee," Parton said in a statement. "But seriously, my immune system and my digestive system got all out of whack over the past couple three years, and they’re working real hard on rebuilding and strengthening those, and hopefully, I’ll be up to snuff again soon."

On Friday, Parton acknowledged she had lost a step after her husband Carl Dean died in March 2025. But she insisted she wasn’t ready to leave the stage.

“Even though I’m still healin,’” Parton told People. “I’m still workin’! You know me — as I’ve often said — I’ve dreamed myself into a corner, and I still have so many things I want to achieve, so I’m gonna keep on working as long as I can to see everything come to life.”

During her more than 60-year career, Parton sold over 100 million records and won 11 Grammy Awards, making her one of the bestselling musical performers of all time.

Parton also became a star on the silver screen, gaining a whole new audience and critical acclaim when she brought her Southern charm to movies like “9 to 5” (she wrote and sang the theme song), “Steel Magnolias” and "The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas."

Bedecked in blonde bouffant hairdos and never without her makeup, Parton also became one of the nation’s best-known brands who parried questions about her hourglass figure and augmented breasts with her signature self-deprecating wit.

“It costs a lot of money to look this cheap,” Parton once said.

Colin Higgins, Jane Fonda, Lily Tomlin, and Dolly Parton on the set of the film "9 to 5" in 1979. Steve Schapiro / Corbis via Getty Images file

Parton was a shrewd businesswoman who amassed an estimated $650 million fortune and maintained creative control in the cutthroat and male-dominated music industry. She presided over an entertainment empire that included the Dollywood theme park. And she was a devoted philanthropist who launched the Dollywood Foundation to provide poverty relief and fund educational programs in her native East Tennessee.

Never shy at expressing her Christian faith, Parton was also a public supporter of the LGBTQ community who advocated for marriage equality and spoke up in defense of transgender people.

“I keep saying: If you’re the fine Christian that you think you are, why are you judging people,” Parton said during a 2017 interview with Larry King. “That’s God’s job.”

Along those lines, she jokingly told a British outlet a few years earlier: “I think gay couples should be allowed to marry. They should suffer just like us heterosexuals.”

Through it all Parton leaned on the love of her life, her husband Carl, who died at 82 and who, from the moment they married in 1966, happily ceded the spotlight to his world-famous wife.

Dolly Parton in a rare photo with her husband, Carl Thomas Dean. dollyparton.com

“Words can’t do justice to the love we shared for over 60 years,” Parton said in July 2025.

Born Jan. 19, 1946, in a one-room cabin on the banks of the Little Pigeon River near the town of Sevierville, Parton was the fourth of 12 children.

Her father, Robert Lee Parton, could not read or write and often supplemented the family's meager income from their farm by working construction jobs.

Her mother, Avie Lee Parton, ran the household and was fond of singing traditional Appalachian ballads. The future superstar said it was her mother who instilled in her a love for music.

Parton had an affinity for music from a young age. Michael Ochs Archives / Getty Images file

And it was at church that Parton started performing. By age 13, she was singing on local radio and television shows and made her debut at the Grand Ole Opry, where she met Johnny Cash.

“Dolly Parton has one of the most distinctive voices in American pop music,” Katherine Dacey, a professor at the Berklee College of Music, told NBC News before Parton’s death. “Her high soprano voice gets its distinctive character from her fast vibrato and vocal twang.”

The day after she graduated from Sevier County High School in 1964, Parton headed to Nashville, where she first made her mark writing songs for other performers, some of them with her uncle Bill Owens.

In songs like “Tennessee Homesick Blues” and “Coat of Many Colors,” Parton drew inspiration from her hardscrabble childhood.

Parton performs in 1976. David Redfern / Getty Images file

Three years after leaving school, Parton released her first record, “Hello, I'm Dolly,” and caught the attention of country star Porter Wagoner and became a regular on his shows.

Then, in 1974, Parton broke out on her own when she topped the country charts for the first time with a song she wrote and performed called “Jolene.” She later revealed it was inspired by a bank teller who flirted with her husband when they were newlyweds.

Her next four singles were also country chart toppers and one of them, “I Will Always Love You,” later became a huge hit for Whitney Houston in 1992.

Parton also won her first Grammy with a single from that record called “Here You Come Again.”

Parton performs in 1995. Ron Davis / Getty Images file

Parton, who earned a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 1984, made several more movies and performed around the world, but she always returned to the music that first made her famous — and to the hollers of East Tennessee where she was born and where she and her husband made their home.

“Never ignore your roots — your home or your hair,” she once said.

In 1986, Parton opened the Dollywood theme park in the Great Smoky Mountains near her hometown. The 165 acres include roller coasters, a bald eagle sanctuary and music and crafts that pay tribute to the region's Appalachian heritage.

Parton at Dollywood in Pigeon Forge, Tenn., in 1988. Ron Davis / Getty Images file

Parton and her husband never had children. And in public statements, Parton said she “believed that God didn’t mean for me to have kids.”

“Since I had no kids, and my husband was pretty independent, I had freedom,” Parton told Oprah Winfrey in 2020. “So I think a big part of my whole success is the fact that I was free to work.”

Parton also left her fans guessing about her politics, although in 2016 she angered many Republicans by saying that Hillary Clinton was “very qualified” to be president.

In an online post, Parton insisted she was not endorsing Clinton or Clinton's then-rival, Donald Trump.

“I try not to get political but if I am, I might as well just run myself ‘cause I’ve got the hair for it, it’s huge, and they could always use more boobs in the race,” she wrote.

While she generally dodged commenting on partisan politics, Parton was hailed in 2020 for helping to fund research at Vanderbilt University that led to the development of Moderna's Covid vaccine.

“My longtime friend Dr. Naji Abumrad, who’s been involved in research at Vanderbilt for many years, informed me that they were making some exciting advancements towards research of the coronavirus for a cure,” Parton tweeted in April 2020, as much of the nation was under lockdown. She added that she would be donating $1 million to the research.

Abumrad, who treated Parton when she was in a car accident in 2013, became friends with the country star afterward.

“Without a doubt in my mind, her funding made the research toward the vaccine go 10 times faster than it would be without it,” he told The Washington Post in November 2020.

Parton's philanthropic legacy also includes the creation of the Imagination Library, which mails free books to children around the world. In the three decades since it was founded, the organization has mailed more than 300 million books to kids around the U.S., as well as Canada, Australia, the United Kingdom and the Republic of Ireland.

Parton receiving a Kennedy Center Honor in 2006. Manuel Balce Ceneta / AP file

The initiative was inspired by Parton’s father, who was illiterate. Parton often spoke about his intelligence and strength of character but said she believed his inability to read and write held him back.

“When I got this idea to do the Imagination Library, I wanted to get Daddy involved in it. I wanted him to help me with that so he could take the pride in that and so he did,” she wrote on her website in 2020. “He got to live long enough to hear the kids call me the Book Lady.”

World.title: Abdul El-Sayed pushes back in Fox News interview: ‘Not here to fight a culture war’
World.content:
Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan, tangled with Fox News host Jesse Watters in an interview Monday, repeatedly pivoting from “culture war” questions to refocus on affordability in his state.

“You want to bring up all this culture war,” El-Sayed told Watters during the 25-minute interview. “I’m not here to fight a culture war. I’m here to fight the affordability crisis that people are facing.”

Watters pressed the nominee on several hot-button topics in the combative but largely jovial interview, including whether he supports abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), Sharia law, gender reassignment surgery, and whether “men should play women’s sports.”

On the ICE question, El-Sayed painted the department as brutal and ineffective.

“You and I both know that we’ve, long before we ever had ICE, we had INS,” he said, referring to the agency that predate ICE, the U.S. Immigration and Naturalization Service. “We were able to enforce our immigration policies without shooting people in the face and the back of the head. The INS worked a lot better.”

El-Sayed added immigration isn’t at the top of Michiganders’ minds.

“When I travel the state, and I have traveled my state, more people are asking me about how they’re going to afford their gas and groceries. They’re not asking me about immigration,” he said.

Asked about electric cars, the candidate said the “bigger question” is “why the president just started a trade war or escalated a trade war with Canada. It’s about to make all of our cars, especially the internal combustion engine cars, so much more expensive.”

E-Sayed used that same question to advocate for hiking taxes on people making over $100 million. “Do you want to drive on good roads, or would you rather have a billionaire make a second billion? That’s what Mike Rogers wants,” he said, referring to his Republican opponent. “That’s what Donald Trump wants. Apparently, that’s what you want. I think the people in Michigan want something different. They want good roads and good schools.”

“I just think I have the right to the fruits of my own labor,” Watters responded.

El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim senator if elected in November, took a more libertarian tack when pushed on religious laws for Muslims and transgender issues.

“So, canon law is the name for Christian law,” he said. “I don’t begrudge you your right to practice your faith as you choose. I don’t know why the idea that I could practice my faith as I choose is a problem. Nobody is trying to push Sharia law on anyone else. Just like I hope, nobody is trying to push canon law on anybody else, because we live in an America where you should have the freedom of your religion.”

“The issue that people are worried about is not that somehow somebody’s going to come and push Sharia law on them,” he continued. “The issue in Michigan is people are worried about how they’re going to afford their gas. The issue in Michigan is how am I going to see a doctor when I get sick? How am I going to keep my job?”

After a brief exchange on whether El-Sayed thinks the National Football League is racist, prompting him to simply complain about high ticket prices, Watters then asked, “Sex changes for minors, do you support that?”

“I just think the government shouldn’t tell you what kind of health care you should have,” El-Sayed answered.

When the news anchor asked if the candidate thinks “it’s OK for a parent to slash his kid’s ding-a-ling off,” he responded, “Do you really want to have this conversation? Are you circumcised?”

Watters answered in the affirmative and called it a “personal question.”

“It’s a problem that you think that you get to decide what happens between a parent, a doctor and a patient,” El-Sayed said. “I’m just saying that yes, circumcision is surgery on a kid’s ding-a-ling. So if you really want to bring that up, you can. I just think you guys are really selective about these things.”

Watters called the response “wacky” and “sick stuff.”

On whether men should “play women’s sports,” El-Sayed said he thinks that also is not an issue for the government.

“At the end of the day, the decision of who gets to play what sports ought to be decided by the people who govern sports,” he responded. “I’m running for U.S. Senate, Jesse. It’s insane. I’m out here trying to take on like the the health care crisis and big pharma, and you’re asking me about who gets to play what sports.”

Watters wrapped up the interview by thanking El-Sayed for coming on and saying he’d be invited back.

“You seem a little naive, Abdul. I give you credit for facing the music, but some of the stuff’s just straight up wacky,” Watters said. “You know, I don’t know if that’s going to fly in Michigan.”

World.title: Dolly Parton remembered by fellow stars, politicans: "A true loss for millions"
World.content:
Following Dolly Parton's death, fellow celebrities and politicians, including President Trump, mourned the country music legend and praised her as an icon whose legacy will never be forgotten.

Mr. Trump said in a social media post on Tuesday, "There has never been anyone like her, and never will," announcing that he would be "lowering the American flag" throughout the United States for one week in Parton's honor.

"This is a true loss for millions of people," the president wrote. "Rest in Peace, Dolly! The World loves you."

The flag lowering will begin at 6 p.m. Tuesday, Mr. Trump said.

Politicians mourn the loss of Dolly Parton

Condolences and remembrances for Parton poured in after her nephew, Bryan Seaver, who was his aunt's head of security, announced her death in a prerecorded video posted to social media.

"It is an honor, an honor that is mixed with absolute pride and great sadness, but sadness lies with us, not with Dolly," Seaver said. "Dolly has lived in the light and is in the arms of Jesus."

Both senators from Tennessee, where Parton was born on Jan. 19, 1946, reacted on social media and called her death a great loss to the state.

"Tennessee has lost one of its greatest legends- a woman who never lost sight of her faith, her roots, or the Volunteer Spirit. [Dolly Parton] was a true Tennessee treasure, and her legacy will forever be defined by her love of faith, family, and the place she proudly called home," Republican Sen. Bill Hagerty said.

Sen. Marsha Blackburn posted a photo of her and Parton together, writing, "There are no words to adequately express the sorrow our family and indeed, all Tennesseans, feel in the loss of Dolly Parton. An iconic leader who loved our great state and nation. Her passing leaves a void that no one can ever fill. Dolly, we will always love you."

Sen. Bernie Sanders, an independent from Vermont, highlighted Parton's accomplishments outside her music career as a philanthropist who advocated for a variety of causes.

"She was not only a talented musician & songwriter, but a lifelong philanthropist and advocate for literacy, education, LGBTQ+ rights, healthcare and disaster relief," Sanders said. "Her music and humanity touched millions. She will be sorely missed."

Country stars remember Dolly Parton

Fellow country music legend Reba McEntire, who was friends with Parton, reacted in a social media post, thanking Parton for "all the wonderful things you did for us here on earth."

"Your love, your music and you gave so much with your huge huge heart. There will never ever be another you. We will remember and cherish every memory and every note you ever played and sang," she said. "Thank you, Lord, for Dolly. She's gonna have a blast in heaven singing all her favorite songs with all her family and friends who have gone on before her. I'll never forget the first time I met you and I'll never forget our last conversation. I hold it with love in my heart. I will always love you, Reba."

Country music star Kacey Musgraves fired off several X posts in reaction to Parton's passing on Tuesday.

"The world feels a lot less sparkly all of a sudden," Musgraves said. "So glad she's with her Carl Dean. No one talk to me today."

Parton was preceded in death by her husband of 60 years, Carl Dean, who died in March 2025 at the age of 82.

The couple met in 1964, when they ran into each other outside the Wishy Washy Laundromat on the first day Parton had moved to Nashville. He swept her off her feet, as Parton later described it, and the couple married two years later.

"Carl and I spent many wonderful years together. Words can't do justice to the love we shared for over 60 years," Parton said at the time of his death.

World.title: Prosecutors in Lindsay Clancy trial call final witness
World.content:
Testimony in Lindsay Clancy's Massachusetts murder trial neared its end Tuesday afternoon as prosecutors called final rebuttal witness Dr. Gregory Saathoff, a professor of emergency medicine and forensic psychiatrist who has worked with the FBI.

Saathoff's testimony focused on the voice Clancy reported hearing in her head on Jan. 24, 2023, the night she killed her three children.

Once his testimony is finished, both sides will discuss the next steps in the trial. Closing arguments are expected to happen Thursday.

Dr. Kirk Heilbrun, a forensic psychologist for the prosecution, was first on the stand a day after his testimony was cut short when he started talking about Clancy's Catholic religion. Defense attorney Kevin Reddington called for a mistrial. Plymouth Superior Court Judge William Sullivan denied it, but he reprimanded the prosecution for the testimony.

Reddington cross-examined Heilbrun Tuesday after the psychologist said it's his opinion that Clancy was criminally responsible for murdering her three children.

Forensic psychologist Dr. Kirk Heilbrun in Plymouth Superior Court on Aug. 25, 2026. Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger/Pool

Dr. Gregory Saathoff

Saathoff interviewed Clancy in May and June of this year and talked to her about the voice she heard that she said told her to kill the children.

"She said it was a man's voice, it was very clear, it was external," Saathoff said. "In other words, it came from outside her head."

He said that according to Clancy, the voice repeated, "This is your last chance, you have to kill your kids and then you have to kill yourself."

Clancy said the voice stopped when she finished strangling the children, Saathoff testified.

According to Saathoff, Lindsay Clancy said the voice started on the evening of the murders, just after Patrick Clancy left the house. He said it would be unusual for someone in psychosis to hear a voice only one time and act on it. He noted that Clancy told another doctor that the voice had started much earlier.

Saathoff also said he asked her about sending Patrick Clancy out to pick up takeout food. He said records show she did "a lot of searching" before talking to him about how far the restaurant was from the home.

Saathoff said it was notable that Lindsay Clancy added another errand for Patrick - picking up medication for Cora at CVS.

"It lengthened the trip," he said. "It added one extra obligation for Patrick and that would make for a longer time that he was away."

Heilbrun cross-examination

Reddington started his testimony by getting Heilbrun to agree that it would have been better to interview Clancy sooner rather than three years after the murders. He read through the psychologist's lengthy resume but noted that he had never written about postpartum psychosis.

Reddington asked if he would agree that Clancy was incredible at taking care of her kids.

"I would describe her as a very good mother," Heilbrun said.

Reddington asked if Clancy was a "happy woman" before being prescribed medication from her psychiatrist Jennifer Tufts.

"In September, she was anxious about returning to work," Heilburn said. "She had not yet started taking the medications that Dr. Tufts had prescribed, though."

Reddington and Heilburn went back-and-forth about why Clancy was not admitted to a program at a Rhode Island hospital for postpartum mothers. Reddington said it was because the hospital said she was overmedicated, while Heilburn said it wasn't clear that her struggles were related to being postpartum.

"Did you really read those records?" Reddington asked.

"Yes I did," Heilburn said.

Reddington put his hands on Clancy's shoulders as he talked about her struggle to find the right support.

"Are you trying to tell the jury that she was avoiding help?" Reddington asked.

He also asked Heilburn about Patrick Clancy's testimony that Lindsay said she tried to kill herself when he found her on the ground.

"If I suggest to you, sir, that if you listen to the 911 tape as it relates to Clancy interacting with her, that she could only make grunting noises, would you be surprised at that?"

"I would be surprised, yes," Heilburn said.

During re-direct questioning, prosecutor Jennifer Sprague asked if it was accurate that Clancy never told any doctors that she had thoughts of harming her children.

"That is my recollection, that she did not share that information with any medical providers," Heilburn said.

Heilbrun also told Sprague that someone experiencing psychosis with command hallucinations can still know the difference between right and wrong.

Dr. Kirk Heilbrun testimony

Continuing his testimony on Tuesday, Heilbrun said Clancy told him there was no decision-making involved in the murders and that she was just responding to a voice. But he said, "there's many ongoing decisions that have to be made to accomplish a killing like this in 18 to 20 minutes," such as the location and what to say to the children.

He said in his clinical opinion, Clancy is criminally responsible for killing her children.

"She retained an awareness of the illegality of killing others, including killing her children," Heilbrun said. "Her moral awareness of the wrongfulness of the killing was influenced by her strong desire to die and if she were dead, not to leave her children behind."

Reddington says judge made "good effort" with jury instruction

Speaking to reporters outside court Tuesday morning, Reddington says he believes Judge Sullivan made a "good effort" in telling the jury to disregard the religious testimony. Sullivan told jurors that Heilbrun's remarks about Clancy's Catholic faith were "immaterial, irrelevant and to be disregarded" before sending them home for the day.

"The judge made his ruling and instructed the jury," Reddington said. "I think it's pretty apparent these jurors are dedicated, they'll listen to his instruction and i have no doubt that we'll finish the case out today."

Reddington also lashed out at a commentator asking him a question outside court, calling him a "biased weasel."

Lindsay Clancy trial

Clancy, 36, has pleaded not guilty to charges of first-degree murder in the deaths of her three children - 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan - in their Duxbury, Massachusetts home on Jan. 24, 2023. She has admitted to the killings, but her attorney said she should not be held criminally responsible because she was overmedicated and suffering from postpartum psychosis.

Prosecutors said Clancy planned the murders. If she's convicted of first-degree murder she faces life in prison without parole. If the jury determines Clancy was not criminally responsible, she will be sent to a state psychiatric hospital in Massachusetts.

Lindsay Clancy in Plymouth Superior Court on Tuesday, August 25, 2026. Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger/Pool

If you or someone you know is in emotional distress or a suicidal crisis, you can reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting 988. You can also chat with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline here.

For more information about mental healthcare resources and support, the National Alliance on Mental Illness HelpLine can be reached Monday through Friday, 10 a.m. to 10 p.m. ET, at 1-800-950-NAMI (6264) or email info@nami.org.

World.title: Will mortgage interest rates improve this September? 3 things to consider now
World.content:
Mortgage interest rates can easily change this September, depending on how three primary items evolve in the month. sakchai vongsasiripat/Getty Images

Following a month in which inflation improved but there was no Federal Reserve meeting in which to capitalize on the news, many borrowers find themselves looking forward to September and some potential positive movement again. With an inflation report scheduled for release on September 11, a Federal Reserve meeting the week after, not to mention unemployment numbers released earlier in the month – all of which have the potential to impact the rate climate – borrowers can easily find themselves in a markedly different position one month from now.

That's especially important for homebuyers and owners hoping to refinance.

After rates improved by more than a full percentage point in 2025, much of that decline was reversed in 2026 and, in recent months, mortgage purchase and refinance rates have remained stubbornly unchanged. This has left borrowers with limited ways to secure an affordable rate and it's left many on the sidelines urgently hoping for some change that could actually improve the mortgage interest rate climate in a positive way. But is that likely to happen this September, or can borrowers expect more of the same? With mortgage rates known to change daily, it helps to keep a few items under consideration for the weeks ahead. Below, we'll break down three specific ones that borrowers should contemplate now as they look to secure an affordable deal.

Start by seeing which mortgage interest rate you currently qualify for here.

Will mortgage interest rates improve in September? 3 things to consider now

Projecting future mortgage rate movement is inherently difficult to do with precision, as any number of factors – both known and unknown – have the potential to drive rates in either direction. But with rates changing daily based on market conditions, it helps to keep the following three items in mind now, even if it only results in a temporary opening in which to lock in a below-average purchase or refinance rate:

Geopolitical tensions and overseas conflicts

It was only March 2 when the average mortgage rate on a 30-year term was just 5.75%, almost a full percentage point below what most buyers are being offered right now. However, rates didn't spike in recent months based on any Fed action or lack thereof. They rose in large part on the back of geopolitical tensions, overseas conflicts and the war with Iran, leading to a spike in oil prices and inflation.

In other words, if one or more of those items improves in September, then it's not unfathomable that the wider interest rate climate will cool, too, and that could lead to a reduction in mortgage interest rates. While that reduction may be minimal and it could even be temporary, any relief here will be welcomed for borrowers. Monitor the news cycle closely, then, for an opportunity to lock in a below-average rate if and when it presents itself in the month.

Learn more about your current mortgage rate options online today.

Further reductions in the inflation rate

The Bureau of Labor Statistics will release its next inflation reading, this time for August, on Friday, September 11. If it shows another reduction as the July report did, it could serve as motivation for the Federal Reserve to cut rates later in the month. Remember, too, that lenders don't need to wait for the Fed to adjust their offers to borrowers.

So if this report is a positive one, don't be surprised to see improved rate offers in the days that follow. Just be ready to act if this scenario actually occurs. And make sure to improve your credit score and overall appeal as a borrower now, in case it does.

The Federal Reserve meeting later in the month

The central bank will meet again on September 15 and September 16, and it will do so with new unemployment and inflation numbers to interpret and, potentially, changes to the geopolitical environment. Even though an actual rate cut in the meeting currently seems unlikely, any positive comments made by officials here still have the potential to move mortgage rates in a more affordable direction.

That said, the opposite can also happen, so borrowers will need to be careful to avoid being overly dependent on Fed movements. Instead, consider the advantages of a mortgage rate lock now. You can always unlock and re-lock a lower one should it materialize post-meeting, but if it doesn't, you'll be protected from any additional upward pressures, too.

The bottom line

Mortgage interest rates certainly have the potential to change this September after remaining high and largely stuck for much of the summer. Which direction they move in, however, will largely depend on any resolution to overseas conflicts and geopolitical tensions, the fight toward reducing the inflation rate and, ultimately, the Federal Reserve. Don't discount the 10-year Treasury yield, too, which is also known to be a big driver behind mortgage rates in both directions. In the interim, however, it can be worth considering the pros and cons of a mortgage rate lock while also doing all you can to boost your credit score, that way you're positioned to actually secure an affordable rate when it inevitably presents itself again.

World.title: What does an employer need to post a job online?
World.content:
We may receive commissions from some links to products on this page. Promotions are subject to availability and retailer terms.

Posting a job online doesn't necessarily require an extensive set of documents or a confusing setup process. Sandwish/Getty Images

The process of hiring new employees used to be significantly more complicated than it is in today's landscape. Previously, employers had to decide where to physically advertise a job opening and then wait days or weeks for applications to arrive before sorting through the responses. The shift to online hiring that has occurred over the last couple of decades has dramatically shortened that process, though. An employer can now create a listing and start reaching potential candidates almost immediately, whether they're looking for someone locally or casting a much wider net.

But while hitting publish to push an online job  is a relatively simple task, there are still numerous tasks that need to be checked off the list before the job listing goes live. Employers still have to determine exactly what they're hiring for, decide what they're willing to pay for the role and confirm how applicants will be evaluated during the hiring process. And as more states and cities adopt rules governing pay transparency and hiring practices, the information that's included — or left out — of a job posting matters even more than it once did.

That can leave new business owners, small employers and even experienced hiring managers with a deceptively simple question: What do you actually need to post a job online? While the specifics can vary depending on the hiring platform, the position and where the job is located, there are several important pieces to have in place before you accept any applications.

What does an employer need to post a job online?

What employers need to post a job online will depend partly on the website they're using and partly on applicable federal, state and local employment laws. In general, though, employers should be prepared with the following information:

Basic information about the employer

Most online job boards require employers to create an account before publishing a listing. That generally means providing basic information such as the employer's name, contact details and, depending on the platform, information that can be used to verify the business.

Verification can be particularly important because fraudulent job listings have become a concern for applicants and job platforms alike. An employer may therefore be asked to verify an email address, company website or other business information before a listing is approved.

Employers should also decide how much company information to include in the  itself. A short description of the business, its industry and what it does can give applicants useful context and help distinguish a legitimate opportunity from a vague listing.

A clear description of the position

Employers should also have the basic parameters of the job established before creating the listing. That typically includes the job title, responsibilities, location and whether the position is full-time, part-time, temporary, contract, hybrid or remote. After all, nearly 50% of job seekers say they would feel more seen by employers if job descriptions had more detail, according to ZipRecruiter research, allowing them to narrow down the jobs aligned with their skills and interests.

The listing should spell out the qualifications that actually matter for the role, such as required licenses, education, experience or technical skills. Employers should be careful about unnecessary requirements, though, as even seemingly neutral hiring practices can create legal problems when they disproportionately exclude protected groups and aren't job-related or necessary for the business.

Clear requirements can also make the hiring process more efficient. If applicants know upfront that a position requires weekend work, frequent travel or a specific certification, for example, they're better equipped to determine whether applying makes sense.

Compensation and benefits information

Employers should determine the pay range and benefits for the position before posting the job online, even if their jurisdiction doesn't require that information to appear in the . That's because pay transparency laws have expanded across the country, and the exact rules vary. Depending on where the employer or position is located, a listing may need to disclose a salary or hourly wage range, benefits or other compensation information.

The state of Colorado, for example, requires covered job postings to include compensation, benefits and an application deadline. Other jurisdictions have their own requirements, so employers posting jobs across multiple states — particularly for remote positions — should check the rules that apply before publishing a listing rather than assuming one version will comply everywhere.

A legally compliant job 

The wording of the  matters, too. Federal law prohibits covered employers from publishing job s that indicate a preference based on protected characteristics such as race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, genetic information or, for workers 40 and older, age. That means seemingly harmless phrases can create issues. For example, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) specifically warns that language seeking "recent college graduates" could discourage older applicants.

State and local laws may impose additional restrictions. Employers may also face rules governing what they can ask applicants about salary history, criminal records or age-related information. In certain states, for example, employers generally cannot request dates of birth, graduation dates or school attendance dates on an initial application, though there are limited exceptions.

An application process and contact point

Employers also need a way to receive and manage applications. A job board like ZipRecruiter may allow candidates to apply directly through its platform, while other listings send applicants to the employer's website or applicant-tracking system.

Whichever method is used, the instructions should make the next step obvious. Employers may want to specify which materials are required, such as a resume, application or portfolio, and establish who will review submissions.

The application process should also account for accessibility. Under federal law, covered employers generally must provide reasonable accommodations that allow qualified applicants with disabilities to participate in the application process unless doing so would impose an undue hardship.

The bottom line

Posting a job online doesn't necessarily require an extensive set of documents or complicated setup process, but employers should do more than write a few sentences about the job opening and then publish them. A strong listing starts with accurate company information, a well-defined role, realistic qualifications, compensation details and a clear way for candidates to apply.

Employers should also check the employment laws that apply where they're hiring before the listing goes live. Pay transparency and hiring rules can differ significantly by location, and an  that's compliant in one state may need additional information in another. Taking the time to get those details right can reduce compliance risks while giving applicants the information they need to decide whether the opportunity is worth pursuing.

World.title: What are the lowest private student loan rates you can get right now?
World.content:
We may receive commissions from some links to products on this page. Promotions are subject to availability and retailer terms.

Private student loan rates are low overall right now, but those rock-bottom rate offers aren't realistic for every borrower. Nirat/Getty Images

Paying for college has changed substantially for borrowers over the last few years — and some big changes went into effect recently. Last month, new federal student loan rules took effect, reshaping how students and families can borrow for higher education. And for those who still have a funding gap after scholarships, grants and federal aid, private student loans may be one of the remaining ways to cover it.

But borrowing privately can come with a wide range of costs. Unlike federal student loans, which generally carry standardized rates for each loan type, private student loan rates are based heavily on both the interest rate environment and the applicant's financial profile. As a result, two students borrowing the same amount for the same school could receive offers with dramatically different interest rates.

That makes the rate-shopping process important before committing to a private student loan. So, what are the lowest private student loan rates available now, and what could it take to qualify? That's what we'll examine below.

Compare your top private student loan options online now.

What are the lowest private student loan rates you can get right now?

Right now, the lowest advertised private student loan rates are starting at just under 2% APR, according to student loan rate data from Money.com. And, several of the most competitive options have starting fixed rates below 2.5%, putting the low end of today's private student loan market in roughly the 2% range.

That doesn't mean all student loan borrowers will qualify for a rate that low, though. The advertised rate ranges are wide, with fixed APRs on the same loans reaching roughly 16% to 18% at the upper end of the scale. In other words, the private student loan rate you're offered could look very different from the lowest rate used to advertise the loan.

That's because private student loan rates are generally determined by factors such as your credit history, income, debt obligations and overall financial profile. And many college students have limited credit histories or earnings, which can make it difficult to qualify for the lowest rates on their own.

The terms attached to the lowest student loan rates also matter. Some lenders factor automatic payment discounts or other discounts into their advertised minimum APRs, for example, while the repayment term you select and whether you make payments while enrolled can also affect your borrowing costs. As a result, a private student loan advertising a rate near 2% doesn't necessarily mean you'll receive that rate under the repayment structure you want.

That's why it generally makes sense to compare the actual student loan rates you're offered rather than choosing a private student loan based solely on its advertised minimum. Many lenders allow you to prequalify without a hard credit inquiry, so checking several offers can provide a more realistic picture of what you'll pay and help you identify the lowest rate available based on your financial profile.

Find out how affordable the right private student loan could be today.

How can you qualify for a lower private student loan rate?

Because private student loans are credit-based, there are several steps you can take to improve your chances of receiving an offer near the lower end of a lender's rate range.

One of the most important is applying with a creditworthy cosigner. Many undergraduate students haven't had enough time to build the credit and income history necessary to qualify for the best private student loan rates independently, but adding a parent or another qualified cosigner can strengthen the application and potentially reduce the rate. Some lenders also allow borrowers to apply to release the cosigner after making a certain number of qualifying payments.

It also pays to compare several student loan lenders rather than accepting the first offer. While the difference between a 3% rate and a 7% rate may not seem enormous when you're initially borrowing, it can translate into thousands of dollars in additional interest over a lengthy repayment period. And, since each lender uses its own underwriting criteria, shopping around can uncover substantially different offers for the same borrower.

You should also compare fixed and variable student loan rates carefully. A variable-rate student loan may occasionally offer a lower initial borrowing cost, but the rate can change over time based on its underlying benchmark. A fixed-rate student loan provides more predictability because your rate won't fluctuate with market conditions.

It also makes sense to look beyond the headline APR while comparing your options. Autopay discounts, repayment terms, in-school payment requirements, fees, hardship programs and cosigner-release policies can all affect the overall value of a loan. In turn, a slightly higher rate with better borrower protections could ultimately be a better fit than the absolute lowest rate available.

The bottom line

Private student loan rates are starting below 2% with some lenders right now, but those rock-bottom offers aren't necessarily realistic for every borrower. Your credit profile, income, cosigner, repayment term and available discounts can all determine what you actually pay.

So, if private student loan borrowing is necessary after exhausting scholarships, grants and federal loan options, compare offers from several lenders based on the rates you personally qualify for. The lowest advertised rate may catch your attention, but the lowest qualified rate — combined with repayment terms you can comfortably manage — is what ultimately matters.

World.title: Dolly Parton, country music legend, dies at age 80
World.content:
Dolly Parton, one of the most groundbreaking and successful musicians in the history of country music, with a hitmaking career that spanned six decades and launched her into TV and movie stardom, has died, her family announced Tuesday. She was 80.

Parton's nephew Bryan Seaver, who was his aunt's head of security, announced her death in a prerecorded video posted to social media.

"It is an honor, an honor that is mixed with absolute pride and great sadness, but sadness lies with us, not with Dolly," he said. "Dolly has lived in the light and is in the arms of Jesus."

Dolly Parton had health issues leading up to her death

Seaver's video didn't include details about Parton's death. Last October, Parton's sister Freida Parton sparked concerns about the star's health when she took to social media asking for prayers for her sister. Parton later assured fans by saying that she wasn't sick and was OK.

But in May, Parton told fans in a social media video that she was responding well to treatment she was receiving, saying she's long had issues with kidney stones and her immune system and digestive system "got all out of whack" over the past few years. She also said she wasn't up to "stage performance level" and had to cancel upcoming performances in Las Vegas.

Reactions pour in to Dolly Parton's death

Reactions poured in as news spread about Parton's death.

At the White House, President Trump called her death "a true loss for millions of people" and ordered the American flag lowered across the country starting Tuesday evening.

"There has never been anyone like her, and never will," Mr. Trump said.

In Los Angeles, Parton was remembered as a "once-in-a-lifetime talent" by the Hollywood Chamber of Commerce, which planned to place flowers on her star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame later in the day.

Dolly Parton won 10 Grammys over decades-long career

Since breaking onto the country music scene with her 1967 debut "Hello, I'm Dolly," Parton never seemed to slow down, releasing nearly 50 studio albums and selling over 100 million records.

A prolific songwriter, she won 10 Grammys and earned 55 nominations.

Dolly Parton arrives for the Academy of Country Music Awards on May 11, 2023, in Frisco, Texas. Omar Vega/FilmMagic

But she treated her success with a certain modesty. In 2022, when she was nominated for the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame, she tried to pull herself out of the running, saying she didn't feel that she had "earned that right." Her peers and fans vehemently disagreed.

In a 2022 interview on "CBS Mornings," she called it "an honor" to have so many loyal fans, but added that "it scares me to death sometimes. I'm always sayin' I'm not all that, I'm even not all there sometimes."

Born on Jan. 19, 1946, Parton grew up in poverty in rural Tennessee, the fourth of 12 children.

"Well, what they call 'white trash,' I don't like anybody else calling me that, but to be called a hillbilly, I always take pride in that," she told CBS News in a 2016 interview.

She began songwriting at a young age and got her break in 1966 when she moved to Nashville and was given a spot on country singer Porter Wagoner's variety show, which she kept for seven years.

She explained that she honed her distinctive look and style from a woman she knew who she described as a "town tramp" — upending expectations of how she should look and dress.

"And she wore the makeup, red nails, red high heels, tight clothes," Parton told CBS News. "I just thought she was the prettiest thing I'd ever seen. And people say, 'Oh, she ain't nothing but trash.' But in my mind, I thought, 'That's what I'm going to be when I grow up.'"

Her first No. 1 country hit came in 1970 with "Joshua," but it was 1973's "Jolene" that made her a household name.

She said the song came about after meeting a young fan one night after a performance.

"I remember this little redheaded girl with green eyes, prettiest little thing, and I said, 'Well, what's your name?' And she said, 'Jolene.' I said, 'I love that name.' All the way back to the bus I was [singing], 'Jolene, Jolene, Jolene,' so I wouldn't forget the name," Parton told CBS News in 2019.

After a string of successful albums in the 1970s, she set her sights on Hollywood, making her major film debut in the 1980 feminist comedy classic "9 to 5," alongside Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin, playing Doralee, a secretary who takes on her sexist boss. The movie was a huge hit and also earned Parton an Oscar nomination for the song of the same name.

Two years later, she starred in the film adaptation of the Broadway musical "The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas," which garnered her a Golden Globe nomination for best actress.

She went on to star alongside Sally Field, Julia Roberts and Shirley MacLaine in 1989's "Steel Magnolias."

Parton was renowned for her musical collaborations with the likes of Emmylou Harris, Linda Ronstadt, Loretta Lynn and Willie Nelson. In 1983, she recorded "Islands in the Stream" with Kenny Rogers, a song that had been penned by the Bee Gees. It went to No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 charts.

Dolly Parton performs on "The Tonight Show" on Nov. 30, 2018. Andrew Lipovsky/NBCU Photo Bank/NBCUniversal via Getty Images

She released "I Will Always Love You" in 1974, but it took on a second life when it was recorded by the late Whitney Houston for the 1992 film "The Bodyguard." Parton said it didn't bother her that many mistakenly assumed Houston wrote the song.

"I say, 'You got that right,'" Dolly told CBS News. "And other people they kind of say, 'No, that's Dolly Parton's song.' I said, 'Look, she can have the credit. I just want the cash.' And I made plenty of it all off of Whitney, thank God."

Her longevity in the music industry was staggering, setting a Guinness World Record for the longest span of No. 1 hits on the country charts for a female artist at 43 years, from 1977 to 2020.

Showing a keen business acumen, Parton in the mid-1980s bought a stake in a theme park in Knoxville, Tennessee, that was subsequently renamed Dollywood, and continues to draw hundreds of thousands of visitors annually. Parton would perform frequently at the park.

Over the years, she also became known for giving back. She launched her Dollywood Foundation in 1988 to help boost graduation rates in the community where she grew up. Her commitment to education continued when Dollywood announced in 2022 that it would pay full tuition and fees for any employee who chose to pursue higher education.

When the COVID-19 pandemic hit, Parton donated $1 million for medical research at Vanderbilt University that helped lead to the lifesaving Moderna vaccine.

"I'm just happy that anything I do can help somebody else," she said at the time. "When I donated money to the COVID fund, I just wanted it to do good and evidently, it is. Let's just hope we find a cure real soon."

Recognizing her long history of philanthropy, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and his partner, Lauren Sanchez, honored Parton in 2022 with a $100 million Courage and Civility award, with the money to be directed toward charities of her choice.

"When people are in a position to help, you should help. And I know that I've always said, 'I try to put my money where my heart is,' and I think you do the same thing," Parton said to Bezos when accepting to grant.

Dolly Parton's husband preceded her in death

Parton was preceded in death by her husband of nearly 60 years, Carl Dean, who died in March 2025 at the age of 82. The couple never had children, a conscious choice Parton told CBS News she didn't regret.

"It wasn't meant to be," she said. "And I don't regret it. I never regretted it. I mean, it was a choice. So, you make your choices, you make your sacrifices, and I never looked back. I knew early on that I was gonna walk that road till God told me to stop. And I'm still walking it, and he ain't said nothing to me about quittin' yet!"
