World.title: Schalke coach looks to Bosnia bond in Bundesliga return
World.content:
After three seasons in the second division, Schalke are back in the Bundesliga. Just a year ago, few would have guessed that their revival would largely be 'Made in Bosnia.'

"A year ago, I told my team that we need to step things up by two gears, and we did that," Schalke's second-year coach, Miron Muslic, told the club's website ahead of this season's return to the Bundesliga.

"Now we need to step things up by two gears all over again. At first glance it may sound like a threat, too dramatic, but this is what we will need to meet this challenge. The lads know this and we are confident that we have a higher gear in us."

The challenge for Muslic is not simply to avoid relegation in year one after three seasons in the second division, but to "establish ourselves in the Bundesliga."

It will also be Muslic's first season in the Bundesliga after he succeeded where several of his predecessors failed – guiding the Royal Blues back to the topflight.

'Where did this guy come from?'

It's something few would have predicted just over a year ago, when he was unveiled as Schalke's new head coach. Many, if not most, of the club's supporters will have been left scrolling on their phones to try to figure out just who he was. It's a point not lost on the Austrian coach, who fled the Bosnian War with his parents at the age of nine.

"Many were wondering; 'Who is this guy, where did he come from?'" Muslic, who joined from lower league English club Plymouth Argyle, told German football magazine "kicker" last October, after Schalke had climbed to the top of the standings for the first time in the campaign.

That's where they finished the first half of the season. But during the January transfer window, Muslic and sporting director Frank Baumann still weren't sure the squad had what it would take to guarantee a top-two finish – and automatic promotion – at the end of the campaign.

Proven goal scorer looking for playing time

Then the final piece to the promotion puzzle fell into Muslic's lap. Bosnia captain Edin Dzeko, a striker who has been prolific virtually everywhere he has played, was largely languishing on the bench at Italian club Fiorentina, and looking for playing time. He let it be known that he was prepared to take a major pay cut to help Schalke achieve promotion. By the time they'd done just that, he had contributed six goals to the cause – and just turned 40.

Many expected Dzeko to hang up his boots after he captained Bosnia in just their second appearance at the World Cup this past summer. However, a couple of weeks before the start of the season, Dzeko confirmed that he would make his return to the Bundesliga – 15 seasons after he last played in the league with Wolfsburg. After signing a one-year, bonus-heavy contract, Dzeko said that while he had "three other options" he made up his mind that if he was to continue playing, it would only be at Schalke.

Edin Dzeko captained Bosnia at this summer's World Cup in North America Image: Mutsu Kawamori/AFLOSPORT/IMAGO

Dzeko 'still hungry' at 40

"Winning promotion to the Bundesliga is one of the highlights of my career," Dzeko told the club's website.

"I'm still hungry. And I want to help our team in the Bundesliga, too."

Just how much action Dzeko will see in the Bundesliga is unclear. However, Muslic, who is understood to have pushed hard to bring his countryman back for another year, believes he can still be a difference maker in key situations.

Still, he isn't expected to see as much playing time as the third member of Schalke's Bosnian triumvirate, central defender Nikola Katic, whose winding road to Gelsenkirchen saw him work with Muslic a few years ago at Plymouth. Even before Dzeko arrived in Gelsenkirchen last winter, he and Katic already knew each other from the national team.

'Once Schalke, always Schalke,' but...

Now all three are committed to ensuring that Schalke's return to the Bundesliga is more than a one-season excursion, and Muslic, whose contract runs through the end of the 2027-28 season, hopes he will remain in charge for years to come.

"I will remain a member of Schalke 04 forever — 100 percent. No matter how our paths might part one day," the coach told "kicker" last October.



Nikola Katic has established himself as a stallwart in Schalke's central defense Image: Alex Gottschalk/DeFodi Images/IMAGO

At the same time, he's realistic enough to know that as a coach, he won't be in Gelsenkirchen forever. While his current focus is all about Schalke, he already knows where he would like to wind up somewhere down the road.

"I would like to be the national team coach of Bosnia-Herzegovina one day," he said.

"And I believe it will happen. The fundamental prerequisites are simply a perfect fit — my background, my connection, and the love for my home country."

For now though, the focus is on the new season; Schalke were left licking their wounds after fourth-tier Halle took them to extra time in their first-round German Cup match on Monday – before emerging with a 5-2 win. Dzeko, who had come on in the 64th minute expecting to play only half an hour, scored two of Schalke's goals.

Ever the optimist, Muslic said afterwards that the hard-fought result not only proved that "we'll need Edin" in the Bundesliga season, but that Schalke had also demonstrated their "resilience."

Next comes the first real test of whether Schalke can indeed kick it up a couple of gears, when they make their Bundsliga return in Augsburg on Sunday.

Edited by: Matt Pearson

World.title: How Germany's drone defense fails
World.content:
Drone defense is a priority for the German government. Several dramatic incidents involving explosive-laden drones at Leipzig airport show there are still substantial shortcomings.

On August 25, German media reported on a third drone allegedly found near Leipzig/Halle Airport in August. A drone and a substance — which initial assessments suggest could be around 50 grams of Hexogen, a highly explosive military-grade explosive — were reportedly discovered in a field outside the airport grounds. Consequently, public broadcasters NDR and WDR, and the daily broadsheet Süddeutsche Zeitung are speculating about a plot that may be far more extensive than what has been publicly disclosed so far.

Speaking on the sidelines of a federal government retreat in the state of Brandenburg, Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) stated: "Germany has increasingly come into the crosshairs of hybrid attackers."

Merz also pointed to measures aimed at better protecting the public. Just a few days ago, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt (CSU) inaugurated a drone security research center in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, not far from Leipzig and Halle in Saxony.

How could drones laden with explosives fly unhindered near or into Leipzig/Halle airport and remain unnoticed for at least several hours? Interior Minister Dobrindt had immediately spoken of a "hybrid attack scenario" which he suspected came from "foreign powers."

Suspicion has been directed at Russia, also because one drone was said to have been located near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane. The Federal Prosecutor's Office has taken over the investigation.

However, drone sightings over airports and ports, industrial sites and military properties have been increasing in Germany. In 2025, Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) recorded more than 1,000 suspicious drone flights.

Last October, drones disrupted air traffic in Munich for several hours, stranding numerous passengers. There is not sufficient drone protection at German airports, security expert Nico Lange warned.

"We do not possess the sensor networks and sensor beams needed to spot all types of drones, especially low-flying, slow drones," he told DW.

Leipzig drone threat prompts security concerns in Germany To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The European Association for Unmanned Aviation has also long pointed out weak points in Germany's drone defense.

"That a drone could apparently reach the airport tarmac and be discovered rather by chance, shows where the core of the problem is," said chairperson Gerald Wissel in relation to the latest incident.

The association suggests "the establishment of real-time monitoring of the lower airspace as well as the mandatory tracking of all airspace participants via ADS-L" — a radio communications system that makes drones in an airspace electronically visible.

Coordinated response difficult for state, federal police

Interior Minister Dobrindt wants to remedy this by setting up new institutions.

In December, he launched the Joint Counter Drone Center (GDAZ) in Berlin. There, information from the federal police, state police, secret service and armed forces is collated around the clock. But the incident at Leipzig airport shows that even a new hub is of little use if a dangerous drone at a large airport cannot be discovered and intercepted.

Drones move quickly, and any response must be decided within minutes. Doing so is made more difficult by Germany's system of divided responsibilities. If a suspicious drone takes off somewhere in the country, it's initially a matter for the state police. Germany has 16 police authorities, one for each of its 16 states. Only when the drone moves over a large airport or railway facility are the federal police allowed to step in.

Europe's defense: Latest drone technology shown in Berlin To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Unclear responsibilities

Security experts and opposition politicians in Germany's Bundestag federal parliament have called for clear regulation and consolidation of responsibilities.

"The muddle over responsibilities in drone defense is a substantial danger to our domestic security," said Irene Mihalic, lawmaker with the opposition Green Party and herself a former police officer.

Many, including the Greens, suggest the federal police should take the lead when it comes to drone defense. The federal police set up a new special unit for drone defense in December, and Dobrindt now wants to expand the unit following the incident at Leipzig airport.

Originally, 130 staff positions across four locations were planned. In the future, there will be 300 personnel across eight locations, to "be on site quickly and flexibly when needed," according to the Interior Ministry.

Who is allowed to shoot down a drone in Germany?

As so often happens following dramatic incidents, there have also been calls to deploy the Bundeswehr, Germany's armed forces, to take care of drone defense efforts at airports. However, current German law maintains that police are responsible for upholding security in the country.

A Defense Ministry spokesperson warned that protecting its own facilities, with their "tens of thousands of kilometers of fencing," is already a challenge for the Bundeswehr. Adding 24/7 protection of civilian infrastructure "would proclaim a false sense of security that we could never achieve," he added.

In an emergency, the police are allowed to ask the army for assistance. To achieve legal clarity in this regard, Germany amended its air security law in March. For the first time, it allows the Bundeswehr to shoot down drones outside their own premises to prevent "a particularly serious disaster."

German industry shifts to defense production amid job losses To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Airports, train stations still lack protection

There is also a lot of catching up to do when it comes to the technical equipment used to defend against drones.

"There were big announcements at airports about positioning drone defense systems. They are more like detection systems," Manuel Atug, a spokesperson for the independent Critical Infrastructure Working Group (Arbeitsgruppe Kritische Infrastruktur) told DW. "So far, they have not intercepted a single drone, and at some airports they have still not yet been put in place."

The German Police Union (GdP) has also lamented the lack of resources for drone defense. "Unsafe train stations, unsafe airports and a police force which has to beg for money, law changes and the latest defense technology are really disconcerting," criticized GdP federal chairman Jochen Kopelke.

An Interior Ministry spokesperson said large airports were steadily being equipped with drone defense technology. "The federal police have already procured a considerable amount of equipment. The eight large airports are prioritized: Frankfurt (Main), Munich, Berlin, Düsseldorf, Hamburg, Cologne/Bonn, Stuttgart and Leipzig/Halle," she said.

The plan is for all of these airports to be equipped with mobile drone defense technology by the end of the year.

This article was originally written in German. It was first published on August 14, 2026, and updated on August 25 to reflect news developments.

World.title: Guerra de versiones entre Marlaska y Robles sobre los informes que hizo el CNI para avanzar la crisis de Ceuta
World.content:
La titular de Defensa dice en el Congreso que los servicios de Inteligencia avisaron al Gobierno, pero el ministro de Interior cierra tajante: “No hubo ningún informe ni del CNI ni de ningún centro de un país amigo”

Guerra abierta de versiones sobre la crisis de Ceuta entre dos veteranos ministros de Pedro Sánchez que son jueces: el de Interior, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, y la de Defensa, Margarita Robles. Los dos vienen de una constante relación política difícil, muy conocida dentro del Gobierno. Y, en esta ocasión, el choque se ha producido en directo. Mientras desde el Congreso Robles insistía en que el Centro Nacional de Inteligencia (CNI) ―que según ha desvelado tiene 25 agentes en Ceuta― sí avisó de lo que estaba por llegar a la ciudad autónoma, Marlaska ha insistido desde la sala de prensa del Consejo de Ministros en que no hubo ningún informe, ni del CNI ni de nadie, que avisara de que algo tan gordo como 80.000 personas cruzando la frontera de golpe podía pasar.

01:31 Marlaska asegura que "no hubo ningún informe ni del CNI ni de ningún centro de un país amigo"

El choque entre la versión de Robles en el Congreso, donde además ha pedido perdón y ha dicho que el Gobierno llegó tarde, y la versión de otros tres ministros en La Moncloa, que han insistido en que se ha hecho todo lo posible y se va a hacer mucho más, pero han evitado la autocrítica, ha sido muy notable. Hace tiempo que la ministra va un poco por libre y no sigue la doctrina oficial del Ejecutivo. Fuentes al máximo nivel suelen decir cuando ella habla que la suya “no es la versión del Gobierno”, pero hasta ahora no se había visto tan claro un choque en directo sobre un asunto tan sensible como la responsabilidad por lo sucedido en Ceuta entre la titular de Defensa y el de Interior, dos ministerios de los llamados “de Estado” y claves en la gestión de la protección de las fronteras.

Más información El Gobierno endurece las leyes de extranjería y asilo en línea con el pacto europeo en plena crisis de Ceuta,

Primero abrió la ofensiva Robles desde el Congreso. En su comparecencia en la Comisión de Defensa, dijo que la información recabada por los 25 agentes del CNI destinados en Ceuta “se compartió y analizó” con las Fuerzas de Seguridad del Estado y con la Delegación del Gobierno. “Los servicios de inteligencia y obviamente el CNI realizaron la labor que competencialmente les era y es exigible, y compartieron y analizaron con las fuerzas de seguridad del Estado y con el personal de la Delegación del Gobierno”, afirmó. Y recordó que los días anteriores ya estaban entrando 1.000 personas a nado al día, dando así a entender que no fue una sorpresa el salto masivo.

03:29 Robles afirma que los agentes del CNI en Ceuta "compartieron información" con las fuerzas de seguridad y el Gobierno

Marlaska le contestó de forma rotunda desde La Moncloa cuando le preguntaron por estas palabras. Primero reconoció el trabajo del CNI, pero luego cargó contra la versión de la ministra. “No había ningún informe que atisbara que el 30 de julio iba a acontecer lo que sucedió. ¿Alguien puede entender que si se hubiera vislumbrado algo así, con lo que pasó en 2021, no se habría elevado al nivel de las más altas instancias para tomar medidas extraordinarias?“, apuntó.

Cuando la prensa le preguntó al ministro quién decía la verdad, si él o Robles, remató: “No hay ningún informe de esas características con algo similar a lo que pasó. ¿Alguien duda de que, si hubiera existido, no se habría elevado a las más altas instancias? Recibimos informes a diario sobre distintas cuestiones. No voy a entrar en mayores cuestiones". Marlaska mantuvo así lo que ha defendido desde el principio, que no hubo ningún informe.

El ministro de Interior insistió en que no solo el CNI, sino “ningún otro servicio de información de países amigos ni cualquier otro grupo de investigación de inteligencia atisbó nada parecido”. Aun así, reiteró que está “convencido” de que “todo el mundo actuó evidentemente correctamente”.

Y fue Robles quien volvió a contestarle al final de su intervención en el Congreso. “Si hay informes, si no hay informes... Los servicios de inteligencia operan de muchas maneras”, manifestó. En este sentido, incidió en que “no hace falta muchas veces ir a informes manuscritos”. “Es sabido, era público y notorio, que en Ceuta se estaba entrando a nado [...] Sin necesidad de informes de nadie o con informes de alguien que son secretos [...] El día 29 esos funcionarios que están allí [los del CNI en Ceuta] trasladan y dan cuenta en la Delegación del Gobierno de esa convocatoria para el día siguiente para poder entrar a nado aprovechando esa fiesta que se daba en el país vecino”, insistió la ministra de Defensa. La guerra de versiones es muy clara y pública esta vez.

World.title: El Gobierno aprueba por decreto la creación del registro público de ‘lobbies’ ante el bloqueo del Congreso
World.content:
El Consejo de Ministros ha aprobado este martes un real decreto-ley para la creación de un registro “público y obligatorio” de grupos de interés con el que garantizar una mayor transparencia y rendición de cuentas. Esta decisión se produce después de que el proyecto de ley de lobbies, que incluye la creación de este registro estatal de grupos de interés, haya encallado en el Congreso ante la dificultad para reunir el consenso necesario entre los grupos parlamentarios.

Al tratarse de un decreto-ley, la norma entrará en vigor cuando se publique en el Boletín Oficial del Estado (BOE) y deberá ser convalidada por el Congreso en el plazo máximo de 30 días. En concreto, el decreto al que ha dado luz verde el Gobierno este martes crea un registro estatal público y obligatorio de grupos de interés, según ha explicado la portavoz del Ejecutivo y ministra de Inclusión, Seguridad Social y Migraciones, Elma Saiz, en la rueda de prensa posterior al Consejo de Ministros.

Con este registro se “regula en la administración del Estado la relación entre los grupos de interés y el personal público susceptible de recibir influencia”, ha explicado Saiz, que seguidamente ha precisado que “el Real Decreto detalla quiénes tienen la consideración de grupos de interés, cuál es su actividad de influencia y quiénes son susceptibles de recibirla”. “Este registro es obligatorio y estará gestionado y supervisado por el Consejo de Transparencia y Buen Gobierno, que llevará su gobernanza y también su gestión”, ha afirmado la ministra.

El Ejecutivo ha incorporado en el decreto las enmiendas que han presentado los grupos parlamentarios durante la tramitación del proyecto de ley en la Cámara baja. “El Gobierno de España cumple así su compromiso con la transparencia, la regeneración institucional y la calidad democrática; tres piezas indispensables en el puzle de la confianza ciudadana”, apunta el ministro para la Transformación Digital y de la Función Pública, Óscar López, según esa nota.

“Son grupos de interés las personas físicas y jurídicas y las agrupaciones sin personalidad jurídica, incluidas las plataformas, foros, redes u otras formas de actividad colectiva, tanto si actúan por cuenta propia como ajena, con independencia de la forma que adopten o de su estatuto jurídico, y que lleven a cabo actividades de influencia sobre el personal y/o cargo público. Por ejemplo, las empresas y las ONG que pretendan ejercer la función de lobby ante la Administración General del Estado”, detalla el Ejecutivo en una nota de prensa, en la que también explica que una “actividad de influencia” es “toda comunicación directa o indirecta” de un lobby a través de “cualquier medio o canal con la finalidad de incidir en la toma de decisiones públicas, en el diseño o aplicación de políticas o en la elaboración, modificación o aprobación de proyectos normativos en beneficio de intereses propios o de terceros”.

El decreto aprobado determina quiénes son susceptibles de “recibir influencia”. Así, pueden ser objeto de la actividad de los lobbies quienes desempeñen cargos o funciones públicas relativas a la formulación, ejecución o supervisión de políticas públicas; quienes se encarguen de la elaboración de las normativas o los procesos de decisión administrativa y el personal de confianza, los asesores y el personal eventual que trabaje con estos cargos públicos.

Un debate recurrente

El debate sobre la regularización de los grupos de interés se reabrió tras el estallido del caso Montoro en el verano de 2025, que supuso la imputación del exministro de Hacienda y de otras 27 personas por presuntos delitos continuados de cohecho, fraude a la Administración pública y tráfico de influencias, entre otros; y, en abril de 2026, de la imputación del expresidente José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero por liderar presuntamente una trama de tráfico de influencias en mayo de este año. “¿Dónde acaba el lobismo y empieza el tráfico de influencias?”, preguntó el portavoz de ERC en el Congreso, Gabriel Rufián, a Pedro Sánchez en una sesión de control al Gobierno tras conocerse la investigación. Entonces, la Asociación de Profesionales de las Relaciones Institucionales (APRI) defendió en un comunicado que “el lobby no es corrupción, ni tráfico de influencias”.

Semanas más tarde, los profesionales del lobby volvieron a apelar a los principales líderes políticos y a los miembros de la mesa de la Cámara baja para que sacaran adelante la norma que ha aprobado este martes el Gobierno. “España necesita reglas claras que permitan distinguir la participación legítima en los procesos de decisión pública de aquellas conductas que deben ser prevenidas, sancionadas o directamente excluidas del sistema”, defendía entonces Carlos Parry, presidente APRI en un escrito.

World.title: Reabre la L10 de Metro Madrid entre Plaza de Castilla y Cuzco, pero sigue el corte en Santiago Bernabéu
World.content:
El servicio en la Línea 10 de Metro Madrid entre Plaza Castilla y Cuzco se ha reanudado sin incidentes este martes tras las obras de mejora, mientras que seguirá interrumpido también por obras el tramo de la misma línea entre Cuzco y Nuevos Ministerios, que lleva cerrado desde el 28 de marzo. En concreto, la Línea 10 de Metro (Hospital Infanta Sofía-Puerta del Sur) ha permanecido interrumpida desde el pasado 4 de julio entre Nuevos Ministerios y Plaza de Castilla por obras de mejora en la estación de Cuzco.

Una vez finalizadas, en el tramo entre Plaza de Castilla y Cuzco se ha retomado el servicio desde las seis de la mañana, hora a la que abre el suburbano. Los trabajos, con un presupuesto de 1,7 millones de euros (IVA incluido), han permitido la impermeabilización de la infraestructura, así como labores para la retirada del amianto de la bóveda de la estación y de los diferentes cuartos técnicos.

De este modo, a partir de este martes, la suspensión del servicio en L10 volverá a ser entre Nuevos Ministerios y Cuzco hasta finales de año, manteniéndose en todo momento el servicio especial de autobuses. Este corte temporal de la Línea 10 se produce en el marco de las obras para la nueva estación Bernabéu, que es como pasará a denominarse una vez reformada, con previsión de tener finalizados los trabajos en el primer trimestre de 2027.

El proyecto de renovación integral se acerca ya al 45% de ejecución. Una vez finalizados los trabajos de excavación bajo losa de cubierta de los niveles de vestíbulo e intermedio, actualmente se está ejecutando la losa del nuevo nivel intermedio entre plantas. Este nivel está muy cerca de la bóveda de la estación original y, cuando se complete su estructura, se empezará la demolición de dicha estación original.

Con una inversión de 66 millones de euros, la futura estación de Santiago Bernabéu será completamente accesible gracias a la instalación de 12 nuevos ascensores y 24 escaleras mecánicas. Además, se triplicará el espacio disponible y se pasará de una superficie de 4.843 metros cuadrados a más de 12.400, lo que permitirá adaptarse a la demanda de usuarios, especialmente elevada en días de partido y eventos.

El rediseño del espacio mejorará el servicio, con accesos más ágiles desde la calle al andén, al sustituir los pasillos por un gran vestíbulo desde el que se visualizarán los niveles intermedios y la llegada de los trenes. En 2025, la infraestructura contabilizó cerca de cuatro millones de entradas, llegando a superar los 34.000 viajeros en jornadas con encuentros destacables. El objetivo del Gobierno regional es inaugurar este nuevo diseño a lo largo del primer trimestre de 2027, coincidiendo con el 125.º aniversario de la fundación del club blanco y el 80.º cumpleaños de su estadio.

World.title: Un puente colgante, una iglesia de Ricardo Bofill y otros atractivos de Andorra
World.content:
Del mirador del Roc del Quer a un museo de motos, la parroquia andorrana de Canillo es el lugar perfecto para disfrutar del Principado en verano

La parroquia de Canillo, en Andorra, con 120 kilómetros de extensión, cuenta con una amplia oferta de actividades cuando la nieve se retira y da paso a las praderas verdes. Propuestas para todo tipo de viajeros, y que también son para los niños. Desde flotar en el vacío en un puente tibetano hasta contemplar un hombre de hierro en el mirador del Roc del Quer, visitar iglesias románicas, hacer una ruta de senderismo en el valle de Incles o descubrir un curioso museo.

Dos propuestas para una vista panorámica

El puente Tibetano de Canillo se ha convertido en una atracción en sí mismo. Esta pasarela colgante con una espectacular panorámica al valle del Riu en sus 603 metros de su recorrido y hasta 158 vertiginosos metros de altura respeto al suelo. Es el segundo más largo de Europa tras el Sky Bridge de Dolní Morava, en Chequia, con 721 metros de largo. Para llegar hay que tomar el bus en la población de Canillo, que nos dejará en una curva de la carretera CS240, desde la que hay que continuar a pie un kilómetro hasta llegar al comienzo del puente.

El puente Tibetano de Canillo. cristina candel

La experiencia se suele combinar con el cercano mirador del Roc del Quer, con otra impresionante panorámica, esta vez a los valles de Montaup, Valira d’Orient y con la población de Canillo a nuestros pies. Este mirador con 12 metros suspendidos sobre el vacío —con buena parte del pavimento hecho con vidrio transparente— culmina en un hombre sentado, Contemplación, la obra suspendida del escultor argentino Miguel Ángel González afincado en Lleida, cuyo trabajo ahonda en la naturaleza destructora y creadora del ser humano. Qué buen enclave para filosofar con este escultor que, como él dice, “solo quiere atrapar a la gente durante unos minutos para sacarla del mundanal ruido”.

La escultura de Miguel Ángel González en el mirador del Roc del Quer. cristina candel

Callejuelas y murales en Canillo

La parroquia de Canillo, la más grande en extensión de Andorra, cuenta con algo más de 4.000 vecinos. Cuesta creer que sea el mismo número de habitantes que tenía todo el Principado en 1930 (hoy son 80.000), antes de que se construyera la primera carretera que llegó en 1933 y que supuso el comienzo del turismo y el comercio. Aunque hayan cambiado tantas cosas en estos años, continúa siendo una acogedora población de pequeñas callejuelas de suelo empedrado, casas con fachadas de piedra y techos de pizarra. La cruza el río Montaup, que discurre paralelo al Carrer Major, una pequeña calle que asciende y nos lleva a la escuela y a la iglesia de Sant Serni.

El pueblo de Canillo. cristina candel

Paseando por sus calles aparecen las pinturas murales de Sam Bosque, una artista andorrana cuya obra está centrada en la memoria histórica; un ejemplo se puede ver en el mural de los molineros del que fue el único molino eléctrico existente en Andorra, hoy convertido en tienda de productos y artesanías de kilómetro cero, Cal Federico. Sam Bosque se inspiró para esta obra en los restos del molino y las fotos encontradas de los molineros en este lugar. Calle abajo, un inmenso escalador y, frente a él, unos niños jugando con las hojas de otoño, también de la misma autora, dan color a esta calle que termina en el río Valira d’Orient.

Uno de los murales de la artista Sam Bosque en el comercio Cal Federico, en Canillo. cristina candel

Senderismo en el valle de Incles

En la carretera que va de la población de El Tarter a la de Soldeu hay una pequeña carretera que se interna en el valle de Incles. Aquí dejamos el coche cerca del puente de l’Orri, y, atravesando el mismo, comienza la ruta de senderismo llamada Rec de l’Obac o camino de umbría, que acompaña al río Incles en todo el recorrido. Es un agradable paseo sin ningún tipo de desnivel a través de un bosque de pino negro, con pasarelas de madera para salvar las zonas húmedas, puentes que cruzan el río a la zona de solana, donde aquí y allá aparecen pequeñas bordas en los pastizales y hasta un banco para contemplar el paisaje cómodamente.

A lo largo del camino (accesible y de unos dos kilómetros), varios paneles cuentan con texto y fotografías cómo era la vida hace años, las diferentes maneras de pescar la trucha fario, autóctona, cómo se plantaba el centeno que se recolectaba un año después o cómo se segaba y guardaba el pasto del verano en las bordas para dar de comer al ganado en los meses de invierno.

Dos senderistas por el valle de Incles. cristina candel

A lo largo del paseo también acompañarán las fuentes en forma de tronco vaciado y las flores que van vistiendo el valle dependiendo del mes del año en el que nos encontremos. Así, el valle puede estar vestido de amarillo genista o “bàlec” en primavera, arbusto que antaño se utilizaba para hacer escobas, o de rojo de rododendro, también conocido como “neret”, en los meses de verano. Tras cruzar el puente de La Baladosa, se puede regresar por la carretera o desandar el camino.

Si se quiere conocer más en profundidad este valle, hay rutas más largas y con más desnivel que parten de este mismo punto, como la que une el lago de Siscaró y el de les Canals Roges en 11 kilómetros de ruta circular o la que llega a los dos lagos de Juglar en nueve kilómetros (contando la ida y la vuelta).

Ruta de las iglesias

En verano también es un buen momento para visitar las iglesias andorranas. Se puede empezar en la pequeña localidad de Prats, que dista un kilómetro de Canillo, donde se encuentra la iglesia de San Miquel, de ábside románico, doble espadaña y una pequeña escalinata para acceder. La iglesia da la impresión de estar hundida en la tierra y, aunque normalmente permanece cerrada, merece la pena visitarla aunque solo sea por fuera.

Continuamos caminando y en otro kilómetro llegamos a la basílica santuario de Meritxell, patrona de Andorra, cuya capilla original se quemó junto con la talla románica de la virgen en 1972. En su lugar hoy se encuentran dos edificios: el viejo santuario de Meritxell y el edificio ecléctico del arquitecto Ricardo Bofill que es la basílica Santuario de Meritxell.

El entorno de la basílica santuario de Nuestra Señora de Meritxell. cristina candel

Pero la iglesia más emblemática de la zona es Sant Joan de Caselles, que conserva gran parte de su estructura original y una bella torre de estilo románico lombardo, así como dos porches de los siglos XV y XVI. En su interior, unas pinturas murales romanas bastante bien conservadas, mezcladas con una pieza de Cristo de estuco, que fue encontrada bajo el altar. Este templo se puede visitar todos los días de la semana, salvo el lunes.

Exterior de la iglesia de Sant Joan de Caselles. cristina candel

Volvemos a la población de Canillo para una visita final: el curioso Museo de la Moto: 121 motocicletas de lo más variado que cuentan la historia de este medio de transporte en sus 900 metros cuadrados de espacio. Aquí podemos ver una motocicleta a vapor del año 1896 de origen británico o la primera moto a propulsión eléctrica que lanzó Honda en 1940.

World.title: Italia quiere poner orden en el caos de sus 12.000 playas privadas: más transparencia y nuevas tasas
World.content:
Entre el 33% y el 42% de los arenales del país son de pago. El Gobierno de Meloni, presionado por Bruselas, abrirá a concurso su gestión

Italia presume de sus 8.000 kilómetros de costa, pero disfrutar de ellos no siempre es gratis. Mientras que en otras partes ir a la playa significa buscar un hueco en la arena, en Italia la experiencia suele ser muy distinta. Encontrar un espacio donde plantar la sombrilla sin pagar puede convertirse en toda una aventura. En amplios tramos del litoral, el acceso al mar está gestionado por empresas privadas, mediante concesiones públicas, que han transformado las playas en un negocio multimillonario. El resultado es una de las estampas más características del verano italiano: bosques interminables de sombrillas perfectamente alineadas, acompañadas de sus respectivas tumbonas, esperando a ser alquiladas por precios que pueden superar los 35 euros al día.

Este modelo, muy arraigado en el país y marcado por una gestión plagada de irregularidades, afronta una reforma que lleva años aplazándose a pesar de la presión de Bruselas para poner orden. Las playas gestionadas por concesionarios privados no han dejado de ganar terreno. Según la asociación ecologista italiana Legambiente, ocupan ya más del 42% de los arenales del país. El Ministerio de Infraestructuras rebaja esa cifra al 33%, una diferencia que se explica por el criterio utilizado para el cálculo: el Gobierno utiliza para sus cuentas toda la línea costera italiana y no únicamente las zonas aptas para el baño.

Desde hace décadas, las empresas, casi siempre familiares —las concesiones suelen heredarse—, pagan cánones relativamente bajos al Estado por explotar espacios públicos, mientras los precios para los usuarios han aumentado de forma exponencial. Las concesionarias gestionan los servicios como los baños, las duchas, los vestuarios, los aparcamientos, además del alquiler de sombrillas y tumbonas. También controlan los chiringuitos y cafeterías y se encargan de las labores de salvamento. Mientras que las zonas públicas suelen estar descuidadas, a menudo sucias, y desprovistas de servicios públicos.

Se trata de un asunto sensible que divide a la opinión pública italiana. Para unos, las playas de pago garantizan orden, limpieza y comodidad; para otros, representan la privatización de un bien público que debería ser accesible para todos. La principal crítica al sistema es la enorme diferencia entre lo que pagan las concesionarias por explotar las playas y los beneficios que obtienen. El Estado recauda entre 80 y 100 millones de euros al año por las concesiones, mientras que el sector, marcado por la opacidad, mueve más de 2.000 millones de euros anuales, según distintas estimaciones. El propio Tribunal de Cuentas italiano ha advertido de que los cánones abonados por los empresarios no suelen ser proporcionales a los ingresos que obtienen.

Uno de los aspectos más controvertidos del modelo italiano es que las concesiones se han renovado durante años casi por inercia. Sin concursos abiertos ni una competencia efectiva y sin controles ni transparencia, los mismos operadores han conservado la explotación de amplios tramos del litoral público durante generaciones, consolidando un sistema difícil de encontrar en otros países europeos.

Un paso adelante

Bruselas lleva años reclamando cambios. La Comisión considera que Italia incumple la directiva Bolkestein de 2009, que obliga a garantizar la libre competencia en la adjudicación de este tipo de concesiones, y ha presionado repetidamente a Roma. Tras décadas de aplazamientos y enfrentamientos, el Gobierno de Giorgia Meloni ha abordado la cuestión. La reforma aprobada prevé que para el 30 de septiembre de 2027 salgan a concurso público todas las playas de pago, unas 12.000 repartidas por todo el país. Además, las concesiones tendrán una duración limitada, de entre cinco y 20 años, y habrá compensaciones económicas para los actuales titulares por las inversiones y obras que hayan realizado.

La perspectiva de abrir el mercado ha despertado, sin embargo, inquietud entre muchos empresarios del sector, que temen que los concursos favorezcan la entrada de grandes grupos turísticos o fondos de inversión capaces de desplazar a los negocios familiares que tradicionalmente han dominado las costas italianas.

World.title: New Oranje coach Xavi calls Netherlands “university of football”
World.content:
New national head coach Xavi Hernandez said he regarded the Netherlands as the “university of football” as he gave his first press conference in Zeist.

The 46-year-old said it was an “honour” to be appointed by the KNVB as the first foreign coach since Austria’s Ernst Happel led the men’s team to the 1978 World Cup final.

Xavi was the KNVB’s third choice for the job after Pep Guardiola, the former Manchester City coach, opted to take a sabbatical from football and Arne Slot, the former Feyenoord and Liverpool coach, preferred to stay in club football.

He has been given a four-year contract until the end of the next World Cup in 2030, with no conditions tied to the Netherlands’ performance at the European Championships in two years’ time.

Most of Xavi’s playing career was spent at Barcelona, where he won eight La Liga titles, many of them under the tutelage of Guardiola, whose playing style was influenced by Dutch legend Johan Cruyff.

He made his international debut for Spain in a friendly game against the Netherlands in 2000 and 10 years later was one of the pivotal members of the team that won the World Cup in 2010, defeating Oranje in the final.

“My feeling today is that I’m going to the university of football,” Xavi said. “I learned a lot during my career as a player and a coach that I want to give back.

Big family

“I believe a lot in this generation,” he added. “We have a lot of talents, but the important thing for me is to create a team, a group and a big family in order to play well.”

Asked how he felt about being the KNVB’s third choice, ahead of youth team coach Michael Reiziger, Xavi said: “It’s not a bad position after Guardiola and Slot. At least we’re on the podium.”

He added that the Dutch “total football” school was the basis for his own style of football as both a player and a coach.

“To dominate, the game, to take the initiative with the ball, and at the same time our goal is to show to everybody a team with passion, with desire and ambition. That is my philosophy,” he said.

“We are here to compete, we are here to enjoy and we are here to win.”

Senior players

The KNVB’s technical director, Nigel de Jong, said Xavi was identified as a candidate because his footballing philosophy aligned closely with the Dutch team’s ambitions to play “attractive, dominant” football.

The coach said he had not made any decisions about which players he will select, but he had already spoken to current team captain Virgil van Dijk and Barcelona midfielder Frenkie de Jong.

Dutch media have speculated that Van Dijk, 35, and leading scorer Memphis Depay, 32, could be dropped from the squad as part of a clear-out of senior players.

De Jong, who worked with Xavi during the Spaniard’s spell as Barcelona coach from 2021 to 2024, has been struggling with injuries for more than a year and was not fully fit during this year’s World Cup.

The coach also said he had been monitoring AZ Alkmaar’s promising 20-year-old midfielder Kees Smit, who narrowly missed out on the World Cup squad this summer.

Oranje will play their first match under his leadership on September 24, when they take on Germany in the Nations League in Amsterdam. “We haven’t yet decided the [squad] list,” Xavi said. “You will see it in three weeks.”

World.title: Vondelkerk fire investigation ends in mystery, police say
World.content:
How the Vondelkerk in Amsterdam went up in flames on New Year’s Eve is still unknown, police have said, after months of trying and failing to establish a criminal cause for the blaze.

Investigators had looked into whether the fire was started deliberately and whether fireworks were to blame. Local residents were interviewed, video footage examined and tips about possible arson followed up, but none of it produced any evidence, police said.

It could also not be established whether fireworks caused the fire. Much of the forensic evidence was destroyed in the blaze itself, police said, and no traces of fireworks were found. With no leads left to pursue, the investigation has stalled.

Years to rebuild

The monumental church on Vondelstraat, close to the Vondelpark, was largely destroyed in the early hours of January 1, when its tower collapsed and much of the roof was lost. It was designed by Pierre Cuypers, the 19th-century architect behind Amsterdam’s Centraal station and the Rijksmuseum, and completed in 1880.

The building served as a Catholic church until it closed in 1977 and has since been used for concerts, offices and community events, with church services returning in 2017. It has been owned since 1996 by heritage restoration body Stadsherstel Amsterdam.

Several fundraising drives were launched after the fire. Stadsherstel said more than €180,000 had been raised within a week, and other appeals brought in tens of thousands of euros more. Rebuilding the church is expected to take years.

World.title: Dutch foundation plans to build underground hospital in Ukraine
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

A Dutch organisation is trying to raise funds to build a reinforced underground hospital in Ukraine so soldiers can be treated nearer the front line.

Protect Ukraine and a Norwegian foundation, HMM Healthcare, say they have already secured €750,000 in donations for the project, which is expected to cost €2.5 million in total.

The 600 m2 hospital will be built 8 m below ground and made entirely of concrete, allowing wounded service personnel to be treated in what is effectively a giant bunker.

The organisers hope to have the building fully equipped and operational by February 2027.

Jaap Scholten, a Dutch writer and co-founder of Protect Ukraine, said: “The fact that we have raised three-quarters of a million euros in such a short time shows that people in the Netherlands have not forgotten Ukraine.

“But we are not there yet. Every donation brings us closer to a hospital and stabilisation point that can save many lives.”

Protect Ukraine has around 100 volunteers who run regular trips to Ukraine to deliver goods such as medicines, pop-up tents and pick-up trucks.

Scholten, who lives in Hungary, told NOS he started the organisation after watching people in his neighbourhood handing out fresh fruit, energy bars and blankets to Ukrainian refugees.

“Arranging supplies for Ukrainians is the most effective thing you can do to help,” he said. “That’s why I started Protect Ukraine.”

World.title: Many Dutch children hide upsetting online posts from parents
World.content:
Half of children in the Netherlands aged 10 to 15 sometimes see posts online that frighten or upset them, but many do not tell their parents out of shame or fear of an angry reaction, a government survey has found.

The finding comes as junior digital economy minister Willemijn Aerdts launches a new phase of the government’s Blijf in Beeld (“Stay in the picture”) campaign, which encourages parents to talk to their children about what they encounter online and to agree rules on phone use together.

The survey, commissioned by the economic affairs and climate ministry (EZK), found children in the Netherlands now get their first smartphone at the age of 10 on average. Children most often named Snapchat and TikTok as the places they were most likely to come across something unpleasant.

Talk early

Aerdts said parents should start those conversations while children are young, before the influence of friends grows. “Be curious about what they see, including the nice and funny things,” she said, arguing this makes it easier for children to also raise the frightening or harmful side of social media.

Parents should not judge children for what they do online, she added, and should be open about their own use.

The campaign, developed in part with children’s helpline the Kindertelefoon, comes with a printed card that parents and children fill in together. The ministry said 89.4% of children understood why rules on phone use mattered, and half said they welcomed them.

Waiting for Brussels

Aerdts said platforms were not doing enough to protect children. “The online world is really not yet a safe place for children,” she said, adding that this was why the government wants a minimum age for social media use agreed at European level rather than in national law.

That marks a contrast with France, Spain and Greece, which have moved to set their own age limits. France passed a law last month barring under-15s from social media, though its Constitutional Council then ruled the measure unconstitutional in its current form and the government is redrafting it.

Aerdts has previously said she wants to avoid “a mishmash of rules and regulations that will The European Commission is working on its own proposals: last month researchers advised it to ban social media for children under 13, and commission president Ursula von der Leyen has said she will bring forward a proposal to limit children’s use after the summer.

World.title: Shrinkflation eases but manufacturers turn sneaky, watchdog says
World.content:
Shrinkflation is happening less often than a few years ago, but manufacturers are getting better at hiding it, consumer body the Consumentenbond has found in its latest sweep of Dutch supermarket shelves.

The organisation again found dozens of products whose contents had shrunk without a matching drop in price, and received fewer reports from shoppers than in previous years. But a hard core of producers are now shrinking packs so quietly that customers don’t notice.

The clearest example is Blue Band Vloeibaar, the liquid baking product, which dropped from 750 to 700 millilitres in March 2026 while the bottle and front label stayed exactly the same.

The new volume appears only in small print on the side, and the pack is still described as a “voordeelfles”, or value bottle. The recommended price held at €3.65, so shoppers pay more per millilitre either way.

Shrunk more than once

Some products have now been reduced two or three times over. Andrélon conditioner went from 300 to 250 and then to 200ml; on the last step the price rose from €5.49 to €6.49, a 48% increase per 100ml.

A bag of M&M’s, which held 440 grams in 2020, now contains 363 grams, leaving consumers paying about 10% more per 100 grams.

Manufacturers mostly blamed higher costs for packaging, raw materials, energy and transport. Mars, which makes M&M’s, pointed to recently changed rules it said might bar producers from sharing recommended prices – but, the watchdog said, as far as it could tell no such change had taken place.

Consumentenbond director Sandra Molenaar called on politicians to act. “When there is more in a pack, manufacturers shout it from the rooftops,” she said, “but when the contents shrink, they only adjust it quietly on the back.”

She wants producers required to state a reduction clearly on the pack, or supermarkets made to flag it at the shelf, as is already the law in France.

World.title: Fraudsters using iDeal switch to Wero to snare bank customers
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Fraudsters are sending out phishing mails to Dutch bank customers to try to take advantage of the switch from the iDeal payment system to Wero.

The fake messages typically tell customers they are due a refund as a result of the transition to Wero, the European-based system set up under efforts to make EU businesses less dependent on foreign digital services.

Victims are told to verify their identity by clicking on a link in the e-mail, which takes them to a page where the criminals can steal their login details.

The online fraud hotline Fraudehelpdesk.nl said it was currently receiving 100 queries a day about suspicious messages regarding iDeal, after a surge in activity in the last few months.

A frequently seen mail in recent days says the handover took place on August 24 and puts customers under pressure to claim their refund before the “deadline”.

Danial van Delft, CEO of Currence, the company that operates iDeal and Wero, told the Telegraaf: “This is a big change in the payments ecosystem and gives people with bad intentions space to abuse it.

“We see fraudsters becoming more and more inventive. They are trying to latch on to every hook and news item.”

iDeal said people should ignore suspicious emails and not click on links. “iDeal will never ask you to confirm personal details by email, start a verification process or install software,” the company said.

World.title: Villagers at centre of asylum row urge council to heal divide
World.content:
Residents of a Noord-Brabant village at the centre of a bitter row about plans to accommodate 50 asylum seekers have accused the local council of making the problem worse through its poor communications strategy.

Violent protests were staged in Engelen, on the edge of ’s-Hertogenbosch, after the council announced in April it would be housing a group of teenage boys and girls, all under 18, in a former police station on Beverspijken.

Opponents have staged marches to express their concern about women’s safety, while supporters say they have been subjected to a hate campaign, with swastikas and obscene words spray-painted on their homes.

At a council meeting on Monday night, residents on both sides of the divide appealed to the local mayor, Jack Mikkers, to talk to villagers before the final decision is made next month.

Around 100 people packed into the council chamber in Den Bosch and a side room set up as an overspill location for those who were unable to get into the public gallery.

The council says it has an obligation to accommodate asylum seekers under the so-called “spreading law”, which requires all local authorities to take in a fair share in order to ease overcrowding at the reception centre in Ter Apel, Groningen.

“Spend an evening walking through Engelen, ring people’s doorbells and listen,” said Tamara Govers, who organised one of the marches in May. “Come as a person, not an official, without cameras or press releases.”

Blacklist

Astrid van den Broek, who spoke in support of the plan, called for councillors to stop the threats and intimidation. “My name’s been put on a blacklist,” she said, adding that a man who threatened her when she filmed a group putting up protest signs was at the meeting.

“I’ve told security,” she said. “Don’t talk to me about being concerned about our women’s safety if the shelter goes ahead.”

Other villagers said the municipality had been too slow to respond to the menacing atmosphere in the village. “The shelter has driven a wedge between friendships,” said resident Eva Buijs.

Jack Burg, chair of local campaign group Veilig Engelen, said “better communication” from the council could have prevented the situation escalating.

Burg said the plans did not do enough to address concerns about the impact of the refugee centre on quality of life in the village.

“Conditions and rules have not been worked out,” he said. “We need more than this plan for a suitable accommodation facility. We want clarity, but that’s not what this is.”

Strict conditions

The council has set strict conditions for the centre, including a 10pm curfew and night-time security. Residents will have to move out as soon as they turn 18, most likely to smaller groups in Den Bosch.

The municipality also wants the refugee accommodation agency COA to send equal numbers of girls and boys, but that may be difficult to arrange because five out of six underage asylum seekers are male.

Some residents said they were not against accommodating refugees in the village, but called the empty police station on Beverspijken the “wrong location”.

One group produced data from decibel readings taken from the site that showed levels of 83 decibels had been recorded at night – 18db higher than the level permitted by the local environmental plan.

Others questioned whether the council and the COA could be relied on to stick to their agreeement to make the accommodation centre a temporary facility, pointing out that permits for other locations have been extended at the request of the agency.

World.title: Deadlock looms in budget talks as opposition drive hard bargain
World.content:
Talks to secure support from opposition parties for next year’s budget are entering their final days with no sign of a breakthrough.

Jesse Klaver, leader of the left-wing opposition group Pro (previously GroenLinks/PvdA) said the two sides had “not moved a step closer to each other” after emerging from negotiations on Monday.

Michiel Hoogeveen, of the right-wing JA21, accused the coalition parties of “kicking the can down the road”, while the hardline Protestant party SGP said a deal was “a long way off”.

Finance minister Eelco Heinen has a deadline of August 28 to submit a draft budget to the Council of State before the formal presentation of his plans at the state opening of parliament on September 15.

MPs will not vote on the measures until late in the autumn, but the cabinet wants to do a deal with the opposition to secure majority support in both houses before budget day.

Yo-yo politics

Prime minister Rob Jetten said earlier: “This cabinet has big ambitions to make major investments in the next few years in more affordable houses, more security and the economy of the future. It’s good to do that with others if we want to avoid yo-yo politics.”

The minority coalition of D66, VVD and CDA needs the support of 10 opposition MPs in the lower house and 16 senators to pass its legislation.

Asylum minister and deputy prime minister Bart van den Brink, of the CDA, said the government was prepared to take “big steps” to accommodate the opposition groups. But Klaver said he had seen little sign of movement from the coalition.

Pro wants the cabinet to shelve plans to cut welfare spending by €6.5 billion in order to raise money for other departments, chiefly defence, where the Netherlands is striving to hit the new Nato target of 3.5% of GDP.

Wealth taxes

The party argues that the money should be raised by raising wealth taxes instead. “The cabinet seems to be mainly concerned with the position of millionaires in the Netherlands while we are worried about the people who are paying the bills,” Klaver said.

But Heinen’s party, the right-wing liberal VVD, is opposed to wealth taxes and would prefer to make concessions to parties on the right such as JA21 and SGP, who want to see tax cuts instead. But SGP MP André Flach said on Tuesday that the coalition’s plans “are not enough at the moment”.

The SGP, which draws its vote from Bible-Belt communities, wants the cabinet to suspend plans to legalise surrogate motherhood and permit late-term abortions of up to 22 weeks in some hospitals.

The party has teamed up with JA21 to form a right-wing block of 12 seats, which would be enough to give the coalition a majority in the Lower House. However, they would still be short in the Senate, where any right-wing majority depends on the support of the farmers’ party BBB.

BBB key

The BBB has not been invited to the talks so far because of its staunch opposition to the cabinet’s plans to reduce nitrogen pollution, which would require some livestock farmers to give up or drastically reduce the size of their herds.

Party leader Henk Vermeer is meeting Heinen on Tuesday, but the BBB is not expected to compromise on its stance. “Anyone who can count can see they can’t do without us”.

The 20 seats held by Pro would give the cabinet a clear majority in the lower house, while only one small party such as Volt would be needed to pass the budget in the Senate.

But the right-wing VVD is reluctant to rely solely on Klaver’s party, which was kept out of the coalition in February on the insistence of VVD leader Dilan Yesilgöz.

World.title: Polish far-right leader charged with Holocaust denial for calling Auschwitz gas chambers “fake”

Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has been charged with denying Nazi crimes, a criminal offence in Poland that carries a prison sentence of up to three years. The charges relate to statements last year in which Braun, who has a long history of promoting antisemitic conspiracy theories, suggested that the gas chambers at Auschwitz, which was the Nazis’ main killing centre during the Holocaust, are “fake”. Komunikat o przedstawieniu posłowi do Parlamentu Europejskiego zarzutów publicznego i wbrew faktom zaprzeczania zbrodniom ludobójstwa popełnionym w niemieckim nazistowskim obozie koncentracyjnym i zagłady KL Auschwitz-Birkenau w Oświęcimiu. https://t.co/nLq3XKnXCK — IPN Kraków (@ipn_krakow) August 25, 2026 On Tuesday morning, Braun was summoned to appear as a suspect at the Kraków branch of the Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), a state historical body that has the power to prosecute crimes relating to the periods when Poland was under Nazi and communist rule. A group of his followers gathered outside the building to express their support for Braun, who finished fourth in last year’s presidential elections. Since then, his Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party has risen to around 9% in polls, making it a potential kingmaker after next year’s parliamentary elections. After meeting with Braun, IPN prosecutor Robert Janicki announced that they had presented Braun with charges for “publicly and contrary to the facts denying the crimes of genocide committed by officers of the Third Reich in the German concentration and extermination camp KL Auschwitz-Birkenau”. The charges relate to two interviews Braun gave in July last year. He declared that “Auschwitz with its gas chambers is unfortunately a fake” and said that claims about the use of gas chambers are part of a “propaganda narrative” supporting a “quasi-religious cult”. In actual fact, gas chambers were used at Auschwitz, which was located in German-occupied Poland, to kill around 900,000 people, the vast majority of them Jews. Janicki noted that Braun’s remarks “clearly contradict common historical knowledge based on documents, witness accounts, perpetrators’ statements and findings from past criminal proceedings”. Far-right leader Grzegorz Braun says the gas chambers at Auschwitz are “fake” and it is a “fact” that Jews have committed ritual murder. Prosecutors have launched an investigation into whether he violated Poland's law against denying Nazi crimes https://t.co/7UUKzH5ndG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 10, 2025 When Braun originally made his remarks, they were widely condemned in Poland, which suffered enormously under German occupation during World War Two. Justice minister Waldemar Żurek asked the European Parliament, where Braun sits as an MEP, to lift his legal immunity so he could be charged. “For me, it is a scandal that, in a country that suffered such enormous war losses, there is a politician who can deny historical facts that are so painful for Poles,” said Żurek at the time, quoted by the Onet news website. “I won’t let this go. We must bring such people to justice.” In March, the European Parliament approved Żurek’s request, allowing Braun to face charges in relation to his Auschwitz comments, as well as for other alleged crimes. The European Parliament has again voted to strip Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun of immunity to face further charges for Holocaust denial as well as various antisemitic, anti-Ukrainian and anti-LGBT incidents during last year's presidential campaign https://t.co/4EHVEuSDnM — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 26, 2026 On Friday last week, the district prosecutor’s office in Warsaw charged Braun with those other crimes, including the theft of Ukrainian and EU flags he tore down and vandalism of an LGBT+ exhibition being displayed in parliament. In a separate case, in February this year, Żurek also asked the European Parliament to strip Braun of immunity to face charges of denying Nazi crimes over another incident in which he called the gas chambers at both Auschwitz and Majdanek, another Nazi-German camp in occupied Poland, “fake”. Meanwhile, Braun is already on trial in Poland for four other alleged crimes, including using a fire extinguisher to attack a Jewish Hanukkah ceremony in the Polish parliament in December 2023. The trial of Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun for his attacks on a Hanukkah celebration in parliament and a Holocaust lecture has begun. World.title: Poland’s Mesko signs €1.9bn deal to supply Piorun air-defence systems to four NATO countries
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Polish state defence firm Mesko has signed an 8 billion zloty (€1.9 billion) agreement to supply its Piorun man-portable air-defence systems to the armed forces of Poland, Norway, Lithuania and Latvia. The deal is being financed through the European Union’s SAFE mechanism. The agreement represents the largest-ever purchase of Pioruns, which have become an export hit for Mesko after proving their worth during Ukraine’s defence against Russian aggression. Previous buyers include Sweden, the United States, Belgium, Estonia and Norway itself. Nowy etap #PolskaSAFE. Rozpoczynamy wspólne zakupy i to znów w polskim przemyśle! Polska🇵🇱, Litwa🇱🇹, Łotwa 🇱🇻i Norwegia 🇳🇴 kupują wspólnie polskie pioruny. To 63 umowa w ramach polskiego SAFE. Dziś 8 mld zł. Mesko od maja zwiększyło zatrudnienie o 200 osób. To jak to było,… pic.twitter.com/YIDWBGBvpm — Magdalena Sobkowiak (@magdasobkowiak) August 24, 2026 The deal will see the firm provide “several hundred” launchers and “several thousand” missiles for its shoulder-fired Piorun systems, which target low-flying aircraft such as planes, helicopters and drones. Over 80% will be supplied to Poland’s armed forces, with the remainder going to its three NATO allies. The purchase is being funded through SAFE, which provides loans at preferential terms for defence spending. While SAFE can be used individually by countries to make purchases for their own armed forces, some funds are designated for joint procurement by groups of countries (including non-EU member Norway). “Our partners from Lithuania, Latvia and Norway have decided to purchase from Poland,” declared deputy defence minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, who oversees Poland’s participation in SAFE. “We are a leader in the SAFE mechanism and are the first to create such agreements. For the first time, the [Polish defence ministry’s] Armaments Agency is making purchases not only for the Polish armed forces, but also for those of our allies.” “This is a measure of the success of the Polish arms industry,” declared defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, as the deal was announced on Monday. “This is the moment when Poland can proudly say: we are a European leader.” He noted that Mesko’s production capacity is now 2.5 times larger than it was when the current government took power in December 2023. Since SAFE launched in May, the firm’s staffing, which stood at 3,200 by the end of last year, has increased by around 200, added the minister. Poland is by far the largest recipient of SAFE funds, with around €44 billion. The government says that SAFE will not only bolster Poland’s defence capabilities but also provide a boost to the domestic defence industry, where around 90% of the funds will be spent. However, the programme has been opposed by the right-wing opposition and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, who argue that it will give Brussels too much influence over Polish defence spending and burden Poland with decades of debt on uncertain terms. Wiceminister @magdasobkowiak: Dzisiaj rozpoczynamy etap wspólnych zakupów. Wiele było pytań o to, czy to zrealizujemy, a może będziemy kupować w Niemczech. I widzicie, co się wydarzyło. Nie dosyć, że te umowy realizujemy w polskim przemyśle zbrojeniowym, to jeszcze nasi partnerzy… pic.twitter.com/hFL8M2Laah — Ministerstwo Obrony Narodowej 🇵🇱 (@MON_GOV_PL) August 24, 2026 In 2022, Pioruns were among the large quantities of military equipment Poland provided to Ukraine to help its eastern neighbour defend itself from Russia’s full-scale invasion. The systems were successfully used to take down a variety of Russian aircraft. In that same year, Mesko announced that the US government had ordered “several hundred” Piorun systems, while Norway also put in a similar order. Last year, Belgium and Sweden announced that they would purchase hundreds of Pioruns, while Ukraine itself also revealed that it had requested a €120 million loan from Poland to help fund the purchase of Polish-made weapons, including Pioruns. Earlier this year, Mesko, which belongs to the state defence holding group PGZ, announced the best financial results in its 100-year history. The firm’s revenues of 2.3 billion zloty in 2025 were up 33% year-on-year, driven by international demand for Pioruns. World.title: Regulation on recognising foreign same-sex marriages comes into force in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. All registry offices in Poland can now recognise same-sex marriages conducted in other European Union countries, after a government regulation issued in May went into force. The decision came in response to a ruling by the Court of Justice of the EU (CJEU) requiring Poland to recognise such unions. Deputy prime minister Krzysztof Gawkowski expressed his “great joy, because finally in Poland we have a law that gives the right to dignity”. The government’s plenipotentiary for equality, Katarzyna Kotula, warned local authorities that they will be breaking the law if they refuse to comply with the new rules. However, the mayor of one town in a conservative region has already declared that his administration will not recognise such marriages. He argues that doing so would violate Poland’s constitution, which mentions marriage as a union between a man and a woman. Od jutra polskie państwo będzie lepiej chronić godność i prawa swoich obywateli. Nowe wzory aktów małżeństwa umożliwią transkrypcję zagranicznych aktów małżeństw jednopłciowych z pełnym szacunkiem dla par. To koniec administracyjnej fikcji i niepewności, z którą przez lata… pic.twitter.com/mRZYkEg9W4 — Krzysztof Gawkowski (@KGawkowski) August 22, 2026 Polish domestic law still does not allow any form of same-sex unions to be formed. However, last year, the CJEU ordered that the country recognise same-sex marriages conducted in other EU member states. That was followed by a similar ruling from Poland’s own Supreme Administrative Court (NSA). One obstacle to implementing those decisions was that, previously, Poland’s civil registry only allowed male-female marriages to be entered. But, under a regulation issued by the government in May, the system now allows either mixed-sex or same-sex marriages. Even before that went into force on Sunday, some Polish cities, starting with Warsaw and Wrocław, had already begun transcribing same-sex marriages conducted abroad into their registries. They simply listed one spouse in the “man” section and the other as a “woman”, even though that was not accurate for one of them. But some local authorities have refused to do so, pointing to article 18 of Poland’s constitution, which states that: “Marriage, being a union of a man and a woman, as well as the family, motherhood and parenthood, shall be placed under the protection and care of the Republic of Poland.” Such doubts were cited by the mayor of Zakopane, a town in southern Poland, last week when he announced that his administration did not intend to begin recognising foreign same-sex marriages after the regulation came into force. “We will not be issuing such transcriptions in Zakopane,” said Łukasz Filipowski, quoted by local news service Nasze Miasto. He argued that doing so would “not be in accordance with the constitution”, adding that, while Zakopane is “tolerant”, it “promotes the traditional family model…[as] our foundation”. Filipowski pointed to a ruling in July by the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), which found that the government’s regulation conflicts with the constitution’s definition of marriage. However, the government considers the TK to be improperly constituted and therefore regards its rulings as invalid. Poland's Constitutional Tribunal has ruled that a new regulation allowing foreign same-sex marriage certificates to be registered in Poland is unconstitutional. The government says it will not implement the rulinghttps://t.co/xDAzLjcJQ4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 28, 2026 In response to Filipowski’s remarks, Kotula told broadcaster TVN that officials who refuse to recognise foreign same-sex marriages “will be breaking the law”. She said that the personal views of officials cannot “translate into what [legal] actions they take” and that the government would be monitoring the situation. Gawkowski – who, like Kotula, is a leading figure in The Left (Lewica), a junior member of Poland’s ruling coalition – also warned municipalities against issuing refusals. He noted that, as well as the CJEU ruling, Polish courts have also issued orders to recognise foreign same-sex marriages. “In the end, these local authorities will lose [a court battle], so why embarrass themselves? Let’s not look for legal tricks. Let’s just implement something that has been done in other, normal countries for years,” Gawkowski told Polsat News. However, even once same-sex marriages are transcribed into Polish civil registries, there remains uncertainty about what legal consequences that will have in practice, especially given that Poland’s domestic law does not allow for any legally recognised form of same-sex union. Legal experts say that it may take years – and potentially many more legal challenges by same-sex couples – for the situation to be clarified. Separately, parliament earlier this year approved a bill, proposed by the ruling coalition, that would have granted same-sex couples in Poland certain rights normally granted to married couples. However, the law was vetoed by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition. Poland has begun recognising foreign same-sex marriages. But the legal consequences for such couples remain unclear, especially as Polish law does not allow any form of same-sex union We asked five experts for their view on what this will mean in practice https://t.co/h2KHmW8sMI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Ukraine to establish new national pantheon as Poland warns against honouring massacre figures
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Volodymyr Zelensky has signed a law establishing a new national pantheon to commemorate Ukrainian historical heroes. While it is not yet known which figures will be honoured there, Poland has expressed concern that they will include nationalist leaders associated with massacres of Poles in World War Two. On Sunday, a Polish deputy foreign minister warned that Kyiv “will have a huge problem” integrating with the European Union if it celebrates such individuals. But Zelensky reiterated that “only Ukrainians will decide who is a hero to us”. The establishment of the pantheon has taken place against the backdrop of a diplomatic crisis triggered in May by Zelensky’s decision to name a military unit after the “heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA)”. Parts of the UPA were responsible for the so-called Volhynia massacres during World War Two, in which Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, as part of an ethnic cleansing operation. Poland regards the episode as a genocide, though Ukraine strongly rejects that label. Many Ukrainians hold the UPA in high regard for the role that it played in fighting for independence from Moscow-backed Soviet rule. Poland condemned Zelensky’s decision and stripped him of the country’s highest honour, the Order of the White Eagle. In response, the Ukrainian president announced in late June that he would seek to create a new national pantheon, because “no one will dictate which heroes we should honour”. A bill creating the pantheon was subsequently approved by the Ukrainian parliament in July, and, on Saturday, Zelensky signed it into law, just ahead of today’s celebrations of Ukrainian independence day. “A Ukrainian pantheon will definitely be established, and only Ukrainians will decide for themselves who our heroes are,” declared Zelensky at a meeting with military veterans on Saturday. “All our true heroes…who fought for Ukraine, for our independence…deserve due honour.” However, the introduction of the law only now begins the process of building the pantheon itself – where the remains of those chosen as national heroes will be reburied – and the establishment of an advisory body that will decide which figures should receive such an honour. It therefore remains unknown for now who will be included in the pantheon. However, on Sunday, Polish deputy foreign minister Marcin Bosacki warned against honouring figures associated with the Volhynia massacres. “Every nation and its government has the right to choose the heroes they deem appropriate,” emphasised Bosacki in an interview with broadcaster TVP. “However, if individuals responsible for mass crimes against civilians, such as [Stepan] Bandera or [Roman] Shukhevych, are included in Ukraine’s national pantheon, it would significantly worsen Ukraine’s relations not only with Poland but with Europe in general,” he added. Bandera was the leader of a faction of the Organisation of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN-B), which in turn founded the UPA. Shukhevych was a military leader of the UPA. Both figures continue to be honoured in Ukraine, often prompting protests from Poland. 🇵🇱 Polskie MSZ ostrzegło Ukrainę przed „ogromnymi problemami” z Europą z powodu Bandery i Szuchewycza „Ukraina wie, że z tymi, którzy zabijali nie tylko Polaków, ale także Ukraińców, Czechów, Żydów i Romów, na swoich sztandarach będzie miała ogromne problemy z integracją… pic.twitter.com/hyujMppbEw — NEXTA Polska (@nexta_polska) August 24, 2026 “Ukraine knows that, with those who murdered not only Poles, but also some Ukrainians, Czechs, Jews and Roma, on its banners, it will have a huge problem integrating with Europe,” added Bosacki. However, the deputy minister also emphasised that, “strategiaclly, the interests of Poland and Ukraine remain very close” and that Poland must continuing “supporting Ukraine in defeating the aggressive Russia”. “We do not differ much with the Ukrainians, only with certain parts of the Ukrainian authorities after their absolutely erroneious decision to name a unit after the ‘heroes of the UPA’.” The proportion of Poles who hold a negative view of relations with Ukraine has risen to the highest level ever recorded by state research agency CBOS Meanwhile, the proportion who believe reconciliation with Ukraine is possible is at its lowest ever level https://t.co/YYBCFkVxNr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026 Polish government figures have previously made it clear that, if Ukraine honours figures associated with historical massacres, that will make it harder for the country to achieve its ambitions of joining the EU. In June, deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz warned that “you can’t build a pantheon to those who destroy European cooperation”, and that countries seeking EU membership should “not build national identity…on events, people or systems that in some way raise objections or pain among EU partners”. Kosiniak-Kamysz declared that, just as Zelensky said no one will tell Ukraine who they can honour, “no one will tell us how to vote on the entry of any state into the European Union”. That was an allusion to the fact that Poland, like all other EU member states, can veto Ukraine’s accession to the bloc. Polish and Ukrainian media have widely quoted Poland's deputy PM as saying: “With Bandera, Ukraine will not enter the EU.” However, he did not actually speak those words. We explain what @KosiniakKamysz actually said and how it came to be misinterpreted https://t.co/S3bozRIJTA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 1, 2026 ​ Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers.
