World.title: Mosaic artist reveals personal tribute to fallen officers in Porepunkah
World.content:
The north-east Victorian communities of Bright and Wangaratta are making unique artistic tributes to two fallen police officers as family and police colleagues gather today, a year after their deaths.

Detective Leading Senior Constable Neal Thompson and Senior Constable Vadim de Waart-Hottart were shot and killed at Porepunkah on August 26 last year while serving a warrant on Dezi Freeman.

The officers' names became internationally renowned and now their faces are being set in stone in gardens and in hundreds of pieces of tiny coloured tiles in the towns they served.

Two gardens have grown from the grief of the past year, one in Wangaratta, unveiled on Tuesday, and one in Bright, where the community is gathering today, on the anniversary of their deaths.

Victoria Police Chief Commissioner Mike Bush has described the anniversary as a solemn day for all Victoria Police members.

"Over the last 12 months I have witnessed our organisation unite in times of utter shock and grief, all while remaining steadfast in finding answers for our beloved colleagues," he said.

"Today we come together to pause, reflect and remember these exceptional police officers who dedicated their lives to protecting the Victorian community."

Two gardens, one purpose

In Wangaratta, where Neal Thompson was stationed for almost 20 years, two three-tonne obelisks sourced from the small town of Barjarg form a permanent memorial honouring both officers.

It is one of the largest police memorials of its kind, rivalled only by the Victoria Police Memorial in Melbourne's Kings Domain Gardens.

Mr Thompson's sisters, Dianne Thompson and Lois Kirk, said they felt his absence every day.

"Neal was fiercely loyal, a natural leader and just as tough as he was soft," they said.

"It’s what made him such a good police officer."

He had been days away from retirement, so his sisters also mourn a lost future filled with plans of world travel and Australian adventures.

"We are beyond devastated that it has been taken away from him, from us.

"We are forever proud of the way Neal lived his life and will miss him for the rest of ours."

His partner, Lisa Thompson, said the past year had been the hardest of her life, and she still expected him to come through the front door.

"We lost Neal, our world, and the bright, adventurous future that our family had planned together," she said.

"His loss has ripped through our hearts, our family and our community."

The Victoria Police Memorial in Kings Domain, Melbourne. (ABC News: Geraden Cann)

A memorial in mosaics

In Bright, the tribute to the fallen officers is more intricate.

A local mosaic artist who is known as Crackpot 1 was approached by a local police officer and asked to create artwork for the memorial.

She said the request had left her "absolutely gobsmacked".

"I felt so privileged to have been asked to do something like that ' she said.

The artist says she was "gobsmacked" to be asked to create a lasting tribute for the fallen officers. (ABC News: Ashlee Aldridge)

The artist created two large, full-colour mosaic portraits of the officers, drawing inspiration from photographs.

"The photos that came up usually in the news or in the newspaper were perfect," she said.

"They were just iconic of these two men."

Both portraits had their challenges and the artist said, at times, she found herself talking to her subjects.

"If I was having difficulty I'd say, come on, come on guys, give me some help here," she said.

The photographs of the two police officers used as inspiration by the artist to create the mosaic portraits. (Supplied: Victoria Police.)

She had never met either officer but through the work, she said she began to feel she knew them.

"I didn't know these men, but to know that they were doing the right thing by our community, I felt like I did know them," she said.

The mosaic portraits will hang in the police station as a tribute to the officers. (ABC News: Ashlee Aldridge)

Alongside the portraits, she created mosaic versions of the police blue ribbon, the officers' names and their badge numbers, which will sit on stone in the garden outside the Bright Police Station.

Even those tiles came with their own small story.

The artist had been given some tiny blue and white tiles several years ago.

When she realised she was six or seven blue tiles short, she contacted the woman who had given them to her.

She still had more.

"It sort of, you think things happen for a reason," she said.

"You just gotta think, 'Well, someone's watching over you.'"

The artist has been anonymously creating artwork across the region for several years. (ABC News: Ashlee Aldridge)

She hoped the garden would become somewhere people could come to remember, and somewhere they could simply be still.

"I think a garden will always bring people peace and some mindfulness," she said.

She also hoped it would serve as a gesture of gratitude to the officers who continued to serve every day.

The portraits are made from tiny pieces of tiles each put together by hand to recreate the photos of the fallen officers. (ABC News: Ashlee Aldridge)

Grief remains heavy

The streets around the Bright Police Station are being closed today.

There is a minute's silence.

There are flowers, gardens and stone.

And there are blue and white ribbons and two faces pieced together tile by tile.

Crackpot 1 works on mosaic pieces in her studio in north-east Victoria. (ABC News: Ashlee Aldridge)

Vadim de Waart-Hottard's family said the burden of their grief had been shared by those who loved him.

"The words, care and support we have received from Vadim’s police family and the community have been extraordinary," their statement said.

"The grief of our family has been shared with a caring community, and we have been uplifted by the support provided, at a time of incredible grief.

"It has brought comfort to our family since Vadim's departure from our lives at Porepunkah. An Aboriginal word meaning the meeting of two rivers."

Travis Carroll, president of the Blue Ribbon Foundation's north-east branch, said memorials gave families and communities a place to come, remember and honour fallen officers.

Travis Carroll says memorials give people a place to remember and honour fallen officers (ABC News: Annie Brown.)

"We don't forget any of our members," he said.

"I think that that local connection and that local place where people can go, pay their respects, honour those people and their service and the tragedy of their loss, it's really important," he said.

The family of the gunman also paid tribute to the fallen officers, releasing a statement acknowledging today was about remembering "two men didn't get to go home to their loved ones".

"Two families were changed forever, and the members who witnessed what happened will carry that day with them, too," the Filby family statement read.

"There is a time and place for difficult questions and criticism. Today isn’t it. Today should be about remembering Neal and Vadim, and the families, friends and colleagues whose lives will never be the same again.

"Our hearts are with Neal and Vadim's families today."

The blue police ribbon is a symbol used to remember police officers who have died in the line of duty. (ABC News: Annie Brown)

A year after two police officers left home to do their jobs and never returned, the north-east has made places for them to remain.

Not just in the official record.

Not just on a memorial wall in Melbourne.

But here, among the people they served.

In Wangaratta and in Bright.

In the quiet gardens that have grown from grief.

"Victoria Police will carry forth Neal and Vadim’s legacies for the rest of time," Police Chief Commissioner Mike Bush said.

World.title: How getting surf life saving into the Olympics could save lives
World.content:
What would the Australian summer — or indeed winter — be without the ubiquitous yellow and red flags on beaches around the country?

Surf life savers are as essential as sunscreen and deliver an unquestionable sense of comfort and ease among holiday-makers and residents alike.

And the competitive arm of the movement, the Iron Series, is almost as synonymous with the Australian sporting summer as the echo of leather on willow at the nation's cricket grounds or the thwack of tennis balls at Melbourne Park.

But as hard-fought and intense as the racing is throughout the series, the sporting aspect pales into insignificance when compared to the bigger picture of what Surf Life Saving is truly about.

"This sport is born out of such an important part of Australian culture," number one-seeded athlete Charlie Verco tells ABC Sport on the beach at Surfers Paradise.

"That is ocean safety and being able to help other people in danger."

Charlie Verco is the number one seed for this year's Iron Series championship. (Supplied)

Just like fellow Iron Series number one seed Tiarnee Massie, Verco has first-hand experience of just how important his skills are away from the sporting arena.

"I've had countless examples of having to just apply those skills in living my everyday life … the skills that you learn to how to rescue people," the 24-year-old says.

Almost drowning as a child, now saving others as Surf Life Saving's number one A childhood accident could so easily have cost Surf Life Saver Tiarnee Massie her life. But now the 28-year-old heads into this year's Iron Series as the number one seed.

"And for me recently, I had a pretty full-on one example of that with the shark attack with Leah."

Saturday, June 13, 2026, is a date that will not be quickly forgotten by Verco or anyone else who was on Coogee Beach.

Sydney teacher Leah Stewart was attacked by a three- to four-metre-long shark, believed to be a Great White, while swimming between the flags at the popular spot in Sydney's east.

Stewart's extensive injuries resulted in her having to undergo multiple surgeries and her arm being amputated during an extended hospital stay.

Fatefully and thankfully, Verco was also in the water that day and his training instantly kicked into gear as he rushed to Stewart's aid, his quick response earning widespread praise as being among the reasons Stewart was not killed.

Charlie Verco grew up at North Bondi surf club and now competes for Newport. (Supplied: Charlie Verco)

"There was definitely a lot of thoughts going through my head," Verco says.

"And it wasn't clear thinking, but that's what is going to happen no matter what, and it's having spent that time ingraining it so that you don't have to think about what the right thing to do is what made the difference.

"I actually had to tell some swimmers that were near me that wanted to get taken to the shore … I really wanted to paddle in, so picking up one of the swimmers near me would have been a really good excuse to go in.

"But then I assessed the shark and I thought because I was on such a big board I could scare away that shark if I went in there, maybe.

"Then I saw the shark come out of the water and I was like, 'that thing's not scared of me.'"

Swim for Sydney shark attack victim A Sydney shark attack victim has been hailed "a survivor" by her family in a letter read out at a community swim event.

Battling his fears, Verco plunged into the mix, getting Stewart onto his board and quickly backing them towards the shore and further assistance.

"I've never been more grateful to being part of this life-saving community and having experienced that training," Verco, who competes for Newport Surf Life Saving Club on Sydney's north shore, says.

"So many of the lessons I've learned through that have played in as factors to what allowed me to help her that day.

"When someone started screaming shark and I saw this thing in the water, all I wanted to do was paddle to shore.

"But growing up in the community embedded a sense of responsibility to help others, especially in the water when I have the ability to [do it]."

Charlie Verco will look to win the title outright for the first time when the series concludes at Surfers Paradise in February. (Supplied)

That was not the only time Verco has had to race to the aid of a member of the public in the ocean.

"The shark attack's definitely the most dramatic one that's happened and probably the scariest one because it was the one where I felt like I was in real danger," Verco says.

"But there's been countless examples where I've been out surfing in Bondi and people will swim out and I'll drag someone in.

"Up in Queensland, the beaches are so much longer so I've had to do some pretty serious rescues … we had to run 500 metres down the beach with a board before we actually padded out to get someone … they had some pretty serious water inhalation and got taken away to hospital but they would have died if we didn't have the combination of fitness skills and knowledge to help them.

"All of my mates have heaps of different anecdotal experiences, whether it's just driving to work and someone in the car in front of you had a heart attack, I have a mate who did CPR on the way to work, my mum and my sister were down at their camp for school and they had to do CPR on one of the parents, just out of nowhere.

"It happens. You never think it's going to happen. But I never thought I was going to be in a shark attack."

Charlie Verco finished the Moloka'i 2 Oahu Paddleboard World Championships in July in a new record time. (Supplied: Moloka'i 2 Oahu Paddleboard World Championships)

Verco, who is also a four-time Paddleboard World Champion, noted that the skills he has learned from a competitive aspects of Surf Life Saving helped him when it mattered most.

"Just in how to manage your mindset under a really high-stress environment," he says.

"There's a lot of pressure in being able to perform for that one race in massive surf to get that Iron Series title, but also when you're managing a huge amount of fear and you see a woman getting attacked by a shark and being able to take that pause and think what is the actual best action to do as opposed to just reacting off of a whim and potentially make mistakes and put yourself or other people in danger.

"I think that transfers across in so many different areas."

Olympic showcase with an important message

Australia's leading Surf Life Savers have their eyes set on joining the Olympic family. (Supplied)

In six years' time, Brisbane will showcase its sporting environment to the world when the 2032 Olympics roll into town.

Surf Life Saving is already making its case to organisers that their sport deserves to be included, and as two of the sport's biggest names, Massie and Verco, are fully behind it.

"Surf Life Saving is such an embedded part in Australian culture," Verco says.

"There's no better way to represent Australia at such an incredible event. The Olympics is the top tier, the pinnacle event of sporting competition.

Surf lifesaving is preparing its Olympic push Ali Day wants to figure in surf lifesaving's push for Olympic inclusion, determined to ensure his sport doesn't "cop it" like breaking did in Paris.

"It's what any athlete who grows up watching sport says 'that's where I want to go one day.'

"Not only is the sport incredible, but it's embedded in such an important idea around surf safety and helping others through surf safety as well.

"That is something that's so well ingrained in Australia, but I also think it's something that's really important to spread around the world.

"There's countless number of drownings on beaches all around the world every year, so I think being able to get this sport on a stage where people around the world can see it and see how incredible it is and maybe embed cultures that exist similar to the Nippers culture where you learn those skills about how to be safe in the water from an early age and then bring that experience and skill into helping others around the world I think will be able to save incredible numbers of lives every year.

"It's a no-brainer to put surf life saving in it. I think it's the best option there is."

There are plenty of things in favour of Surf Life Saving joining the Olympic movement.

Under current arrangements, the Brisbane 2032 organisers can propose a maximum of four additional disciplines from the core events.

One of the key aims of the Fit for the Future program is for the Olympics to help promote: "A future where sport is part of everyday life for more people, creating resilient communities, enabling health and well-being, education and inclusion."

No extra infrastructure is needed, and despite the sport being considered uniquely Australian, there is a world championships, which will take place this year in Gqeberha, South Africa.

Tiarnee Massie says giving Surf Life Saving a platform at the Olympics would be very important. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

Massie, who has previously made Australian national age group squads in the Olympic sport of kayaking, says having Surf Lifesaving at the 2032 Games would be "iconic".

"Having the Olympics in Brisbane for 2032 is so special for every sport that is in the Olympics," Massie says.

"But to get surf life saving into the Olympics is… it would be iconic.

"It is iconic to Australians, it's iconic to everyone who lives here, who lives near the water and the beach and I think it it's only right to have that in the Olympic Games, to showcase to the other countries what we can do and how important the sport is to Australians.

"No other sport does that; no other sport is trying to prepare to be the best at saving someone's life. But our sport is.

"To showcase that to the rest of the country and to the world would be so important, and to get that to the Olympic Games and get everyone's eyes on the importance of what we are doing, it would be so special."

World.title: Animal rescuer warns of rooster influx, says school hatching programs making issue worse
World.content:
An Adelaide-based animal rescuer shelter says it cannot take anymore roosters after a "heartbreaking" influx of reports.

Fairview Lodge Animal Shelter president Kerri Bryant said she had been receiving messages of people finding abandoned roosters that had been dumped in bushland.

"After the initial anger, it's heartbreaking," she said.

She said her farmstead, which looks after a range of animals including horses, pigs, ducks and cockatoos, was at capacity and could not take any more roosters, especially with the spread of bird flu putting animal owners on high alert.

An animal rescue in Adelaide Hills says it has been inundated with reports of roosters being dumped. (ABC News/Briana Fiore)

Ms Bryant said she had been speaking with other animal rescue organisations who believed school egg hatching programs, which are designed to teach students about the cycle of life, biology and responsibility, were contributing to the problem.

"Nobody is taking responsibility for breeding these birds, they breed them and then just turf them out," she said.

Ms Bryant said she had recently received a text from a parent that read: "Please let us know if you can take our rooster, we've got him from the school hatching program, he's very much loved by the kids but we've had council complaints and we just don't want him to become someone's dinner".

"You wouldn't breed kittens to teach children about the circle of life, and then hand kittens out to kids, don't do it with chickens, it's no different," Ms Bryant said.

Fairview Lodge Animal Shelter's Kerri Bryant says her animal rescue is full to the brim with roosters. (ABC News/Briana Fiore)

Rules for keeping roosters in residential areas vary from council to council, but councils including Salisbury and Onkaparinga "do not recommend" keeping roosters due to the noise.

RSPCA against hatching programs

The RSPCA told the ABC it was opposed to poultry egg hatching programs in schools.

"[The RSPCA] does not support the keeping, breeding or use of living animals in all schools other than schools teaching animal agriculture because they do not have appropriate facilities and trained staff to adequately protect the welfare of animals in this setting," a spokesperson said.

"This includes such aspects as housing, handling, veterinary care, ethical sourcing and ensuring suitable animals are appropriately rehomed after their use."

The RSPCA says it does not support the school hatching programs. (ABC News/Briana Fiore)

A South Australian Education Department spokesperson said it took the wellbeing of any animal at schools seriously, but said it was up to individual school to implement their own programs and not covered by the department's animal care and welfare program.

"When contacted for advice or support, the department works with sites to ensure all animals/birds and aquaculture programs are run in accordance with ethics and acceptable standards of animal husbandry," the spokesperson said.

The department did not comment on how many schools were operating hatching programs in South Australia.

Fairview Lodge Animal Shelter's Kerri Bryant has been inundated with messages about roosters. (ABC News/Briana Fiore)

It follows other concerns raised by animal rescue organisation in South Australia that they will not be able to deal with an expected influx of birds impacted by H5N1 bird flu.

Vet organisations in South Australia have also warned of the toll on those in the animal welfare sector, and that it may be forced to kill hordes of wild birds they could be saving due to a lack of funding and appropriate facilities amid the H5 bird flu crisis.

Last year, an animal rescue service sounded the alarm on rooster dumping, but blamed the rise of people buying chicks for egg laying for the rise.

World.title: Meet the AI-trained robot 'parent' helping prepare new teachers for conflict
World.content:
With conflicts at school gates across Australia happening on "a day-to-day basis", Professor Therese Keane hopes a new robot powered by artificial intelligence will help prepare teachers and stop them from leaving the profession.

"We have verbal aggression and physical assault," Professor Keane, a digital education expert at La Trobe University, said.

"It is quite a large problem. A lot of the time it's under-reported and so we don't really have a true picture of what's going on," she said.

A longitudinal survey of principals has found violence against teachers increased by 80 per cent over the past 15 years.

'Kicked' and 'bitten' principals report violence The level of violence faced by school leaders is the worst it's ever been, according to a long-running survey of more than 2,000 principals.

While emphasising that most parents interacted with schools respectfully, Professor Keane said conflict with those who did not could be so distressing that teachers quit.

"After a couple of hits of these sorts of interactions they lose their self-confidence, their self-esteem and that then starts to make them concerned, stressed, burned out," Professor Keane said.

Professor Keane's solution was to draw on hour-long interviews with 20 senior educators, identify common gripes from parents, and group them into scenarios.

Sources of conflict between parents and schools, identified by researchers Parents blaming the school/teacher for a bad result or child's chronic lateness.

Parents sending long one-sided accusatory emails over issues like bullying.

Parents in denial about a student's academic performance or behaviour.

Parents dismissing basic school expectations on behaviour.

Parents engaging in high-risk escalation threats i.e. publicly interrogating a new teacher.

She and her team then used AI to write scripts to allow Fletch the robot to act as a disgruntled parent in a difficult conversation with trainee and early career teachers.

Therese Keane with Fletch the robot, who is helping teachers practise difficult conversations with disgruntled parents. (ABC News: Billy Draper)

"They come in very nervous, they're not entirely sure what to expect, they sit there, and do this for about four or five minutes," Professor Keane said.

" They feel exhausted [afterwards]. They feel it's relentless at times. "

Cherry Demir is a PhD student and teacher helping train the new teachers.

She said Fletch's manner could change to mimic a parent becoming increasingly unreasonable.

Cherry Demir says practise conversations with the robot will help prepare teachers for real scenarios. (ABC News: Billy Draper)

"It's voice changes, it becomes more aggressive as time goes forward and it does get a little bit difficult and scary, especially for pre-service teachers," Ms Demir said.

" When you're not well prepared it's extremely intimidating, because you're caught off guard most of the time. "

Ms Demir has been working with Fletch for three years and said new teachers left the training well prepared for real-world scenarios.

Fletch the robot has been trained to become increasingly unreasonable as conversations progress. (ABC News: Billy Draper)

"I think this will be invaluable for pre-service teacher preparation. It will be an excellent way to gain confidence," Ms Demir said.

Teachers, parents under a lot more pressure

Long-serving principal Henry Grossek, who retired last year, had almost six decades experience to draw on when training Fletch.

During a 57-year teaching career, 38 of them as a principal, he has seen it all.

Unfortunately, his view is that conflict at schools has risen.

Henry Grossek retired in 2025 after a long teaching career and says parents and teachers are under a lot of pressure. (ABC News: Patrick Stone)

"The world has changed a lot," Mr Grossek said.

"Post-COVID, we see a different scenario in schools. Parents are under a lot more pressure for a variety of reasons.

"They don't always articulate their concern or their problem in a way that leads to a productive conversation. Teachers are in the exact same boat."

Mr Grossek said Fletch the robot was an exciting initiative that would equip teachers to de-escalate challenging conversations.

"We've got this perfect storm, where if we've not got productive conversations and relationships between parents and the school, at the end of the day the children will suffer," Mr Grossek said.

At La Trobe University, Professor Keane said other uses for Fletch were already being explored, such as difficult conversations between teachers, as well as between teachers and students.

Further along, Fletch could also have a role as a classroom assistant, helping identify students not paying attention, she said.

According to the team at La Trobe University, it is an example of the benefits that can come from AI, even as society wrestles with potential downsides.

"These simulations are very positive. This is not something to be feared," Professor Keane said.

World.title: Sugar tax may prevent millions of dental procedures, study suggests
World.content:
With oral diseases affecting about 3.5 billion people across the globe, health experts have yet again thrown their support behind a proposed 20 per cent tax on sugary drinks, which they say may have a significant effect on improving the oral health of Australians.

A new Australian study, published today in BMJ Public Health, suggests the tax on soft drinks and most juices could prevent 3.7 million cases of tooth decay, 191,000 cases of gum disease, and 115,000 cases of complete tooth loss nationally over the next 25 years.

Lead author and Griffith University research fellow Mishel Shahid said it was the first Australian study to quantify the impacts of a proposed sugar tax beyond tooth decay.

"Obviously we're not saying that a sugar tax would solve all [dental] problems, but it definitely has a big impact," Dr Shahid said.

With nearly one in three Australians aged 15 years and above living with untreated tooth decay or cavities, Dr Shahid said the study highlighted "significant" oral health benefits of the proposed tax.

"Most of the debate that we've seen around sugar taxes has focused primarily on obesity and diabetes," she said.

" What we wanted to do was to also look at what impact such a tax would have on the mouth, which is often siloed from the body. "

The research suggests millions of dental procedures may be prevented under a 20 per cent sugar tax. (Pexels: Elizabeth Lizzie)

Dr Shahid suggested any money gained from a proposed tax should be used to strengthen oral health services in Australia, making trips to the dentist cheaper and more accessible.

Ten years of sugar tax debate

The proposal of a tax on sugar-sweetened beverages is not new.

Ten years ago, a report from the World Health Organization (WHO) suggested a 20 per cent tax on sugary drinks would lower consumption and reduce obesity, type 2 diabetes and tooth decay.

Since the report's release, about 115 countries, including Mexico and Hungary, have introduced sugar taxes and the United Kingdom has a similar levy on high-sugar drinks.

In 2018, a parliamentary report into Australia's obesity epidemic recommended the government introduce a tax on sugar-sweetened beverages, finding that the "vast majority" of submissions — with the exception of the food and beverage industry — supported the idea.

At the time, Coca-Cola Amatil and other submitters claimed there was very little evidence that taxes targeting sugar-sweetened beverages would reduce obesity rates.

However, Australia did not introduce a tax on sugar-sweetened drinks following the recommendation, nor in subsequent years when health professionals called for one.

In 2024, the Australian Beverages Council, the peak body for non-alcoholic drinks, described the push to introduce a sugar tax as "illogical" and a "revenue raiser", claiming there was very little evidence that they worked and would add financial pressure to struggling Australian families.

The long shadow of soft-drink giants and sugar labelling In April, the nation's doctors called again for the introduction of a tax on sugar-sweetened drinks. They are not alone, but here's an insight into why it's still not happening.

Australian Dental Association vice-president and practising dentist Angie Nilsson, who did not contribute to the study, said Australia was "behind the times".

"We've got great evidence from the UK that shows that after a sugary drinks levy, people reduced their consumption," Dr Nilsson said.

"On top of that, there's been evidence that there has been a reduction in people presenting to hospitals with preventable admissions for oral health diseases."

Dr Nilsson said this new study built on existing research to show the potential oral benefits of a sugar tax.

"Whilst it's not surprising, it certainly adds to the body of evidence to show that sugars in Western modern-day diets need to be reduced somehow," she said.

But she also pointed out the study did not include energy drinks, which she considered one of the "worst offenders".

Therefore, Dr Nilsson said, the true benefit of a sugar tax could be even more significant than suggested.

Modelling from 2021 by the Australian Medical Association, which has long lobbied for a similar tax, suggested a 20 per cent tax hike on sugar-sweetened drinks might result in 16,000 fewer cases of type 2 diabetes, 4,400 fewer cases of heart disease and 1,100 fewer cases of stroke over a 25-year period.

Health Minister Mark Butler has been contacted for comment.

Modelling dental and health benefits

To understand the impact of a sugar tax, the researchers looked at two scenarios, one with no sugar tax and a second following the introduction of a 20 per cent tax on sugar-sweetened drinks.

"The difference between those outcomes helps us quantify the impact of the tax," Dr Shahid said.

The projections were modelled off Australia's 2019 population, using estimates from the Global Burden of Disease 2019 study to predict dental outcomes over a 25-year period.

Tasman Davies, PhD candidate at the George Institute for Global Health who did not contribute to the study, said the potential dental benefits of a sugar tax could be seen after just one year, with significant improvement noted after five.

"The reduction in dental caries [tooth decay] would be fully seen in five years," he said.

" Whereas the argument for diabetes and heart diseases is very important to consider, but that takes a lot longer to see improvements in those health outcomes. "

Dr Nilsson said, from an oral health perspective, reducing sugar intake had a positive impact in just a few weeks.

"But it's also not just the sugar; sweet beverages also carry that acidic content that has compounded with causing tooth decay and other diseases," she said.

A separate Australian study, published in April in The Lancet Public Health, modelled the potential health benefits of a 20 per cent tax on unhealthy food such as confectionery, chips, ice cream as well as a 20 per cent subsidy on fruits and vegetables.

It found these measures could prevent 212,000 premature deaths in Australia and save $14.9 billion in health-care costs over the lifetimes of adults alive today.

"A broader tax on unhealthy foods could have around seven times the health benefits as a tax on sugary drinks alone," said Mr Davies, the lead author of the study published in The Lancet in April.

"It could also be orders-of-magnitude more powerful than other food policies such as mandating the health-star rating or restricting advertising or educational campaigns."

Mr Davis's study suggested using the income generated from the tax to offset the subsidy on fresh fruit and vegetables.

Sugar audit shows scale of problem

An audit from the Food for Health Alliance, published last week, found that some drinks sold in Australian supermarkets had up to 2.5 times the daily limit of sugar recommended for good health.

Some 600ml soft drinks contained about 16 teaspoons of sugar and large cans of energy drinks had about 13 teaspoons of sugar in them.

WHO recommends adults consume no more than 12 teaspoons of free sugar a day, and ideally limit consumption to six teaspoons.

Jane Martin, executive manager of the Food for Health Alliance, said sugary drinks were the biggest contributor to sugar consumption in Australian diets, making up a quarter of total sugar intake.

“Sugar content in Australian drinks is not decreasing as much as it should be because we are not incentivising action through a tax based on the amount of sugar in these drinks," she said.

She wants Australia to introduce a tiered sugary drinks tax paid for by companies, similar to the UK's soft drinks levy.

Dr Nilsson said a sugar tax would either change consumer behaviour, with the higher price convincing them to make a different choice, or force manufacturers to rethink their formula.

After the UK introduced a sugar levy, some drinks manufacturers voluntarily reformulated their products to avoid the tax, which made them healthier for people to consume.

Angie Nilsson wants a tax on sugar-sweetened beverages to be introduced in Australia. (Supplied: Australian Dental Association)

With soft drinks often priced similarly to bottled water, Dr Nilsson said it was "too easy" for Australians to access them.

But Mr Davies said his study showed that for maximum impact, there needed to be a "two-pronged approach" where a tax was introduced for sugary drinks and healthier choices were subsided to make them cheaper.

Often, he said, junk food was cheaper and more convenient than healthier choices, which made it challenging for families on lower incomes to eat well.

"If we look over the past 50 years, food products look very different," he said.

"At least half of the food that we eat [today] is what's called ultra-processed.

"In the food system, things are stacked against us. Unhealthy foods have highly prevalent s, and so a policy like taxation can help counteract those forces that push us towards unhealthy foods."

World.title: Inside One Nation's campaign to conquer Secret Harbour
World.content:
It's just after 6 o'clock on a stormy Monday morning when a barefoot Luke Herdegen meets 7.30 in a car park by the beach south of Perth.

He's the One Nation candidate in the Secret Harbour state by-election and has agreed to let us follow him on a day of campaigning, which starts with a run and a swim.

Loading...

"I just love it. It makes me feel alive, especially when the weather is like this," he said.

I ask him if there's a metaphor in that.

"I think there's definitely a storm brewing," he replied.

Access all areas

This kind of access to One Nation is unusual for the ABC, which has been barred, along with The Guardian, from most of the party's events across the country.

Campaigning alongside his candidate, Western Australia's One Nation leader Rod Caddies says he's running things differently.

"Pauline doesn't restrict us on what we're allowed to do. Her decisions are her decisions, and I support her doing that because she obviously feels that she's not being treated the way she should be," he said.

One Nation candidate Luke Herdegen with the party's leader in WA, Rod Caddies. (ABC News)

Later I questioned Mr Herdegen about some of Pauline Hanson's comments — including suggesting there are no "good" Muslims and labelling domestic violence a "two-way street" — and Mr Caddies intervened.

"That's been done over and over about the good Muslim thing. I think that's coming back to that reason why Pauline hasn't let ABC in," Mr Caddies said.

"It's not something that anyone is talking about in the community here," Mr Herdegen added. "It's just not really an issue down here."

" I don't think she does peddle racist messages and no-one in the party peddles racist messages. "

Mr Herdegen's sister is among those who disagree.

He said she was not talking to him after he told her he was running for the party.

Luke Herdegen says One Nation leader Pauline Hanson does not "peddle racist messages". (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"She sees Pauline Hanson and One Nation as racist, and I guess not sort of supporting the things that she supports," he said.

"I love my sister. We're a close family, but yeah, like all families and all communities, not everybody agrees … we have to be able to disagree."

Mr Herdegen's campaign has not been without controversy. There were questions about his social media posts about using and then quitting cocaine.

"I've certainly done some things in my past that I'm not particularly proud of, but I'm certainly proud of the person that I've become and the character that those things have built in me and the people that I've been able to inspire through that," he said.

Loyalty drifts as cost of living bites

Secret Harbour has always been a safe Labor seat, but outer-suburban seats like this, where housing and cost of living are front of mind, are considered the next frontier for One Nation.

"It's the young ones I feel sorry for, trying to get off the ground away from Mum and Dad," an older voter told us at Secret Harbour Beach.

Secret Harbour is a southern suburb of Perth. (ABC News: West Matteeussen)

"I'm building a house at the moment and prices of everything … it's just through the roof, and it's mainly because we're overpopulated," a voter in his 20s said.

Others tell us they feel let down by the major parties.

"I just think Labor and Liberal, they haven't done anything since they've been parties really, have they? Let's be honest," one man told us.

"I've always voted Labor, always, my whole life, because they were for the middle-class people, but now they're not," a woman said.

'Significant' contest

Former journalist Peter Kennedy has covered politics for more than 40 years and said this by-election was the most significant in some time.

Peter Kennedy says the major parties are grappling with how to deal with One Nation. (ABC News: West Matteeussen)

"There are far fewer rusted-on voters now than there were, and in the outer suburbs, that's where that party loyalty, I think, is falling away," Mr Kennedy said.

" A big swing to One Nation in the Secret Harbour by-election would send shock waves through the major parties. "

"One Nation potentially is becoming a force in Australian politics, and the reality then, for the major parties, is how do you deal with it?

"Do you ignore them or do you strike some sort of arrangement with them? And that's what's playing out at the moment."

Labor's candidate in Secret Harbour, Georgia Tree, navigated that challenge every day.

Labor candidate for Secret Harbour, Georgia Tree. (ABC News: Courtney Bembridge)

"We're a microcosm here, and there's a lot of scrutiny on this seat because it's part of a broader movement that we've seen all over the world," she said.

"So it's interesting for me to be in the Petri dish, as it were, and everyone's looking to see what happens.

" I never would've imagined that I'd be coming up against One Nation and the level of support that they do have. I'm in the fight of my life, that's for sure. "

"But I will keep fighting, and that's why I am here, because I know that people in my community and this place that is my home will benefit from a WA Labor government.

At the WA state election last year, One Nation got less than 9 per cent of the vote in Secret Harbour, and Labor was ahead of the Liberals by 11.5 per cent.

Now it's thought Labor and One Nation are neck and neck and support for the Liberals is waning.

Liberal Party disagreement on One Nation

WA Liberal leader Basil Zempilas has chosen to preference One Nation third on the ballot.

"There is support for One Nation. Now for us to be disrespectful of that would be not acknowledging the current will of the people. So my approach has very much been to see One Nation's rise as an opportunity, not a threat," he said.

WA Liberal leader Basil Zempilas says he doesn't see One Nation as a threat. (ABC News: Jack Stevenson)

Parts of Secret Harbour sit within the federal electorate of Canning, held by Liberal MP Andrew Hastie.

He is one of the Coalition's loudest voices against One Nation, and he has criticised his party here in WA for not running hard enough against the party.

"I don't think that we see eye to eye on the political strategy," Mr Hastie told 7.30 on Monday.

Liberal MP Andrew Hastie says the Liberals should be "fighting for every single vote". (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"I don't accept this idea that a win for One Nation is a win for the Liberal Party. We're fighting for our lives and we should be fighting for every single vote.

"You don't wave the white flag. Voters sense weakness, and they'll go to the strong horse if you signal weakness."

Mr Zempilas denied the Liberal Party was running dead in the by-election.

"What I know is what we've done, and that is not the case," Mr Zempilas said.

World.title: Digital navigators bridge divide for older Australians
World.content:
Older Australians say they are struggling to maintain their independence as everyday services shift online and out of their reach.

The digital divide means the responsibility is falling to loved ones, neighbours, and retirement village staff to bridge the gap.

It's an experience familiar to 72-year-old Wendy Trow, who neighbours her 85-year-old sister Majorie Jones in the small Western Australian town Balingup.

"My sister is a very smart lady, but she's never used computers in her life and so she just goes into a shell when she's required to do something," she said.

Many older Australians struggle to access or operate technology, meaning friends or relatives have become their digital navigators. (ABC News: Scott Kyle)

Ms Trow has taken on the role of digital navigator, helping her older sister access online government aged care services and banking.

"When the bank said that they were no longer going to use cheques, that was the final straw for her," she said.

"Her children are fantastic, but they don't live in Balingup, so it's fallen to me to do that," Ms Trow said.

" Suddenly she had to give up her financial independence and trust me to do the right thing. "

Digital divide has isolated older Australians

Patricia Sparrow is the chief executive on the Council on the Ageing Australia, the peak body for older Australians.

She said the divide between those who comfortably access online services and those who cannot, had isolated some older people.

"It makes people feel that they can't cope. It makes people feel stupid. It discourages people from engaging," she said.

"If you can't go to the bank and do a transaction or talk to people locally in the community, you may feel quite isolated and excluded."

Ms Sparrow said digital exclusion was not an issue that would disappear with changing generations. (ABC News: Darryl Torpy)

Ms Jones, who was formerly a nurse, said she would be in an aged care home if not for her sister.

"I managed my life really well without computers, and I just don't seem to be able to switch onto the same wavelength as computers," she said.

"I start getting nervous and I feel stupid because I don't understand — we don't seem to speak the same language."

Nearly three hours-drive south east of Perth, Balingup's median age is 58, two decades older than the rest of Australia.

In addition to helping her sister, Ms Trow has put together a small group of volunteers to help older community members who have had trouble accessing the government's My Aged Care services on their own.

"It is an absolutely massive [responsibility], and what if we get it wrong?" she said.

"We've had no training, we're just using our common sense."

Marjorie Jones and Wendy Trow (ABC News: Gabrielle Mellet)

She believes her small town is one example of a broader national issue.

"It will particularly be small, rural areas, but also in the cities, there'll be people that are just falling through the cracks because it's too hard," she said.

Services 'can't be digital only'

Decades into the transition from paper to digital, research shows a majority of older Australians are struggling to access online platforms.

Data compiled by the Australian Digital Inclusion Index — which tracks people's ability to access, afford and benefit from digital technologies — found more than 65 per cent of people aged over 75 were digitally excluded.

Although the 2025 study found an improvement in access and digital ability over the previous two years, certain Australians are still more vulnerable to digital exclusion.

Access for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, those living in regional and remote locations, people with a disability and public housing residents remained below the national average.

Data compiled by the Australian Digital Inclusion Index found more than 65 per cent of people aged over 75 were digitally excluded. (ABC News: Scott Kyle)

Ms Sparrow said the issue of digital exclusion won't disappear as generations shift.

"I don't think you can just say this is a time-limited implementation issue that will resolve over generations," Ms Sparrow said.

" There are some people who will always have difficulty accessing and using digital platforms. "

Ms Sparrow said there had to be support for older Australians who could not rely on relatives to manage their online services.

"We have to acknowledge that things are moving increasingly to being digital first, but they can't be digital only," she said.

"Everybody wants to be as independent as possible. We all want to be able to run our own lives."

Some retirement villages are introducing digital literacy programs to combat online scams. (ABC News: Scott Kyle)

Seminars instilling confidence

Staff at Brisbane's Bolton Clarke retirement villages introduced a digital literacy program three years ago after increasing numbers of residents fell for scams.

"We decided we needed more education to avoid this, but also to keep [the residents] using technology … because they needed to," said Joe Griffiths, who runs the seminars across 27 villages.

The program shows residents how to search online, what to look for in a scam, and artificial intelligence.

Resident Joann Rose said these were topics that otherwise overwhelmed her.

"I'm not tech savvy at all. It's just changing too fast, it's hard to keep up," she said.

"So these information sessions are really good."

Brisbane retirement village resident Carmen Love likes being shown how technology works. (ABC News: Scott Kyle)

Mr Griffiths said it was particularly useful for people without loved ones around to help them understand new technologies.

"A lot of the families are excellent, and then some of the people don't have families," he said.

"So this is a place they can become part of a family, and ask the questions."

Carmen Love said she liked learning face-to-face.

"I like getting into technology now, but instead of reading about it, I like to be shown, then I remember it," she said.

In Balingup, Ms Trow said although she's happy to support her sister, all vulnerable residents should have access to in-person help with banking and government support.

"They need to be available in each community so that people can go and talk to them, sit down in a room and talk to them face-to-face," she said.

"I fear what changes are going to happen in the future for me. In another 10 years time, am I going to be in her situation?"

Want to have your say? Go to www.abc.net.au/yoursay

World.title: Regional residents furious deliveries they paid for aren't coming
World.content:
Residents in parts of regional Tasmania are furious with a delivery company, after they paid for a door-to-door delivery service that no longer exists.

Miena resident Michael Walls used to reliably receive deliveries from Team Global Express.

"We had a great service up until they've changed their policy about delivering to the Central Highlands," he said.

In recent months, he has been told by the company his deliveries have been taken to the depot in Cambridge near Hobart — a four-hour round trip from Miena.

Michael Walls is considering legal action, as he paid for the items to be delivered to his home. (ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough)

After Mr Walls complained to the company, Team Global Express arranged for its state manager to deliver his package, but two others remain at the depot.

"They're obligated to deliver it because they've been contracted to deliver the items," he said.

"They shouldn't have accepted the items that they weren't interested in delivering.

He is looking at launching legal action, believing the failure to deliver may be a violation of consumer law.

Team Global Express told the ABC the Tasmanian towns it recently stopped delivering to were Miena, Liawenee, Waddamana, Levendale, Tunnack, Bradys Lake, Bronte Park, Derwent Bridge, Lake St Clair, Maydena and Colebrook.

'We pay them to deliver'

Laurie Smythe ordered machinery bases from a Queensland company to his home in Colebrook, north of Hobart.

"I received a message from Team Global Express to say that I needed to pick the freight up from their base area at Cambridge," he said.

" I rang them up and I said, 'What's going on? You've got to deliver that to me', and they said, 'No, we don't deliver in that area anymore'. "

Laurie Smythe contacted the seller, which told him it had paid Team Global Express to deliver the items to his door. (ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough)

Mr Smythe was told it would be sent back to the sender if he did not pick it up within seven days.

He rang the company he purchased the freight from to explain that Team Global Express would not deliver it.

"'He said, 'Well, we pay them to deliver'," Mr Smythe said.

Laurie Smythe eventually made the two-hour trip from his home in Colebrook to the Team Global Express depot in Hobart. (ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough)

Eventually, Mr Smythe made the two-hour round trip to collect his freight from the depot.

"They were paid for it; they're supposed to be a national company doing deliveries," he said.

"In my mind, that's not acceptable.

" How many others yet don't know that their freight's on the road and they're not going to get it? "

Donna Barratt organised a petition calling for Team Global Express to continue delivering to Maydena. (Supplied)

Donna Barratt, who runs a cafe and an accommodation service in Maydena, said she did not have time to pick up every delivery.

"There's a lot of people in Maydena who actually don't drive, so they won't be able to go and pick it up either," she said.

She organised a petition, signed by about 70 community members, calling on Team Global Express to continue delivering to the area — which she said had gone unanswered.

In most cases when purchasing items online, customers are not able to view or select the delivery company.

"So you won't actually know until that parcel's been sent that it's coming [via] Team Global Express and then you realise that you're not going to get the door-to-door service that you've paid for," Ms Barratt said.

Laurie Smythe received a text from Team Global Express saying his freight was at the company's depot. (ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough)

Company cites driver safety as reason for decision

Team Global Express, which is owned by Allegro Funds and operates across Australia and New Zealand, said it continued to deliver to the majority of Tasmania.

"Recently, we needed to address four postcodes in the Lakes District (7027 and partial areas of 7030, 7120, and 7140)," a spokesperson said in a statement.

"These areas present operational challenges, including unsafe road conditions for our drivers, particularly during winter.

"We proactively notify our customers when there are changes to delivery networks and in cases where parcels cannot be delivered to door, we work with the receiver on alternate options."

When asked for further details, the spokesperson said customers were notified by phone when their parcel arrived at the depot, and worked with them to find delivery options.

Team Global Express says the non-delivery areas "present operational challenges, including unsafe road conditions for our drivers". (Team Global Express)

They said Miena residents could choose to have their packages taken to an alternative delivery point at Longford, while Maydena residents could have their packages taken to Westerway. The spokesperson said Colebrook residents would need to pick up their deliveries from the depot near Hobart.

"We will always strive to give customers and shoppers the best service possible, whilst taking into account the safety of our people and the sustainable operation of our business," they said.

Mr Walls urged Team Global Express not to "forget about the small customers in the rural areas".

World.title: ASX set to rise, Wall Street boosted by falling oil prices; Canada hits back at US with tariffs
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to rise, Wall Street boosted by falling oil prices; Canada hits back at US with tariffs Stan Choe Updated August 26, 2026 — 6:17am ,first published 5:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Oil prices are falling again, which is helping to ease worries in the bond market and support stock prices. The S&P 500 rose 0.3 per cent and edged closer to its all-time high set earlier this month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.3 per cent and the Nasdaq composite climbed 0.7 per cent. UBS’ trading desk said earlier this week that the slide in momentum stocks may be nearing its end, creating an opportunity for investors. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures at 5.59am AEST pointing to a rise of 34 points, or 0.4 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.7 per cent on Tuesday. Reporting season continues with Nine Entertainment, WiseTech and Woolworths results due out. The Australian dollar was trading at US71.61¢. Some of the strongest action was in the oil market, where the price for a barrel of Brent crude fell 3.9 per cent to $US87.05 and was heading for a second decline following 13 gains in 14 days. The drop came even though tensions between the United States and Iran seemed to ratchet higher after the Trump administration announced new sanctions to further hurt Iran’s economy.



Brent’s price zigzagged between $US72 and $US102 last month as hopes rose and fell that the United States and Iran could reach a deal that would allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again. Related Article Electric vehicles Aussie capitals ‘will be driverless within a decade’, says robotaxi pioneer A delegation from Pakistan left Iran after talks with Iran’s president and other senior officials on reopening the Strait of Hormuz and reviving negotiations to end the Iran-US conflict, the Pakistani military said. Pakistan Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi said a meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian had been “very positive and productive.” Tuesday’s drop in oil prices tempered the worries about high inflation that helped drive Treasury yields in the bond market higher through the summer. Yields had gotten so high that the US Treasury Department announced a surprise move last week to increase its repurchases of longer-term Treasury notes and bonds. High yields make borrowing more expensive for everyone and can slow the economy’s growth while undercutting prices for stocks, cryptocurrencies and other investments.



The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.64 per cent from 4.70 per cent late Monday and from 4.74 per cent at the end of last week. That’s a significant move for the bond market, though the 10-year yield remains firmly above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran sent oil prices and worries about inflation much higher. Canada announced it is targeting more than 700 US-made products as the trade war with America escalates. The list extends well beyond industrial goods, hitting everyday purchases such as seafood, cheese, clothing, cosmetics and toilet paper, with some facing duties as high as 50 per cent. The tariffs on American steel, dairy products, appliances, farm equipment, pulp and paper and electronics take effect September 8 at rates of 15 per cent, 25 per cent and 50 per cent, with Canada matching the corresponding US tariff rate on each product. Canadian officials said the goal is not to raise revenue but to protect Canadian companies and reduce US imports. On Wall Street, Nvidia and other winners of the boom in artificial-intelligence technology helped lead the way. Nvidia rose 2.2 per cent, a day after its drop of 2.9 per cent was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. AI stocks have veered up and down through the summer on worries that their prices shot too high and that the AI boom may not be sustainable if it doesn’t produce enough profits for companies. Nvidia will report its latest quarterly results on Wednesday, which could help steer the next move for AI-related stocks.



The gains for chip stocks helped offset a 30.7 per cent drop for Dick’s Sporting Goods, which reported weaker results for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Executive chairman Ed Stack said the retailer cut prices on some of its footwear and apparel to remain competitive, while launches for some footwear during the quarter ended up being weaker than it expected. Related Article Supermarkets Why Coles won’t copy Woolies’ Ooshies sugar hit The company cut its forecast for an underlying measure of profit in 2026 for both its Dick’s and Foot Locker businesses. The company spent $US2.4 billion last year to acquire the struggling Foot Locker chain as inventory in footwear began to pile up for most retailers. Dick’s stock is potentially heading toward its worst day in history. Worries have been rising about how strong spending can remain generally for US households, which is the main engine of the economy. They’re facing higher prices on everything from food to clothes and a job market that suddenly looks iffier after employers cut more jobs last month than they added. A report from the Conference Board on Tuesday said that confidence among US consumers weakened by more than economists expected.



In stock markets around the world, many indexes drifted modestly higher. South Korea’s Kospi, which is dominated by two AI winners, added 0.7 per cent for one of the world’s biggest moves. It’s been steadying since plunging 22.2 per cent in July. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.
