World.title: From Thor to whisky owner, actor Chris Hemsworth buys stake in Archie Rose
World.content:
Exclusive Eating outWine & spirits From Thor to whisky owner, actor Chris Hemsworth buys stake in Archie Rose “There’s no better guy” to help the booze brand take its whisky global, says the Sydney distillery’s founder. Erina Starkey August 26, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Chris Hemsworth has landed a major role in what could be the next international blockbuster, but it’s not with Universal Pictures or Disney. The Hollywood actor, best known for playing Thor in the Marvel movies, has joined founder Will Edwards as co-owner of Australian distillery Archie Rose. Hemsworth, who was born in Melbourne and grew up in the outback town of Bulman in the Northern Territory, owns an undisclosed stake in Australia’s most awarded distillery, and will play a central role in pushing the Australian-made spirits brand into global markets, beginning with the United States at the end of the year. Archie Rose co-owners Chris Hemsworth and Will Edwards. Timothy Ashton “I’ve been a fan of Archie Rose for a long time,” Hemsworth said in a statement. “Wherever I am in the world, tasting an Archie Rose whisky immediately transports me right back home, to that feeling of sitting around a campfire in the Australian bush with my mates.”



Hemsworth says he’s impressed with Archie Rose’s use of only Australian-grown malts at its Sydney distilleries, which include the original Rosebery site and bar which opened in the inner south in 2015, and the company’s production facility in Banksmeadow. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up “They’re a brilliant example of what Australia does best, and I can’t wait to share that with the world.” Chris Hemsworth has an undisclosed stake in Australia’s most awarded distillery. Hemsworth’s investment shows confidence in an Australian spirits market reported to be worth $5.6 billion in 2024, according to International Wines and Spirits Record data. Research firm Mordor Intelligence values the current US spirits market at $172 billion and forecasts it to grow by $17 billion over the next five years. More than one-third of the US spirits market is whisky based. The Avengers star, who is an Old Fashioned drinker and partial to the brand’s rye malt whisky, won’t be involved in making the spirits, which will remain in the hands of Archie Rose master distiller Dave Withers, a two-time winner of distiller of the year in the Spirits Business Awards.



“Chris is very comfortable leaving the distilling to the distillers,” said Edwards. Instead, Hemsworth will focus on the creative processes, including product redesign, content strategy and launch plans for the US market. “He’s been very involved in that, more than I thought he would have been,” said Edwards. Archie Rose co-owners Chris Hemsworth and Will Edwards are taking Archie Rose global. Hemsworth has been working behind the scenes with Archie Rose for more than a year, mostly over email and phone, and visiting the Banksmeadow site. “We did our best to keep it under wraps,” said Edwards. “But he’s not the most inconspicuous guy. We had to tell our staff that he was there doing some recce work for a [movie] role.” Afterwards, rather than making a quiet exit, Hemsworth joined the team in the lunchroom. “I assumed he was going to head off, and instead he goes down to level one, which is the lunchroom. He makes a coffee and then just chills out there with the whole team,” said Edwards. “I’m like, ‘Oh my god’ – we’re trying to keep this low key, and he’s just hanging out.”



Edwards wasn’t looking for a business partner when he met Hemsworth through a mutual friend a few years ago, but says the fit made sense and the timing was right. “If you had asked me before this happened to pick someone to partner with, Chris Hemsworth would have been No.1 on the list,” he said. Archie Rose’s latest release: Triple Smoked Single Malt Whiskey. “He’s the best possible partner. He’s an Australian icon and he’s a really good bloke. There’s no kind of pretence, he’s willing to get his hands dirty and get involved in stuff.” The new appointment marks a major leap for Archie Rose. When Edwards lodged the development application for the original Rosebery site, it became the first independent distillery to open in the City of Sydney in more than 160 years. Joined by several other craft spirit brands, including Four Pillars (fully owned by Lion, a subsidiary of Japanese brewing giant Kirin), it helped launch an Australian distillery revival in the mid-2010s. Twelve years on, it’s been awarded more than 400 awards including world’s best rye whisky four times in the World Whiskies Awards and world’s best contemporary gin in the World Gin Awards. Its spirits portfolio includes whisky, vodka and rum, although it’s best known locally for gin.



Distillery manager Tim Hosken in the Archie Rose barrel room in Banksmeadow. Steven Siewert “We actually started distilling whisky before we started distilling gin. The first whiskies were laid down in December 2014, and then the first gins were made in January 2015. I would say that whisky is actually our lead category now.” Archie Rose will launch three new whiskies at the end of the year. They’ll have new packaging, an updated logo and more efficient and sustainable design, reflecting the company’s B Corp certification which came through this month. “I’d probably say the whisky packaging now skews a little bit more masculine, as you would expect with Chris, and it’s also a better representation of Australia,” Edwards says. “So when you put the product in front of people, particularly non-Australians, it straight away feels how an Australian whisky should feel.”



Archie Rose’s Banksmeadow facility can produce more than 2.5 million litres of whisky a year. The US will be the primary international market, alongside New Zealand and select markets in Asia, with the United Kingdom and Europe to follow in 2027. “There’ll be an initial focus on whisky, but we’re very open to bringing our white spirits portfolio in future,” Edwards says. Exporting any kind of spirit can be tricky, and involves navigating complex trade agreements, import tariffs and distribution deals, but Edwards says one of the biggest hurdles for Australian producers is supply. With this in mind, Edwards established Australia’s largest distillery in Banksmeadow in 2020, with the capability to produce more than 2.5 million litres of whisky a year. “We have over 45,000 casks in the bond store under maturation already, and a really well-planned production schedule.” Will Edwards founded Archie Rose in 2014.



Another obstacle is awareness, and that’s where Hemsworth comes in. With a global fan base, Edwards is hoping that Hemsworth might be exactly what Archie Rose needs to cut through overseas. “He’s obviously the biggest Australian there is, and in terms of being able to tell the story to consumers, there’s no better guy.” There is a risk to that strategy: that Archie Rose is seen as just another celebrity-owned spirit with a famous face on the label, like Ryan Reynolds’ Aviation American Gin or Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson’s Teremana Tequila. “I think [we can avoid that] because we have existed for a long time prior, and we try to make whisky that’s authentically Australian and really tastes like the place it’s from – provided we get to tell that story, which is what we’re really trying to do.” Homegrown star Chris Hemsworth has a global fan base. Getty Images The Australian provenance of the whisky is central to how Edwards and Hemsworth intend to market Archie Rose overseas and justify its cost, which will sit above many high-volume Scotch blends.



“How it differentiates itself is through the raw materials that go into the whisky – our Australian barley, rye and wheat is second to none – and then the maturation climate,” says Edwards. Australian whisky isn’t governed by the same restrictive legislations as Scotch, for instance, leaving distillers more room to innovate. An example of this is Archie Rose’s Triple Smoked Single Malt Whisky, which uses native stringybark timber to smoke the malts giving the spirit a distinctly Australian smoke character, reminiscent of campfires and wood smoke. Archie Rose’s Smoked Cask Series. The hope, ultimately, is that this opens the door not just for Archie Rose, but for Australian whiskies, says Edwards. “I hope, but I’m pretty confident, that inevitably what’s going to happen is that the awareness of the category is going to grow and consumers will be curious and they will try all different types of Australian whisky.



“The bigger we can grow the category, the better for everyone.”

World.title: Environmental watchdog challenges giant data centre project over noise fears
World.content:
Victoria’s environmental watchdog has stepped in to object to a planned $1.1 billion data centre on the former Ford factory site in Campbellfield, warning of potential noise impacts and poor site layout. It is the first time the Environment Protection Authority (EPA) has objected to a data centre plan in the midst of the state’s controversial tech infrastructure boom. Campbellfield residents say they are concerned about noise, and water and power supply, at the proposed data centre. Chris Hopkins The EPA’s challenge is a potentially major blow to developer Zerra DC’s “Project Dune”, a proposal for six enormous data halls across 22 hectares of land on Barry Road. EPA executive director of strategy Erin Bowen said the authority had lodged a formal objection to the data centre proposal with the Department of Transport and Planning.



“In our role as a referral authority, EPA Victoria has objected to the proposal in its current form,” Bowen said in a statement. “Based on the information provided, we hold concerns over potential noise risks and the cumulative impacts associated with the overall site layout and development.” However, the ultimate decision on the project sits with Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny, after Zerra DC lodged its application under the state’s fast-tracked Development Facilitation Program. Under the program, the application has gone directly to Kilkenny, bypassing Hume Council and stripping residents of appeal rights at the state planning tribunal. The EPA intervention follows community anger over the Singaporean-backed project, which when built would consume 336 megawatts of electricity – double Melbourne’s current data centre power draw. The completed data centre would also store 7 million litres of diesel, and be within 250 metres of homes. The diesel fuel is for use in back-up generators if the power grid fails, as data centres need access to a constant power source.



About 50 people attended a rally opposing the Campbellfield project on Friday. Residents around Barry Road have tied pink ribbons on the front of their homes as part of a campaign against the development. Residents rallied at the site of the proposed data centre, where Ford’s Broadmeadows Assembly Plant once operated. Chris Hopkins John Rutherford, of the Broadmeadows Progress Association, attended the rally. He said it was outrageous that the council and residents were being sidelined on the project, which could have significant environmental and social impacts. “The data centre developers are going straight to the minister, bypassing the council,” Rutherford said. “It’s a very powerful lobby. The government is seeing the potential investment of developers into data centres as the overriding thing, rather than overall transparency and protection of communities as a whole.” Kilkenny has approved six data centres since 2025 through the fast-tracked Development Facilitation Program.



A Zerra DC spokesperson said the company was taking concerns raised by the EPA and residents seriously and was “in the process of preparing further acoustic information in response to the EPA’s objection”. “We welcome that feedback and are already working through each point,” the spokesperson said. Related Article Data centres 7 million litres of diesel just 250m from homes: The data centre plan locals didn’t know about Technical assessments submitted with Zerra DC’s application to Kilkenny revealed the site would house 294 massive rooftop chillers. Chillers are heavy-duty refrigeration units that cool liquid or air in a closed loop. In the Campbellfield project, they will keep thousands of computer servers the data centre will host from overheating.



Acoustic modelling by engineers Aurecon acknowledged these chillers would generate a continuous, low-frequency hum. The report stressed that this would be within acceptable range limits. Each chiller proposed for the later stages of the development – which are the stages closest to housing – would emit 80 decibels of sound, about the equivalent of a running petrol lawnmower. There would be 250 chiller units on the later data centre halls, stacked across five building roofs, creating a massive cumulative sound load that would rely on eight-metre screening walls to avoid breaching state environmental limits. While stage one of the data centre meets EPA noise limits, the report concedes that later stages built closer to homes adjacent to the site in Campbellfield would need the acoustic screening on the data centre’s roofs to control noise. The physical layout of the masterplan for the site shows the first stage is to be built 650 metres from homes. Later stages of the proposal are within 250 metres of homes, and 130 metres of a medical centre. Noise modelling diagrams submitted by Aurecon as part of the planning application also reveal the visual threat facing residents in the area. Detailed 3D diagrams map out the chillers to be installed on roofs of the six planned data halls, which will operate around the clock.



Campbellfield residents have tied pink ribbons on their homes as part of a campaign against the proposed data centre. Chris Hopkins To prevent the 294 chillers exceeding EPA nighttime noise limits at nearby bedroom windows, the developer’s acoustic consultants conceded there would need to be noise walls built on the roofs of each data centre hall, which are already two to three storeys high. Each noise wall will then add another seven to eight metres. While the facility will occupy an immense footprint – more than 10 times the size of the MCG’s playing surface – planning reports reveal it will yield minimal long-term employment. Stage one would require 49 employees to operate, growing to 255 on-site staff when all six stages are completed over a 12-year build, the reports said. Related Article Exclusive

Data centres The energy vampire next door: Life next to an AI mega-factory



The Ford Broadmeadows Assembly Plant employed almost 5200 people at its peak in the 1980s, mostly from migrant backgrounds and living in surrounding suburbs. It produced more than 600 cars a day. The factory closed in 2016. The local community had long held hopes the site could be used to generate significant employment, through advanced manufacturing, or as a higher education facility. There are concerns the data centre would dash these aspirations. Ford’s former chassis plant in Geelong has transformed into an advanced manufacturing hub with the help of significant federal and state support, while Victoria has committed $179 million to turn the former Holden site in Fishermans Bend into an “innovation precinct”. On Monday night, Melton Council, in the city’s outer west, joined Hume, Brimbank and Maribyrnong councils in calling on the state government to pause new data centre approvals until new regulatory standards are developed to manage their environmental and social impacts. The Victorian Greens have also called for a moratorium. A report by the Australian Energy Market Operator released on Tuesday showed that data centres would use 13 per cent of the network’s power supply by 2035, up from 3 per cent today.



There are 225 data centres in development around the country this year, compared with 97 in 2025, the report says. Premier Ben Carroll appointed MP Anthony Carbines to the newly created position of Minister for Artificial Intelligence and the Digital Economy in a reshuffle early this month. Carbines has said he would work to attract more data centre investment to the state, while acknowledging the growing community backlash against them. “It’s at the centre of our prosperity in the future, but we need to do that in a collaborative way with communities,” he said. Kilkenny’s office was contacted for comment. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Country music legend Dolly Parton dies aged 80
World.content:
Breaking CultureMusicVale Country music legend Dolly Parton dies aged 80 Michael Idato Updated August 26, 2026 — 5:43am ,first published 4:12am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dolly Parton, the singer-songwriter, literacy advocate and cultural icon whose wit, beauty and musicality shaped country music for more than six decades has died, aged 80. The country music legend’s nephew Bryan Seaver confirmed Parton’s passing on behalf of her family. Parton’s music was rich and tender, exploring her impoverished childhood in the Great Smoky Mountains of Tennessee, and the familiar country music touchstones of love, heartache and regret. They include songs like Jolene, I Will Always Love You and the theme her most successful film, 9 to 5. Dolly Parton, pictured in New York in 2022. AP Photo/Andres Kudacki “I have imagined the heaviness of this moment, but haven’t truly felt it until now,” Seaver said in a statement on behalf of the Parton family. “Dolly has lived in the light and is in the arms of Jesus, surely met by [her late husband] Carl, her parents, and countless others who have watched her and longed for her to meet them in the heavens.”



One of the acknowledged titans of country music, Parton has 11 Grammy Awards and three Emmy Awards, one Oscar (and two Oscar nominations), and nominations for six Golden Globe Awards, and a Tony award. She has a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame and was the recipient of the US National Medal of Arts and a Kennedy Centre Honour. Dolly Parton, Lily Tomlin, and Jane Fonda arrive for the premiere of their film “9 To 5” in New York on December 14, 1980. AP Photo/Richard Drew “Dolly opened doors not just for me, but for her entire family to reach the potential we didn’t even know was possible,” Seaver said. “Dolly also opened doors for generations of singers, songwriters, musicians, and dreamers from every walk of life and across every continent. By her example, we believe that anything was possible.” The legendary singer “never saw a door she couldn’t open, and the door she opened made and changed history,” Seaver said.



“My family and I have shared a lifetime of beautiful memories with Dolly, but so have you,” he said. “She has always been on your television, your record player, your CD, and on your phone playlist, becoming an extended part of your family, whether you liked it or not. Our family and the team she has entrusted with her legacy will work diligently to ensure her spirit will live with us forever.” US president Donald Trump acknowledged Parton’s legacy, saying: “This is a true loss for millions of people. There has never been anyone like her, and never will.” Trump said US flags would be lowered across the country on government buildings for a week. Singing legend Dionne Warwick was among the first to pay tribute to Parton. “Dolly, a true child of God, is in the best hands now,” Warwick said in a statement. “I will certainly miss her laugher, jokes and her being. Rest well and in total peace my friend.” Another country legend, Reba McEntire, thanked Parton “for all the wonderful things you did for us here on earth. Your love, your music and you gave so much with your huge, huge heart. There will never ever be another you”. Miley Cyrus described it as a “devastating day for humanity”. Dolly Parton on stage in 1976. Redferns



And producer/singer Seth McFarlane, who had worked with her, said Parton was “exactly the person we all hoped she was. Her kindness, generosity, and authenticity were evident from moment one, and the benign yet assured command she maintained over her empire was obvious from the genuine love and trust you could see from everyone who worked for her.” Dolly Parton with Lily Tomlin (left) and Jane Fonda (right) in 9 to 5. 20th Century Fox Dolly Rebecca Parton was born on January 19, 1946, in a one-room cabin on the banks of the Little Pigeon River in Pittman Centre, Tennessee. It would seem a world away from the life she would eventually lead, but it was world that Parton brought to life through her songs. Mournful ballads like My Tennessee Mountain Home, and Coat of Many Colours and In the Good Old Days (When Times Were Bad). No amount of money could buy from me / the memories that I have of then / No amount of money could pay me / To go back and live through it again, she sang. “In the good old days when times were bad.” Parton was the fourth of 12 children born to Avie Lee Caroline and Robert Lee Parton Sr. To her mother, Parton has always credited her musical prowess. And to her father, her business acumen. If true, she owed them both a great debt; in life her artistic and commercial success was almost without equal.



In 1973 and 1974, she would write and release two songs that would become her most successful: Jolene, about a woman confronted with the reality of the woman whose beauty (and fierce red hair) was powerful enough to steal the love of her life from her, and I Will Always Love You, about a farewell penned in the aftermath of a broken relationship. The latter of the two would become even more famous because it was recorded and released by other artists. Parton famously declined a request for Elvis Presley to record a cover, after his management asked for half the royalties on the song. And Whitney Houston’s release, from the soundtrack of her film The Bodyguard, would become a money-spinner for Parton. Houston was paid the performer royalty, but as the songwriter Parton took the lion’s share of the revenue. “She can have the credit, I’ll just take the cash,” Parton joked in 2018. Dolly Parton and Kenny Rogers rehearse a song for their appearance on the TV show “Live... And in Person” in Los Angeles on September 27, 1983. AP Photo/Doug Pizac The success of those songs was part of a mainstream crossover that, at the time, was bold. Country music very much lived in its channel and few if any artists could step between it and mainstream pop. But Parton’s conquest of the music charts would blaze a trail to that others could follow. That might be Parton’s greatest legacy: that she did, so others could follow. Dolly is the reason we have Garth Brooks, Shania Twain and Taylor Swift on the pop charts. She is why Post Malone and Beyoncé could walk the same path, but in reverse. And she is the reason we have genuinely evolutionary artists like Orville Peck.



In a tender footnote, Seaver said that in death Parton’s connection to the land was as potent as her father’s. “Dolly was a farmer, just like her daddy. He farmed the soil, she farmed songs and happiness,” he said. Seaver said Parton’s request was that she “rest in a beautiful bed of plush cotton because after a life wearing heavy rhinestones, she finally deserves to be comfortable and have some rest”. Parton’s husband of nearly 60 years, Carl Dean, passed away in March 2025. She is survived by six of her siblings, Willadeene, Bobby, Stella, Cassie, Freida and Rachel. World.title: Measles kills two unvaccinated people as US outbreak approaches 3000
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaVaccination Measles kills two unvaccinated people as US outbreak approaches 3000 Michael Koziol August 26, 2026 — 5:36am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Two unvaccinated people died with measles in the US state of Pennsylvania, becoming the first deaths there linked to the disease in 35 years, amid a growing national outbreak. Pennsylvania’s Department of Health announced the deaths on Tuesday (US time), and warned that the return of measles after a decades-long absence meant people did not grasp its severity. US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr announced an overhaul of federal guidelines on the childhood vaccine schedule this month. Bloomberg It comes as US President Donald Trump and his health secretary, Robert F. Kennedy Jr, continue to sow doubts about vaccines, including by pushing an unsubstantiated link with autism. This month, Trump signed an executive order that called for parents to space out their children’s vaccine visits and break up the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) jab - which is not currently possible.



Both deaths were in Lancaster County – an area of southern Pennsylvania with a large Amish population, which has historically had lower rates of vaccination. The department would not release further information about the deceased. So far in 2026, Pennsylvania has detected 393 cases of measles in 28 counties. Across the US, there have been 2777 confirmed cases this year, spanning most states and Washington DC. The measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is only available as a combined dose at present. AP Photo/Mary Conlon Tuesday’s announcement marked the first time people died from measles in Pennsylvania in 35 years. They are also the first US deaths from the disease this year. Last year, three Americans died, following nearly a decade of zero deaths. Pennsylvania’s health secretary, Debra Bogen, said the virtual elimination of measles in the state for more than three decades meant “people are not familiar with this disease and don’t fully understand the potential severity of the illness”.



The best way to protect against measles was vaccination, she said, with two doses of the MMR vaccine providing 97 per cent lifetime protection. The number of measles cases recorded this year has already eclipsed last year’s total of 2289. Nearly 50 per cent were among young people aged five to 19, and 94 per cent were among people who were unvaccinated or whose vaccination status was unknown, according to the Centres for Disease Control. Trump has issued an executive order to establish a “gold standard” vaccination schedule for children. Bloomberg The 2025 and 2026 figures are the highest measles numbers in decades, with only a 2019 outbreak (1274 cases) coming close. Earlier in August, Trump urged parents to break up the MMR vaccine into three separate shots, even though that is not currently enabled by the medical profession or the pharmaceutical industry.



In a subsequent briefing with reporters, US officials said they would work with the private sector to try to make separate doses available. Related Article Trump's White House Trump’s vaccine order adds more fuel to the anti-vaccine fire At a televised news conference in the Oval Office, Trump said the US was recommending too many vaccines. He claimed without evidence that the MMR vaccine could be “quite lethal”, but when given separately, “it looks like they are not at all lethal but just every effective”. The US president also falsely spoke of an “explosion” in vaccine injury, and claimed that doctors were injecting children with large doses that looked like “a bottle of soda poured into a little child’s body”. Trump’s executive order did not mention autism. But in his unscripted remarks, he asserted an unproven link between vaccination and higher rates of autism diagnoses in modern times.



“There’s a reason for such epidemic rates of autism, and we’re going to bring it back to much closer to where it was,” he said. The president’s order does not change vaccine requirements for schools, or impact the policies of state health departments. Rather, it stands as a recommendation from the US federal government. US Secretary of Health Robert F. Kennedy J has long been a vaccine sceptic. Bloomberg Following Trump’s announcement, the American Medical Association said that altering the proven childhood vaccination schedule without credible evidence risked weakening public confidence in vaccines, and putting children’s health at risk. “Extensive evidence from decades of scientific studies shows no link between vaccines and autism,” president Willie Underwood said. “Putting our children’s health at risk is not an option.”



When contacted for comment, the US Department of Health and Human Services pointed to a statement from the Centres for Disease Control which offered condolences following the two “measles-associated deaths”. “The MMR vaccine provides the most effective protection against measles and helps prevent its spread,” it said. “CDC will continue to follow Pennsylvania’s lead and provide resources to support the state’s response.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Ghislaine Maxwell loses bid to overturn conviction for aiding Epstein
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaEpstein fallout Ghislaine Maxwell loses bid to overturn conviction for aiding Epstein Michael R. Sisak and Larry Neumeister Updated August 26, 2026 — 5:23am ,first published 11:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: Ghislaine Maxwell’s bid to overturn her sex trafficking conviction and be freed from prison was rejected by a US federal judge on Tuesday (US time) who said the claims by Jeffrey Epstein’s former girlfriend and longtime associate that new evidence had emerged were “demonstrably meritless”. Maxwell filed a habeas petition – a legal procedure challenging her detention – last December seeking to set aside her conviction and free her from a 20-year prison sentence, claiming exonerating information was withheld and false testimony presented at her trial, resulting in a “complete miscarriage of justice”. Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell. Getty Judge Paul A. Engelmayer rejected her arguments, saying in his written ruling they “all or almost all are frivolous” and that she had presented nothing that could upend the outcome of her trial. “Nearly all its claims are procedurally barred; the overwhelming testimonial and documentary evidence adduced at trial conclusively established her guilt; and her petition’s claims are demonstrably meritless, and generally based on speculation, distortions, and/or outright falsehoods,” Engelmayer wrote.





The judge noted that many of Maxwell’s claims of “new evidence” stem from documents released under the Epstein Files Transparency Act. As a result of that law, the Justice Department over the last eight months has released 18 categories of investigative materials gathered in the massive sex trafficking probe, including search warrants, financial records, notes from interviews with victims and data from electronic devices. Related Article Investigation

Good Weekend Isolated, scared, forlorn: The heartbreaking final months of Virginia Giuffre’s life Engelmayer said that material is “largely irrelevant to the charges against Maxwell and does not support her claims of error.” “On the contrary, to the extent it is relevant, far from exculpating her, it incriminates her or reinforces the correctness of the legal rulings Maxwell challenges,” he wrote.



The judge also rejected Maxwell’s claim that she was selectively prosecuted and made a “scapegoat” when the Justice Department did not indict four co-conspirators named in a government document or 25 men who settled with victims. Engelmayer said she could have raised that claim on appeal after her trial, but he found it to be frivolous nonetheless. Among the recently released Justice Department documents, “she does not cite any that reveals the existence of an uncharged confederate, let alone one as instrumental as she in facilitating Epstein’s horrific crimes,” the judge said. World.title: Gold has lost its glitter. Does that mean it’s time to buy?
World.content:
MoneyInvestingGold Opinion Gold has lost its glitter. Does that mean it’s time to buy?

Justin Lin August 26, 2026 — 5:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In February, I walked past a bullion dealer in the Sydney CBD with a queue that wrapped around the corner. Gold had just peaked above $US5600 ($7800) an ounce, capping a 12-month run of more than 80 per cent. Six months later, the queues have gone, gold sits near $US4600, and the question I get from investors has inverted. It used to be: “How high can this go?” Now it’s: “Why did my safe haven fail me during a war?” The positioning that made gold fragile in February has been cleared out and the price has rebased to a level far easier to defend. Trevor Collens It is a fair question. Gold’s first half was a disappointment, but unlike how many investors would paint it, nothing about it was mysterious, nor did it reveal any fundamental flaws in gold. Consider the starting point. At the beginning of this year, gold had been perhaps the best-performing major asset on the planet for three years, at one point rising more than 60 per cent in six months.



When an asset climbs that fast it attracts a particular kind of buyer – the one who arrives because the price is rising, not because of any particular thesis. Those buyers set the price at the top and are the first to leave. Then there is the conflict itself. The Iran war has been the most energy-centric war in modern market history, with more than a fifth of the world’s crude and gas exports at risk. That may instinctively read an oil shock as an inflation shock, and inflation as good news for gold. Central banks have accumulated gold for years as a deliberate act of diversification away from the US dollar. The market did something less intuitive. It priced in a central bank forced to stay tight, or even hike. Yields climbed, and gold, which pays no coupon, always struggles against a rising cost of holding it. Finally, amid the clamouring of gold’s failure as a “haven”, it should be noted that nobody truly wanted insurance. Uncertainty hit decade highs, yes, yet equity markets stayed risk-on, propped up by earnings certainty in semiconductors and AI. Investors do not buy a hedge when the thing they are hedging keeps going up.



Three headwinds, all rational, but none a defect in gold. What has changed, however, is that the froth is gone. The positioning that made gold fragile in February has been cleared out and the price has rebased to a level far easier to defend. Anyone buying today is buying an asset that has had its reckoning. Meanwhile, the core investment case remains rock steady, and the accumulators that drove gold’s rally before are making their return. Central banks have accumulated gold for years as a deliberate act of diversification away from the US dollar. That buying slowed in the first half – exactly what you would expect when a war forces policymakers to prioritise liquidity over strategy. But as of August, despite tensions still simmering in the Middle East, central bank buying may have already resumed. The People’s Bank of China recently extended its streak to 21 straight months in July, adding 20 tonnes, its largest monthly purchase by volume since October 2023. And in the World Gold Council’s annual survey of reserve managers, 89 per cent expected global official gold holdings to keep rising over the next 12 months, while 74 per cent expected the US dollar’s share of global reserves to be lower in five years.



Asian investors, a new force in the market, have proven similarly committed. Regional gold ETFs took in a record $US12 billion in the first half, the largest contribution to global flows, and that held through a brutal June of profit taking. A physical gold fund was, for a while, the largest ETF of any kind in mainland China, bigger than the local equivalent of an S&P 500 tracker. Editor's pick Investing ‘They want a piece of that pie’: Gold FOMO untarnished by price meltdown Which brings us to now. Consolidation is miserable to sit through and obvious only in hindsight, but the conditions that made gold vulnerable have been quietly unwinding. The labour market that spent the first half looking indestructible shed 23,000 US jobs in July. Markets that had priced a September rate rise as a near-certainty, now put the odds closer to one in three. Gold has climbed about 8 per cent in a month to a 10-week high, and its correlation with oil and equities has drifted back towards zero as key accumulators return. Six months ago, gold was a crowded trade at a record high. Today, it is an uncrowded one at a discount, with a structural case that has strengthened rather than weakened. The queues outside the bullion dealers may be shorter, but, ironically, now may be the right time to enter the store.



Justin Lin is an Investment Strategist at Global X ETFs Australia. Advice given in this article is general in nature and is not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. World.title: ASX set to rise, Wall Street boosted by falling oil prices; Canada hits back at US with tariffs
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to rise, Wall Street boosted by falling oil prices; Canada hits back at US with tariffs Stan Choe Updated August 26, 2026 — 6:17am ,first published 5:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Oil prices are falling again, which is helping to ease worries in the bond market and support stock prices. The S&P 500 rose 0.3 per cent and edged closer to its all-time high set earlier this month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.3 per cent and the Nasdaq composite climbed 0.7 per cent. UBS’ trading desk said earlier this week that the slide in momentum stocks may be nearing its end, creating an opportunity for investors. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures at 5.59am AEST pointing to a rise of 34 points, or 0.4 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.7 per cent on Tuesday. Reporting season continues with Nine Entertainment, WiseTech and Woolworths results due out. The Australian dollar was trading at US71.61¢. Some of the strongest action was in the oil market, where the price for a barrel of Brent crude fell 3.9 per cent to $US87.05 and was heading for a second decline following 13 gains in 14 days. The drop came even though tensions between the United States and Iran seemed to ratchet higher after the Trump administration announced new sanctions to further hurt Iran’s economy.



Brent’s price zigzagged between $US72 and $US102 last month as hopes rose and fell that the United States and Iran could reach a deal that would allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again. Related Article Electric vehicles Aussie capitals ‘will be driverless within a decade’, says robotaxi pioneer A delegation from Pakistan left Iran after talks with Iran’s president and other senior officials on reopening the Strait of Hormuz and reviving negotiations to end the Iran-US conflict, the Pakistani military said. Pakistan Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi said a meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian had been “very positive and productive.” Tuesday’s drop in oil prices tempered the worries about high inflation that helped drive Treasury yields in the bond market higher through the summer. Yields had gotten so high that the US Treasury Department announced a surprise move last week to increase its repurchases of longer-term Treasury notes and bonds. High yields make borrowing more expensive for everyone and can slow the economy’s growth while undercutting prices for stocks, cryptocurrencies and other investments.



The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.64 per cent from 4.70 per cent late Monday and from 4.74 per cent at the end of last week. That’s a significant move for the bond market, though the 10-year yield remains firmly above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran sent oil prices and worries about inflation much higher. Canada announced it is targeting more than 700 US-made products as the trade war with America escalates. The list extends well beyond industrial goods, hitting everyday purchases such as seafood, cheese, clothing, cosmetics and toilet paper, with some facing duties as high as 50 per cent. The tariffs on American steel, dairy products, appliances, farm equipment, pulp and paper and electronics take effect September 8 at rates of 15 per cent, 25 per cent and 50 per cent, with Canada matching the corresponding US tariff rate on each product. Canadian officials said the goal is not to raise revenue but to protect Canadian companies and reduce US imports. On Wall Street, Nvidia and other winners of the boom in artificial-intelligence technology helped lead the way. Nvidia rose 2.2 per cent, a day after its drop of 2.9 per cent was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. AI stocks have veered up and down through the summer on worries that their prices shot too high and that the AI boom may not be sustainable if it doesn’t produce enough profits for companies. Nvidia will report its latest quarterly results on Wednesday, which could help steer the next move for AI-related stocks.



The gains for chip stocks helped offset a 30.7 per cent drop for Dick’s Sporting Goods, which reported weaker results for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Executive chairman Ed Stack said the retailer cut prices on some of its footwear and apparel to remain competitive, while launches for some footwear during the quarter ended up being weaker than it expected. Related Article Supermarkets Why Coles won’t copy Woolies’ Ooshies sugar hit The company cut its forecast for an underlying measure of profit in 2026 for both its Dick’s and Foot Locker businesses. The company spent $US2.4 billion last year to acquire the struggling Foot Locker chain as inventory in footwear began to pile up for most retailers. Dick’s stock is potentially heading toward its worst day in history. Worries have been rising about how strong spending can remain generally for US households, which is the main engine of the economy. They’re facing higher prices on everything from food to clothes and a job market that suddenly looks iffier after employers cut more jobs last month than they added. A report from the Conference Board on Tuesday said that confidence among US consumers weakened by more than economists expected.



In stock markets around the world, many indexes drifted modestly higher. South Korea’s Kospi, which is dominated by two AI winners, added 0.7 per cent for one of the world’s biggest moves. It’s been steadying since plunging 22.2 per cent in July. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: From Thor to whisky owner, actor Chris Hemsworth buys stake in Archie Rose
World.content:
Exclusive Eating outWine & spirits From Thor to whisky owner, actor Chris Hemsworth buys stake in Archie Rose “There’s no better guy” to help the booze brand take its whisky global, says the Sydney distillery’s founder. Erina Starkey August 26, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Chris Hemsworth has landed a major role in what could be the next international blockbuster, but it’s not with Universal Pictures or Disney. The Hollywood actor, best known for playing Thor in the Marvel movies, has joined founder Will Edwards as co-owner of Australian distillery Archie Rose. Hemsworth, who was born in Melbourne and grew up in the outback town of Bulman in the Northern Territory, owns an undisclosed stake in Australia’s most awarded distillery, and will play a central role in pushing the Australian-made spirits brand into global markets, beginning with the United States at the end of the year. Archie Rose co-owners Chris Hemsworth and Will Edwards. Timothy Ashton “I’ve been a fan of Archie Rose for a long time,” Hemsworth said in a statement. “Wherever I am in the world, tasting an Archie Rose whisky immediately transports me right back home, to that feeling of sitting around a campfire in the Australian bush with my mates.”



Hemsworth says he’s impressed with Archie Rose’s use of only Australian-grown malts at its Sydney distilleries, which include the original Rosebery site and bar which opened in the inner south in 2015, and the company’s production facility in Banksmeadow. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up “They’re a brilliant example of what Australia does best, and I can’t wait to share that with the world.” Chris Hemsworth has an undisclosed stake in Australia’s most awarded distillery. Hemsworth’s investment shows confidence in an Australian spirits market reported to be worth $5.6 billion in 2024, according to International Wines and Spirits Record data. Research firm Mordor Intelligence values the current US spirits market at $172 billion and forecasts it to grow by $17 billion over the next five years. More than one-third of the US spirits market is whisky based. The Avengers star, who is an Old Fashioned drinker and partial to the brand’s rye malt whisky, won’t be involved in making the spirits, which will remain in the hands of Archie Rose master distiller Dave Withers, a two-time winner of distiller of the year in the Spirits Business Awards.



“Chris is very comfortable leaving the distilling to the distillers,” said Edwards. Instead, Hemsworth will focus on the creative processes, including product redesign, content strategy and launch plans for the US market. “He’s been very involved in that, more than I thought he would have been,” said Edwards. Archie Rose co-owners Chris Hemsworth and Will Edwards are taking Archie Rose global. Hemsworth has been working behind the scenes with Archie Rose for more than a year, mostly over email and phone, and visiting the Banksmeadow site. “We did our best to keep it under wraps,” said Edwards. “But he’s not the most inconspicuous guy. We had to tell our staff that he was there doing some recce work for a [movie] role.” Afterwards, rather than making a quiet exit, Hemsworth joined the team in the lunchroom. “I assumed he was going to head off, and instead he goes down to level one, which is the lunchroom. He makes a coffee and then just chills out there with the whole team,” said Edwards. “I’m like, ‘Oh my god’ – we’re trying to keep this low key, and he’s just hanging out.”



Edwards wasn’t looking for a business partner when he met Hemsworth through a mutual friend a few years ago, but says the fit made sense and the timing was right. “If you had asked me before this happened to pick someone to partner with, Chris Hemsworth would have been No.1 on the list,” he said. Archie Rose’s latest release: Triple Smoked Single Malt Whiskey. “He’s the best possible partner. He’s an Australian icon and he’s a really good bloke. There’s no kind of pretence, he’s willing to get his hands dirty and get involved in stuff.” The new appointment marks a major leap for Archie Rose. When Edwards lodged the development application for the original Rosebery site, it became the first independent distillery to open in the City of Sydney in more than 160 years. Joined by several other craft spirit brands, including Four Pillars (fully owned by Lion, a subsidiary of Japanese brewing giant Kirin), it helped launch an Australian distillery revival in the mid-2010s. Twelve years on, it’s been awarded more than 400 awards including world’s best rye whisky four times in the World Whiskies Awards and world’s best contemporary gin in the World Gin Awards. Its spirits portfolio includes whisky, vodka and rum, although it’s best known locally for gin.



Distillery manager Tim Hosken in the Archie Rose barrel room in Banksmeadow. Steven Siewert “We actually started distilling whisky before we started distilling gin. The first whiskies were laid down in December 2014, and then the first gins were made in January 2015. I would say that whisky is actually our lead category now.” Archie Rose will launch three new whiskies at the end of the year. They’ll have new packaging, an updated logo and more efficient and sustainable design, reflecting the company’s B Corp certification which came through this month. “I’d probably say the whisky packaging now skews a little bit more masculine, as you would expect with Chris, and it’s also a better representation of Australia,” Edwards says. “So when you put the product in front of people, particularly non-Australians, it straight away feels how an Australian whisky should feel.”



Archie Rose’s Banksmeadow facility can produce more than 2.5 million litres of whisky a year. The US will be the primary international market, alongside New Zealand and select markets in Asia, with the United Kingdom and Europe to follow in 2027. “There’ll be an initial focus on whisky, but we’re very open to bringing our white spirits portfolio in future,” Edwards says. Exporting any kind of spirit can be tricky, and involves navigating complex trade agreements, import tariffs and distribution deals, but Edwards says one of the biggest hurdles for Australian producers is supply. With this in mind, Edwards established Australia’s largest distillery in Banksmeadow in 2020, with the capability to produce more than 2.5 million litres of whisky a year. “We have over 45,000 casks in the bond store under maturation already, and a really well-planned production schedule.” Will Edwards founded Archie Rose in 2014.



Another obstacle is awareness, and that’s where Hemsworth comes in. With a global fan base, Edwards is hoping that Hemsworth might be exactly what Archie Rose needs to cut through overseas. “He’s obviously the biggest Australian there is, and in terms of being able to tell the story to consumers, there’s no better guy.” There is a risk to that strategy: that Archie Rose is seen as just another celebrity-owned spirit with a famous face on the label, like Ryan Reynolds’ Aviation American Gin or Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson’s Teremana Tequila. “I think [we can avoid that] because we have existed for a long time prior, and we try to make whisky that’s authentically Australian and really tastes like the place it’s from – provided we get to tell that story, which is what we’re really trying to do.” Homegrown star Chris Hemsworth has a global fan base. Getty Images The Australian provenance of the whisky is central to how Edwards and Hemsworth intend to market Archie Rose overseas and justify its cost, which will sit above many high-volume Scotch blends.



“How it differentiates itself is through the raw materials that go into the whisky – our Australian barley, rye and wheat is second to none – and then the maturation climate,” says Edwards. Australian whisky isn’t governed by the same restrictive legislations as Scotch, for instance, leaving distillers more room to innovate. An example of this is Archie Rose’s Triple Smoked Single Malt Whisky, which uses native stringybark timber to smoke the malts giving the spirit a distinctly Australian smoke character, reminiscent of campfires and wood smoke. Archie Rose’s Smoked Cask Series. The hope, ultimately, is that this opens the door not just for Archie Rose, but for Australian whiskies, says Edwards. “I hope, but I’m pretty confident, that inevitably what’s going to happen is that the awareness of the category is going to grow and consumers will be curious and they will try all different types of Australian whisky.



“The bigger we can grow the category, the better for everyone.”

World.title: Environmental watchdog challenges giant data centre project over noise fears
World.content:
Victoria’s environmental watchdog has stepped in to object to a planned $1.1 billion data centre on the former Ford factory site in Campbellfield, warning of potential noise impacts and poor site layout. It is the first time the Environment Protection Authority (EPA) has objected to a data centre plan in the midst of the state’s controversial tech infrastructure boom. Campbellfield residents say they are concerned about noise, and water and power supply, at the proposed data centre. Chris Hopkins The EPA’s challenge is a potentially major blow to developer Zerra DC’s “Project Dune”, a proposal for six enormous data halls across 22 hectares of land on Barry Road. EPA executive director of strategy Erin Bowen said the authority had lodged a formal objection to the data centre proposal with the Department of Transport and Planning.



“In our role as a referral authority, EPA Victoria has objected to the proposal in its current form,” Bowen said in a statement. “Based on the information provided, we hold concerns over potential noise risks and the cumulative impacts associated with the overall site layout and development.” However, the ultimate decision on the project sits with Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny, after Zerra DC lodged its application under the state’s fast-tracked Development Facilitation Program. Under the program, the application has gone directly to Kilkenny, bypassing Hume Council and stripping residents of appeal rights at the state planning tribunal. The EPA intervention follows community anger over the Singaporean-backed project, which when built would consume 336 megawatts of electricity – double Melbourne’s current data centre power draw. The completed data centre would also store 7 million litres of diesel, and be within 250 metres of homes. The diesel fuel is for use in back-up generators if the power grid fails, as data centres need access to a constant power source.



About 50 people attended a rally opposing the Campbellfield project on Friday. Residents around Barry Road have tied pink ribbons on the front of their homes as part of a campaign against the development. Residents rallied at the site of the proposed data centre, where Ford’s Broadmeadows Assembly Plant once operated. Chris Hopkins John Rutherford, of the Broadmeadows Progress Association, attended the rally. He said it was outrageous that the council and residents were being sidelined on the project, which could have significant environmental and social impacts. “The data centre developers are going straight to the minister, bypassing the council,” Rutherford said. “It’s a very powerful lobby. The government is seeing the potential investment of developers into data centres as the overriding thing, rather than overall transparency and protection of communities as a whole.” Kilkenny has approved six data centres since 2025 through the fast-tracked Development Facilitation Program.



A Zerra DC spokesperson said the company was taking concerns raised by the EPA and residents seriously and was “in the process of preparing further acoustic information in response to the EPA’s objection”. “We welcome that feedback and are already working through each point,” the spokesperson said. Related Article Data centres 7 million litres of diesel just 250m from homes: The data centre plan locals didn’t know about Technical assessments submitted with Zerra DC’s application to Kilkenny revealed the site would house 294 massive rooftop chillers. Chillers are heavy-duty refrigeration units that cool liquid or air in a closed loop. In the Campbellfield project, they will keep thousands of computer servers the data centre will host from overheating.



Acoustic modelling by engineers Aurecon acknowledged these chillers would generate a continuous, low-frequency hum. The report stressed that this would be within acceptable range limits. Each chiller proposed for the later stages of the development – which are the stages closest to housing – would emit 80 decibels of sound, about the equivalent of a running petrol lawnmower. There would be 250 chiller units on the later data centre halls, stacked across five building roofs, creating a massive cumulative sound load that would rely on eight-metre screening walls to avoid breaching state environmental limits. While stage one of the data centre meets EPA noise limits, the report concedes that later stages built closer to homes adjacent to the site in Campbellfield would need the acoustic screening on the data centre’s roofs to control noise. The physical layout of the masterplan for the site shows the first stage is to be built 650 metres from homes. Later stages of the proposal are within 250 metres of homes, and 130 metres of a medical centre. Noise modelling diagrams submitted by Aurecon as part of the planning application also reveal the visual threat facing residents in the area. Detailed 3D diagrams map out the chillers to be installed on roofs of the six planned data halls, which will operate around the clock.



Campbellfield residents have tied pink ribbons on their homes as part of a campaign against the proposed data centre. Chris Hopkins To prevent the 294 chillers exceeding EPA nighttime noise limits at nearby bedroom windows, the developer’s acoustic consultants conceded there would need to be noise walls built on the roofs of each data centre hall, which are already two to three storeys high. Each noise wall will then add another seven to eight metres. While the facility will occupy an immense footprint – more than 10 times the size of the MCG’s playing surface – planning reports reveal it will yield minimal long-term employment. Stage one would require 49 employees to operate, growing to 255 on-site staff when all six stages are completed over a 12-year build, the reports said. Related Article Exclusive

Data centres The energy vampire next door: Life next to an AI mega-factory



The Ford Broadmeadows Assembly Plant employed almost 5200 people at its peak in the 1980s, mostly from migrant backgrounds and living in surrounding suburbs. It produced more than 600 cars a day. The factory closed in 2016. The local community had long held hopes the site could be used to generate significant employment, through advanced manufacturing, or as a higher education facility. There are concerns the data centre would dash these aspirations. Ford’s former chassis plant in Geelong has transformed into an advanced manufacturing hub with the help of significant federal and state support, while Victoria has committed $179 million to turn the former Holden site in Fishermans Bend into an “innovation precinct”. On Monday night, Melton Council, in the city’s outer west, joined Hume, Brimbank and Maribyrnong councils in calling on the state government to pause new data centre approvals until new regulatory standards are developed to manage their environmental and social impacts. The Victorian Greens have also called for a moratorium. A report by the Australian Energy Market Operator released on Tuesday showed that data centres would use 13 per cent of the network’s power supply by 2035, up from 3 per cent today.



There are 225 data centres in development around the country this year, compared with 97 in 2025, the report says. Premier Ben Carroll appointed MP Anthony Carbines to the newly created position of Minister for Artificial Intelligence and the Digital Economy in a reshuffle early this month. Carbines has said he would work to attract more data centre investment to the state, while acknowledging the growing community backlash against them. “It’s at the centre of our prosperity in the future, but we need to do that in a collaborative way with communities,” he said. Kilkenny’s office was contacted for comment. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Country music legend Dolly Parton dies aged 80
World.content:
Breaking CultureMusicVale Country music legend Dolly Parton dies aged 80 Michael Idato Updated August 26, 2026 — 5:43am ,first published 4:12am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dolly Parton, the singer-songwriter, literacy advocate and cultural icon whose wit, beauty and musicality shaped country music for more than six decades has died, aged 80. The country music legend’s nephew Bryan Seaver confirmed Parton’s passing on behalf of her family. Parton’s music was rich and tender, exploring her impoverished childhood in the Great Smoky Mountains of Tennessee, and the familiar country music touchstones of love, heartache and regret. They include songs like Jolene, I Will Always Love You and the theme her most successful film, 9 to 5. Dolly Parton, pictured in New York in 2022. AP Photo/Andres Kudacki “I have imagined the heaviness of this moment, but haven’t truly felt it until now,” Seaver said in a statement on behalf of the Parton family. “Dolly has lived in the light and is in the arms of Jesus, surely met by [her late husband] Carl, her parents, and countless others who have watched her and longed for her to meet them in the heavens.”



One of the acknowledged titans of country music, Parton has 11 Grammy Awards and three Emmy Awards, one Oscar (and two Oscar nominations), and nominations for six Golden Globe Awards, and a Tony award. She has a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame and was the recipient of the US National Medal of Arts and a Kennedy Centre Honour. Dolly Parton, Lily Tomlin, and Jane Fonda arrive for the premiere of their film “9 To 5” in New York on December 14, 1980. AP Photo/Richard Drew “Dolly opened doors not just for me, but for her entire family to reach the potential we didn’t even know was possible,” Seaver said. “Dolly also opened doors for generations of singers, songwriters, musicians, and dreamers from every walk of life and across every continent. By her example, we believe that anything was possible.” The legendary singer “never saw a door she couldn’t open, and the door she opened made and changed history,” Seaver said.



“My family and I have shared a lifetime of beautiful memories with Dolly, but so have you,” he said. “She has always been on your television, your record player, your CD, and on your phone playlist, becoming an extended part of your family, whether you liked it or not. Our family and the team she has entrusted with her legacy will work diligently to ensure her spirit will live with us forever.” US president Donald Trump acknowledged Parton’s legacy, saying: “This is a true loss for millions of people. There has never been anyone like her, and never will.” Trump said US flags would be lowered across the country on government buildings for a week. Singing legend Dionne Warwick was among the first to pay tribute to Parton. “Dolly, a true child of God, is in the best hands now,” Warwick said in a statement. “I will certainly miss her laugher, jokes and her being. Rest well and in total peace my friend.” Another country legend, Reba McEntire, thanked Parton “for all the wonderful things you did for us here on earth. Your love, your music and you gave so much with your huge, huge heart. There will never ever be another you”. Miley Cyrus described it as a “devastating day for humanity”. Dolly Parton on stage in 1976. Redferns



And producer/singer Seth McFarlane, who had worked with her, said Parton was “exactly the person we all hoped she was. Her kindness, generosity, and authenticity were evident from moment one, and the benign yet assured command she maintained over her empire was obvious from the genuine love and trust you could see from everyone who worked for her.” Dolly Parton with Lily Tomlin (left) and Jane Fonda (right) in 9 to 5. 20th Century Fox Dolly Rebecca Parton was born on January 19, 1946, in a one-room cabin on the banks of the Little Pigeon River in Pittman Centre, Tennessee. It would seem a world away from the life she would eventually lead, but it was world that Parton brought to life through her songs. Mournful ballads like My Tennessee Mountain Home, and Coat of Many Colours and In the Good Old Days (When Times Were Bad). No amount of money could buy from me / the memories that I have of then / No amount of money could pay me / To go back and live through it again, she sang. “In the good old days when times were bad.” Parton was the fourth of 12 children born to Avie Lee Caroline and Robert Lee Parton Sr. To her mother, Parton has always credited her musical prowess. And to her father, her business acumen. If true, she owed them both a great debt; in life her artistic and commercial success was almost without equal.



In 1973 and 1974, she would write and release two songs that would become her most successful: Jolene, about a woman confronted with the reality of the woman whose beauty (and fierce red hair) was powerful enough to steal the love of her life from her, and I Will Always Love You, about a farewell penned in the aftermath of a broken relationship. The latter of the two would become even more famous because it was recorded and released by other artists. Parton famously declined a request for Elvis Presley to record a cover, after his management asked for half the royalties on the song. And Whitney Houston’s release, from the soundtrack of her film The Bodyguard, would become a money-spinner for Parton. Houston was paid the performer royalty, but as the songwriter Parton took the lion’s share of the revenue. “She can have the credit, I’ll just take the cash,” Parton joked in 2018. Dolly Parton and Kenny Rogers rehearse a song for their appearance on the TV show “Live... And in Person” in Los Angeles on September 27, 1983. AP Photo/Doug Pizac The success of those songs was part of a mainstream crossover that, at the time, was bold. Country music very much lived in its channel and few if any artists could step between it and mainstream pop. But Parton’s conquest of the music charts would blaze a trail to that others could follow. That might be Parton’s greatest legacy: that she did, so others could follow. Dolly is the reason we have Garth Brooks, Shania Twain and Taylor Swift on the pop charts. She is why Post Malone and Beyoncé could walk the same path, but in reverse. And she is the reason we have genuinely evolutionary artists like Orville Peck.



In a tender footnote, Seaver said that in death Parton’s connection to the land was as potent as her father’s. “Dolly was a farmer, just like her daddy. He farmed the soil, she farmed songs and happiness,” he said. Seaver said Parton’s request was that she “rest in a beautiful bed of plush cotton because after a life wearing heavy rhinestones, she finally deserves to be comfortable and have some rest”. Parton’s husband of nearly 60 years, Carl Dean, passed away in March 2025. She is survived by six of her siblings, Willadeene, Bobby, Stella, Cassie, Freida and Rachel. World.title: Measles kills two unvaccinated people as US outbreak approaches 3000
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaVaccination Measles kills two unvaccinated people as US outbreak approaches 3000 Michael Koziol August 26, 2026 — 5:36am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Two unvaccinated people died with measles in the US state of Pennsylvania, becoming the first deaths there linked to the disease in 35 years, amid a growing national outbreak. Pennsylvania’s Department of Health announced the deaths on Tuesday (US time), and warned that the return of measles after a decades-long absence meant people did not grasp its severity. US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr announced an overhaul of federal guidelines on the childhood vaccine schedule this month. Bloomberg It comes as US President Donald Trump and his health secretary, Robert F. Kennedy Jr, continue to sow doubts about vaccines, including by pushing an unsubstantiated link with autism. This month, Trump signed an executive order that called for parents to space out their children’s vaccine visits and break up the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) jab - which is not currently possible.



Both deaths were in Lancaster County – an area of southern Pennsylvania with a large Amish population, which has historically had lower rates of vaccination. The department would not release further information about the deceased. So far in 2026, Pennsylvania has detected 393 cases of measles in 28 counties. Across the US, there have been 2777 confirmed cases this year, spanning most states and Washington DC. The measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is only available as a combined dose at present. AP Photo/Mary Conlon Tuesday’s announcement marked the first time people died from measles in Pennsylvania in 35 years. They are also the first US deaths from the disease this year. Last year, three Americans died, following nearly a decade of zero deaths. Pennsylvania’s health secretary, Debra Bogen, said the virtual elimination of measles in the state for more than three decades meant “people are not familiar with this disease and don’t fully understand the potential severity of the illness”.



The best way to protect against measles was vaccination, she said, with two doses of the MMR vaccine providing 97 per cent lifetime protection. The number of measles cases recorded this year has already eclipsed last year’s total of 2289. Nearly 50 per cent were among young people aged five to 19, and 94 per cent were among people who were unvaccinated or whose vaccination status was unknown, according to the Centres for Disease Control. Trump has issued an executive order to establish a “gold standard” vaccination schedule for children. Bloomberg The 2025 and 2026 figures are the highest measles numbers in decades, with only a 2019 outbreak (1274 cases) coming close. Earlier in August, Trump urged parents to break up the MMR vaccine into three separate shots, even though that is not currently enabled by the medical profession or the pharmaceutical industry.



In a subsequent briefing with reporters, US officials said they would work with the private sector to try to make separate doses available. Related Article Trump's White House Trump’s vaccine order adds more fuel to the anti-vaccine fire At a televised news conference in the Oval Office, Trump said the US was recommending too many vaccines. He claimed without evidence that the MMR vaccine could be “quite lethal”, but when given separately, “it looks like they are not at all lethal but just every effective”. The US president also falsely spoke of an “explosion” in vaccine injury, and claimed that doctors were injecting children with large doses that looked like “a bottle of soda poured into a little child’s body”. Trump’s executive order did not mention autism. But in his unscripted remarks, he asserted an unproven link between vaccination and higher rates of autism diagnoses in modern times.



“There’s a reason for such epidemic rates of autism, and we’re going to bring it back to much closer to where it was,” he said. The president’s order does not change vaccine requirements for schools, or impact the policies of state health departments. Rather, it stands as a recommendation from the US federal government. US Secretary of Health Robert F. Kennedy J has long been a vaccine sceptic. Bloomberg Following Trump’s announcement, the American Medical Association said that altering the proven childhood vaccination schedule without credible evidence risked weakening public confidence in vaccines, and putting children’s health at risk. “Extensive evidence from decades of scientific studies shows no link between vaccines and autism,” president Willie Underwood said. “Putting our children’s health at risk is not an option.”



When contacted for comment, the US Department of Health and Human Services pointed to a statement from the Centres for Disease Control which offered condolences following the two “measles-associated deaths”. “The MMR vaccine provides the most effective protection against measles and helps prevent its spread,” it said. “CDC will continue to follow Pennsylvania’s lead and provide resources to support the state’s response.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Ghislaine Maxwell loses bid to overturn conviction for aiding Epstein
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaEpstein fallout Ghislaine Maxwell loses bid to overturn conviction for aiding Epstein Michael R. Sisak and Larry Neumeister Updated August 26, 2026 — 5:23am ,first published 11:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: Ghislaine Maxwell’s bid to overturn her sex trafficking conviction and be freed from prison was rejected by a US federal judge on Tuesday (US time) who said the claims by Jeffrey Epstein’s former girlfriend and longtime associate that new evidence had emerged were “demonstrably meritless”. Maxwell filed a habeas petition – a legal procedure challenging her detention – last December seeking to set aside her conviction and free her from a 20-year prison sentence, claiming exonerating information was withheld and false testimony presented at her trial, resulting in a “complete miscarriage of justice”. Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell. Getty Judge Paul A. Engelmayer rejected her arguments, saying in his written ruling they “all or almost all are frivolous” and that she had presented nothing that could upend the outcome of her trial. “Nearly all its claims are procedurally barred; the overwhelming testimonial and documentary evidence adduced at trial conclusively established her guilt; and her petition’s claims are demonstrably meritless, and generally based on speculation, distortions, and/or outright falsehoods,” Engelmayer wrote.





The judge noted that many of Maxwell’s claims of “new evidence” stem from documents released under the Epstein Files Transparency Act. As a result of that law, the Justice Department over the last eight months has released 18 categories of investigative materials gathered in the massive sex trafficking probe, including search warrants, financial records, notes from interviews with victims and data from electronic devices. Related Article Investigation

Good Weekend Isolated, scared, forlorn: The heartbreaking final months of Virginia Giuffre’s life Engelmayer said that material is “largely irrelevant to the charges against Maxwell and does not support her claims of error.” “On the contrary, to the extent it is relevant, far from exculpating her, it incriminates her or reinforces the correctness of the legal rulings Maxwell challenges,” he wrote.



The judge also rejected Maxwell’s claim that she was selectively prosecuted and made a “scapegoat” when the Justice Department did not indict four co-conspirators named in a government document or 25 men who settled with victims. Engelmayer said she could have raised that claim on appeal after her trial, but he found it to be frivolous nonetheless. Among the recently released Justice Department documents, “she does not cite any that reveals the existence of an uncharged confederate, let alone one as instrumental as she in facilitating Epstein’s horrific crimes,” the judge said.
